34.text: If the names dataset is not already on disk, download it automatically so the tutorial is self-contained.

37.text: URL pointing to the raw names dataset hosted in Karpathy's GitHub repository.

40.text: Read the text file and split it into individual name strings. Each line becomes one training document.

41.text: Shuffle the names so the model encounters them in random order rather than memorizing alphabetical patterns.

44.text: Build the character-level vocabulary: 26 lowercase letters, each mapped to a unique integer ID.

45.text: The beginning-of-sequence token doubles as the end-of-sequence marker for name boundaries.

46.text: The real vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 letters plus the BOS/EOS marker. PAD is separate and never predicted.

47.text: PAD token for batch alignment. Sequences in a batch have different lengths, so shorter ones get padded to match the longest.

48.text: Expanded vocab includes PAD, the embedding table needs a row for it, even though it's never a real prediction target.

54.text: 4x larger embedding dimension than lab 03. Batching amortizes the overhead, so we can afford a bigger model.

55.text: Same 4 attention heads, but now each has 16 dimensions instead of 4.

56.text: 2 layers instead of 1, deeper model for richer representations.

57.text: Same 16-character context window as previous labs. Names longer than this get truncated.

58.text: Each head now has 16 dimensions (64 / 4), four times larger than in lab 03. More dimensions per head means richer attention patterns.

59.text: 32 sequences per training step, the model sees 32 names simultaneously and averages their gradients.

60.text: 1000 steps, same as previous labs. But each step processes 32x more data.

66.text: RMSNorm, identical to lab 03. The architecture doesn't change, just the scale.

71.text: Same x * rsqrt(mean(x^2) + eps) formula.

75.text: Attention module, now with a pad_mask parameter. This is the key addition for batching.

78.text: Same Q, K, V projections as lab 03.

79.text: Project the normalized input into key vectors that other positions will compare against.

80.text: Project the input into value vectors that carry content to be aggregated by attention weights.

83.text: Attention now accepts a padding mask, the model needs to know which positions are real vs. padding.

84.text: Unpack batch, time, channel dimensions.

85.text: Q projection and multi-head reshape.

86.text: Project into key vectors and reshape into separate attention heads. Keys let each position advertise its content for query matching.

87.text: Project into value vectors and reshape into heads. Values carry the content that attention weights will blend together.

89.text: Compute attention scores by taking the dot product of queries and keys, scaled by the square root of head dimension to prevent saturation.

91.text: Causal mask: same as lab 03, prevents attending to future positions.

92.text: Set future positions to negative infinity so the model cannot cheat by looking ahead.

105.text: The padding mask is here for shape rather than for effect. Padding is always appended and never interleaved, and the causal mask already stops a query at position t from seeing any key beyond t, so every key a real query can reach is a real token.

107.text: Fill PAD keys with -inf. The only logits this changes belong to pad queries, whose targets are -100 and dropped from the loss anyway; run a batch with and without it and the loss agrees to the last decimal. It stops being a no-op the moment you left-pad, switch to bidirectional attention, or pack several documents into one row, which is why the line stays.

108.text: Turn raw attention scores into a probability distribution so weights sum to one across keys.

111.text: Defensive, and in this configuration unreachable. Softmax over an all--inf row does return NaN, but no row here can be fully masked: row 0 always keeps position 0, which is BOS and never PAD.

113.text: Weighted value sum and reshape.

114.text: Project the concatenated multi-head attention output back into the embedding space.

117.text: MLP, identical to lab 03.

120.text: Widen the representation to 4x the embedding dimension for richer nonlinear transformations.

121.text: Compress the expanded hidden state back to the original embedding dimension.

123.text: Apply ReLU activation between two linear layers, forming the feed-forward sub-network.

124.text: The entire MLP compresses into a single chained expression in PyTorch.

127.text: Transformer block, now passes pad_mask through to attention.

130.text: Normalize the input before passing it to the attention sub-layer for stable training.

131.text: The attention sub-layer now receives the padding mask so it knows which positions hold real tokens versus filler.

132.text: Normalize the input before the MLP sub-layer, following the pre-norm transformer pattern.

133.text: The feed-forward network that processes each position independently after attention mixing.

135.text: Forward propagates the padding mask.

136.text: Attention is the only sub-layer that mixes information across positions, so it is the only one that could ever care about the mask. The MLP on the next line sees each position on its own.

137.text: The MLP operates one position at a time, so it needs no mask.

141.text: Complete model, embedding table is now larger to accommodate the PAD token.

144.text: padding_idx=PAD tells the embedding to output zeros for PAD tokens and exclude them from gradient updates. A clean way to handle variable-length sequences.

145.text: Position embeddings, same as lab 03.

146.text: Normalize embeddings before entering the transformer stack. This initial normalization keeps activations stable from the start.

147.text: Register all transformer layers so PyTorch can discover and optimize their parameters.

148.text: Output head maps to real vocab only (27 tokens, not 28). PAD is never a valid prediction.

149.text: Walk through every sub-module and apply N(0, 0.08) initialization, ensuring consistent starting conditions across all labs.

152.text: Re-zero the PAD row that _init_weights just overwrote. padding_idx keeps gradients away from this row, but it does not undo an initializer that has already written to it.

156.text: Only Linear and Embedding carry weights to initialize; RMSNorm here has none, so it is skipped.

157.text: N(0, 0.08) for all weights, the same initialization as every previous lab.

159.text: Forward pass accepts padding mask.

160.text: Unpack batch size B and sequence length T from the input shape. These dimensions drive all the downstream tensor operations.

161.text: Token embeddings, PAD tokens get zero vectors thanks to padding_idx.

162.text: Position embeddings broadcast across the batch.

163.text: Combine token and position embeddings and normalize before entering the transformer stack.

164.text: Pass the representation through each transformer layer in sequence. With two layers now, the model builds progressively richer representations.

165.text: The mask travels down to every layer's attention. Worth keeping in mind while reading it: the mask that actually shapes this lab's loss is ignore_index in the loss call, not this one.

166.text: Output logits over the real vocabulary.

172.text: Batch creation: the infrastructure needed for mini-batch training. This is where you see the engineering overhead of batching.

175.text: Gather batch_size documents, cycling through the dataset.

176.text: Select the document for this batch position.

181.text: Truncate to max context length.

184.text: Find the longest sequence in this batch, everything gets padded to this length.

185.text: Allocate lists that will hold the padded input tokens, shifted targets, and boolean masks for every sequence in the batch.

188.text: For each sequence, create aligned input, target, and mask.

189.text: Actual sequence length (minus 1 for the target shift).

190.text: Input: real tokens + PAD fill.

193.text: Targets: shifted tokens + -100 fill. PyTorch's cross_entropy ignores positions marked -100.

194.text: Boolean mask, False for real tokens and True for padding. It feeds attention, while the -100 targets on the line above are what genuinely keep padding out of the loss and the gradient.

199.text: Pack into tensors and return.

200.text: The input tensor of shape (B, max_T) containing token IDs, with PAD filling shorter sequences to the batch's maximum length.

201.text: The target tensor of shape (B, max_T) with shifted tokens as labels. Padded positions use -100 so cross-entropy ignores them.

202.text: A boolean mask of shape (B, max_T) marking which positions are real tokens (False) and which are padding (True).

209.text: Run training on CPU, which is sufficient for this small model and dataset size.

210.text: Create the model with the scaled-up architecture: 64-dim embeddings, 4 heads, and 2 transformer layers.

211.text: Parameter count, much larger than lab 03 due to bigger dimensions and 2 layers.

213.text: Same Adam optimizer configuration as all previous labs: lr=0.01, betas=(0.85, 0.99). Only the model size and batch size changed.

215.text: Iterate over training steps, processing a batch of 32 names at each step.

216.text: Assemble a padded batch of 32 tokenized names, aligning them to the same length with PAD tokens and building the corresponding masks.

217.text: Transfer input token IDs to the compute device. On CPU this is a no-op, but the pattern generalizes to GPU training.

218.text: Transfer target labels to the compute device, matching where the model's output tensors will live.

219.text: Transfer the padding mask to the same device so it can be applied directly to the attention score matrix.

221.text: Forward pass with padding mask, the model knows which positions to ignore.

222.text: ignore_index=-100 means the loss is only computed on real tokens, not padding. This is crucial, otherwise shorter sequences would be penalized differently than longer ones.

224.text: Clear accumulated gradients from the previous step before computing new ones.

225.text: Backward pass, autograd computes gradients for all parameters through the batched forward pass.

226.text: Linearly reduce the learning rate toward zero over the course of training.

227.text: Update learning rate for all parameter groups.

228.text: Write the decayed learning rate into the optimizer's parameter group.

229.text: Use the Adam optimizer to update all model weights based on the computed gradients.

231.text: Print the loss periodically so we can monitor whether the model is learning.

237.text: Temperature 0.5 makes generation more conservative: the model favors high-confidence predictions, producing more typical-sounding names.

239.text: Switch the model to evaluation mode, which disables training-specific behaviors like dropout.

240.text: No gradient tracking for inference.

241.text: Generate 20 brand-new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution.

242.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token as the initial prompt.

244.text: Feed generated sequence as a batch of 1. No padding needed for single-sequence inference.

245.text: Forward pass, no pad_mask needed for single sequences.

246.text: Grab the logits from the last generated position and divide by temperature. Lower temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top predictions.

247.text: Convert the temperature-scaled logits into a proper probability distribution that sums to one, ready for sampling.

248.text: Draw one token from the probability distribution to continue generating the name.

249.text: When the model outputs the BOS token during generation, it signals the name is complete and we stop adding characters.

251.text: Append the newly sampled token to the growing sequence so it becomes context for predicting the next character.

252.text: Map each token ID back to its character. Skip the leading BOS to get just the generated name text.

253.text: Display the completed generated name after all characters have been sampled.

units.title: JAX
units.tagline: Purely functional style. No classes, no hidden state, no mutation.
units.description:
JAX takes a radically different approach: everything is a pure function. No classes, no mutable state, no .backward() method.

Model parameters are plain dictionaries of arrays. The forward pass is a function that takes parameters and data, returns a loss. jax.grad transforms that function into one that returns gradients. jax.jit compiles it for speed. Random numbers require explicit keys that must be split, with no hidden global state.

This functional style makes it trivial to compose transformations: differentiate, vectorize, parallelize, compile, all by wrapping functions.
learning_objectives: Implement a transformer using pure functions without mutable state
Apply jax.grad and jax.jit to transform and compile functions
Compare functional and object-oriented ML programming paradigms

exercises.prompt: The loop separates first-time-shape steps from cached-shape steps and prints a mean for each, because @jit specialises train_step on input shapes and one name per step keeps producing new sequence lengths. Drop the @jit decorator and re-run: what happens to the two means, and what does the gap between them cost over 1000 steps?
exercises.hint: Without jit there is no tracing and no shape specialisation, so no step is ever the first of its shape. Compare the single uncompiled mean against the cached-shape mean from the jitted run, since that difference is what compilation buys. Then note how small the per-shape tracing penalty is next to it, and look at 06_jax_batched for the fix: pad to a fixed length and there is only one shape to trace.

exercises.prompt: Try reusing a random key instead of splitting it at each step. What goes wrong with the generated output and why?
exercises.hint: JAX random keys are deterministic. Reusing the same key means every random operation produces identical results, breaking sampling diversity.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: JAX edition.

Same decoder-only GPT architecture as the PyTorch version, based on
"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017),
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762, but expressed in JAX's purely functional
paradigm, with no classes, no mutation and explicit PRNG keys. The functional
approach reflects the style described in "Compiling machine learning programs
via high-level tracing" (Frostig et al., 2018),
https://mlsys.org/Conferences/doc/2018/146.pdf.

Key differences from the PyTorch version:
  - All parameters are explicit pytrees (no hidden state)
  - Forward pass is a pure function (no side effects)
  - Gradients via jax.value_and_grad (automatic, like PyTorch, but functional)
  - The whole training step (loss, gradients, Adam) is one jitted function
  - Explicit PRNG key threading, with modern typed keys (jax.random.key)

The training loop also reports where XLA compiles: jit specializes on input
shapes, and one name per step means a new sequence length every so often. The
corpus allows 14 lengths and a 1000-step run hits 12 of them, so the same
function is traced a dozen times, scattered through training. That is the JAX
gotcha this lab makes visible instead of hiding.
"""

import math
import os
import random
import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import jit, value_and_grad

random.seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parameters as a flat dict (pytree)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 16  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 1  # number of layers
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length
head_dim = n_embd // n_head  # dimension of each head

# jax.random.key is the modern typed-key constructor; jax.random.PRNGKey is the
# legacy uint32-pair form. Same algorithm, but a typed key carries its
# implementation in its dtype, which is what current JAX expects everywhere.
key = jax.random.key(42)


def init_param(key, shape, std=0.08):
    return jax.random.normal(key, shape) * std


# One key per parameter tensor: wte, wpe, lm_head, plus six per layer.
num_param_tensors = 3 + 6 * n_layer
keys = jax.random.split(key, num_param_tensors)
ki = iter(keys)

params = {
    "wte": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size, n_embd)),
    "wpe": init_param(next(ki), (block_size, n_embd)),
    "lm_head": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size, n_embd)),
}
for i in range(n_layer):
    params[f"l{i}.wq"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wk"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wv"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wo"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc1"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, 4 * n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc2"] = init_param(next(ki), (4 * n_embd, n_embd))

num_params = sum(p.size for p in jax.tree.leaves(params))
print(f"num params: {num_params}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pure-function forward pass
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def rmsnorm(x):
    ms = jnp.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return x / jnp.sqrt(ms + 1e-5)


def forward(params, input_ids):
    """
    params: dict of arrays
    input_ids: (n,) int array
    Returns: logits (n, vocab_size)
    """
    n = input_ids.shape[0]
    tok_emb = params["wte"][input_ids]  # (n, D)
    pos_emb = params["wpe"][jnp.arange(n)]  # (n, D)
    x = rmsnorm(tok_emb + pos_emb)

    for li in range(n_layer):
        x_res = x
        x_n = rmsnorm(x)

        Q = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wq"]  # (n, D)
        K = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wk"]
        V = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wv"]

        # Multi-head reshape: (n, nh, hd) -> (nh, n, hd)
        Q_h = Q.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        K_h = K.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        V_h = V.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)

        att = Q_h @ K_h.transpose(0, 2, 1) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        causal_mask = jnp.triu(jnp.ones((n, n)), k=1).astype(bool)
        att = jnp.where(causal_mask, -1e9, att)
        att = jax.nn.softmax(att, axis=-1)

        attn_out = att @ V_h  # (nh, n, hd)
        attn_cat = attn_out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, n_embd)
        x = attn_cat @ params[f"l{li}.wo"] + x_res

        # MLP
        x_res2 = x
        x_n2 = rmsnorm(x)
        h = x_n2 @ params[f"l{li}.fc1"]
        h = jax.nn.relu(h)
        x = h @ params[f"l{li}.fc2"] + x_res2

    logits = x @ params["lm_head"].T  # (n, V)
    return logits


def loss_fn(params, input_ids, targets):
    """Cross-entropy loss, pure function suitable for jax.value_and_grad."""
    logits = forward(params, input_ids)
    log_probs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1)
    n = input_ids.shape[0]
    loss = -jnp.mean(log_probs[jnp.arange(n), targets])
    return loss


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Adam optimizer (functional, with no hidden state mutation)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
learning_rate, beta1, beta2, eps_adam = 1e-2, 0.85, 0.99, 1e-8
m_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)
v_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One jitted training step: loss + gradients + Adam
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two things worth noticing here.
#
# 1. Use value_and_grad rather than grad. jax.grad alone returns only the gradients,
#    so printing the loss as well would mean running the forward pass twice. The
#    backward pass already computes the loss on its way through, so
#    value_and_grad hands it back for free.
#
# 2. The optimizer is expressed with jax.tree.map instead of a Python loop over
#    dict keys. Same arithmetic, but now the whole step (forward, backward and
#    update) is a single pure function that jit can compile as one XLA program,
#    instead of a compiled gradient call surrounded by interpreted Python.
@jit
def train_step(params, m_state, v_state, input_ids, targets, step, lr):
    loss, grads = value_and_grad(loss_fn)(params, input_ids, targets)
    new_m = jax.tree.map(lambda m, g: beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g, m_state, grads)
    new_v = jax.tree.map(lambda v, g: beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2, v_state, grads)
    bias1 = 1 - beta1 ** (step + 1)
    bias2 = 1 - beta2 ** (step + 1)
    new_params = jax.tree.map(
        lambda p, m, v: p - lr * (m / bias1) / (jnp.sqrt(v / bias2) + eps_adam),
        params,
        new_m,
        new_v,
    )
    return loss, new_params, new_m, new_v


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training loop
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
num_steps = 1000
seen_lengths = set()  # every new sequence length costs one XLA compilation
compile_ms, cached_ms = [], []

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)

    input_ids = jnp.array(tokens[:n])
    targets = jnp.array(tokens[1 : n + 1])

    is_new_shape = n not in seen_lengths
    seen_lengths.add(n)

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    loss_val, params, m_state, v_state = train_step(
        params, m_state, v_state, input_ids, targets, step, learning_rate * (1 - step / num_steps)
    )
    # JAX dispatch is asynchronous: without blocking, we would be timing the
    # enqueue and not the work.
    jax.block_until_ready((loss_val, params))
    dt = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    if is_new_shape:
        compile_ms.append(dt)
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} | new sequence length n={n:2d} -> XLA trace #{len(seen_lengths)} | {dt:7.1f} ms")
    else:
        cached_ms.append(dt)

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss_val:.4f} | {dt:6.2f} ms")

# The point of the two numbers below: jit is not "slow once, then fast". It is
# "slow once per input shape", and the shapes here keep arriving throughout
# training because names have 14 different lengths.
print(f"\ndistinct sequence lengths: {len(seen_lengths)} -> {len(compile_ms)} traces of the same train_step")
print(f"  first-time-shape steps: {sum(compile_ms) / len(compile_ms):8.1f} ms mean (compilation included)")
print(f"  cached-shape steps:     {sum(cached_ms) / len(cached_ms):8.2f} ms mean")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high
print("\n--- inference (new, hallucinated names) ---")
rng_key = jax.random.key(0)
for sample_idx in range(20):
    tokens = [BOS]
    for _ in range(block_size):
        input_ids = jnp.array(tokens)
        logits = forward(params, input_ids)
        logits = logits[-1] / temperature
        rng_key, subkey = jax.random.split(rng_key)
        token_id = jax.random.categorical(subkey, logits).item()
        if token_id == BOS:
            break
        tokens.append(token_id)
    name = "".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:])
    print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {name}")

26.text: The architecture is still the same transformer, but JAX changes the style of thinking completely: from objects with hidden state to pure functions and explicit parameter passing.

27.text: Keep the task fixed so the real contrast is PyTorch's imperative style versus JAX's functional one.

28.text: This split already foreshadows JAX's philosophy: even randomness becomes explicit data you pass around instead of ambient framework state.

31.text: JAX is the same model seen through a different lens: no modules with internal state, just functions that transform inputs, parameters, and RNG keys.

32.text: The surface syntax looks NumPy-like, which is deceptive in a good way: beneath it sits a much more explicit functional execution model.

35.text: Keep the data order fixed so the conceptual jump to functional programming does not get muddied by run-to-run noise.

40.text: Dataset path, shared across labs.

41.text: Download the names dataset from the internet if it is not already present locally.

44.text: URL pointing to the raw names dataset hosted in Karpathy's repository.

47.text: Read the text file and split it into individual name strings, one per line.

48.text: Randomize the training order so the model does not memorize sequences of names.

51.text: The set of unique characters in the dataset forms our vocabulary. Each character gets a fixed integer ID for the model to work with.

52.text: The beginning-of-sequence token doubles as the end-of-sequence marker for name boundaries.

53.text: The vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 lowercase letters plus the BOS/EOS marker.

60.text: Split attention into 4 parallel heads so each can focus on different character relationships.

61.text: A single transformer layer, keeping the model minimal for this small-scale experiment.

62.text: Names up to 16 characters long fit in the context window. Longer names get truncated, but most fit easily.

63.text: Each of the 4 heads gets 4 dimensions of the 16-dimensional embedding, letting heads specialize on different character relationships.

68.text: JAX has no global random state: you create a key and split it for every random operation. jax.random.key is the modern typed constructor, where the key carries its generator implementation in its dtype; PRNGKey is the older raw uint32 pair. Same numbers, but a lab about explicit randomness may as well use the API JAX actually wants.

71.text: Parameter initializer, same N(0, 0.08) distribution, but using JAX's RNG.

72.text: JAX random requires an explicit key for every call. This makes randomness reproducible and parallelizable.

76.text: Derive the key count from the model rather than hard-coding it. Add a layer and the iterator below would otherwise run dry halfway through initialization.

77.text: Pre-split one key per parameter tensor. JAX forces you to say where every random number comes from, which is exactly what makes an initialization reproducible across devices.

78.text: Iterator over keys, each parameter gets its own unique key.

80.text: Parameters are a plain Python dict, no nn.Module, no parameter registration. In JAX, parameters are just data you pass to functions.

81.text: Initialize the token embedding table that maps each character to a learned vector.

82.text: Position embeddings give the model a sense of order. Each slot in the sequence has its own learned vector encoding 'where' a token sits.

83.text: The output head weight matrix that maps from embedding space back to vocabulary logits for next-token prediction.

85.text: Per-layer weights, same structure as previous labs, just stored in a dict.

86.text: Weight matrix that projects the normalized input into query vectors for attention.

87.text: Weight matrix that produces key vectors for positions to be matched against queries.

88.text: Weight matrix that produces value vectors carrying content to be mixed by attention.

89.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output back into the embedding space.

90.text: First MLP weight matrix that expands the representation to 4x the embedding dimension.

91.text: Second MLP weight matrix that compresses back to the original embedding dimension.

93.text: jax.tree.leaves extracts all arrays from the nested dict. JAX treats dicts as "pytrees", a core abstraction for working with nested parameter structures.

100.text: RMSNorm as a bare function, no class, no state. JAX style: functions in, functions out.

101.text: Mean of squares, same math as every other lab.

102.text: Divide by the root mean square to normalize. This keeps all vectors at roughly unit scale, preventing activations from growing or shrinking as they flow through layers.

105.text: The forward pass is a pure function: the same inputs always produce the same outputs, with no side effects. That is what lets jax.grad and jax.jit work, since they transform mathematical functions rather than stateful objects.

"""
microGPT: JAX edition.

Same decoder-only GPT architecture as the PyTorch version, based on
"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017),
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762, but expressed in JAX's purely functional
paradigm, with no classes, no mutation and explicit PRNG keys. The functional
approach reflects the style described in "Compiling machine learning programs
via high-level tracing" (Frostig et al., 2018),
https://mlsys.org/Conferences/doc/2018/146.pdf.

Key differences from the PyTorch version:
  - All parameters are explicit pytrees (no hidden state)
  - Forward pass is a pure function (no side effects)
  - Gradients via jax.value_and_grad (automatic, like PyTorch, but functional)
  - The whole training step (loss, gradients, Adam) is one jitted function
  - Explicit PRNG key threading, with modern typed keys (jax.random.key)

The training loop also reports where XLA compiles: jit specializes on input
shapes, and one name per step means a new sequence length every so often. The
corpus allows 14 lengths and a 1000-step run hits 12 of them, so the same
function is traced a dozen times, scattered through training. That is the JAX
gotcha this lab makes visible instead of hiding.
"""

import math
import os
import random
import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import jit, value_and_grad

random.seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parameters as a flat dict (pytree)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 16  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 1  # number of layers
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length
head_dim = n_embd // n_head  # dimension of each head

# jax.random.key is the modern typed-key constructor; jax.random.PRNGKey is the
# legacy uint32-pair form. Same algorithm, but a typed key carries its
# implementation in its dtype, which is what current JAX expects everywhere.
key = jax.random.key(42)


def init_param(key, shape, std=0.08):
    return jax.random.normal(key, shape) * std


# One key per parameter tensor: wte, wpe, lm_head, plus six per layer.
num_param_tensors = 3 + 6 * n_layer
keys = jax.random.split(key, num_param_tensors)
ki = iter(keys)

params = {
    "wte": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size, n_embd)),
    "wpe": init_param(next(ki), (block_size, n_embd)),
    "lm_head": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size, n_embd)),
}
for i in range(n_layer):
    params[f"l{i}.wq"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wk"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wv"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wo"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc1"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, 4 * n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc2"] = init_param(next(ki), (4 * n_embd, n_embd))

num_params = sum(p.size for p in jax.tree.leaves(params))
print(f"num params: {num_params}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Pure-function forward pass
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def rmsnorm(x):
    ms = jnp.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return x / jnp.sqrt(ms + 1e-5)


def forward(params, input_ids):
    """
    params: dict of arrays
    input_ids: (n,) int array
    Returns: logits (n, vocab_size)
    """
    n = input_ids.shape[0]
    tok_emb = params["wte"][input_ids]  # (n, D)
    pos_emb = params["wpe"][jnp.arange(n)]  # (n, D)
    x = rmsnorm(tok_emb + pos_emb)

    for li in range(n_layer):
        x_res = x
        x_n = rmsnorm(x)

        Q = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wq"]  # (n, D)
        K = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wk"]
        V = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wv"]

        # Multi-head reshape: (n, nh, hd) -> (nh, n, hd)
        Q_h = Q.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        K_h = K.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        V_h = V.reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)

        att = Q_h @ K_h.transpose(0, 2, 1) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        causal_mask = jnp.triu(jnp.ones((n, n)), k=1).astype(bool)
        att = jnp.where(causal_mask, -1e9, att)
        att = jax.nn.softmax(att, axis=-1)

        attn_out = att @ V_h  # (nh, n, hd)
        attn_cat = attn_out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, n_embd)
        x = attn_cat @ params[f"l{li}.wo"] + x_res

        # MLP
        x_res2 = x
        x_n2 = rmsnorm(x)
        h = x_n2 @ params[f"l{li}.fc1"]
        h = jax.nn.relu(h)
        x = h @ params[f"l{li}.fc2"] + x_res2

    logits = x @ params["lm_head"].T  # (n, V)
    return logits


def loss_fn(params, input_ids, targets):
    """Cross-entropy loss, pure function suitable for jax.value_and_grad."""
    logits = forward(params, input_ids)
    log_probs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1)
    n = input_ids.shape[0]
    loss = -jnp.mean(log_probs[jnp.arange(n), targets])
    return loss


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Adam optimizer (functional, with no hidden state mutation)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
learning_rate, beta1, beta2, eps_adam = 1e-2, 0.85, 0.99, 1e-8
m_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)
v_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# One jitted training step: loss + gradients + Adam
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Two things worth noticing here.
#
# 1. Use value_and_grad rather than grad. jax.grad alone returns only the gradients,
#    so printing the loss as well would mean running the forward pass twice. The
#    backward pass already computes the loss on its way through, so
#    value_and_grad hands it back for free.
#
# 2. The optimizer is expressed with jax.tree.map instead of a Python loop over
#    dict keys. Same arithmetic, but now the whole step (forward, backward and
#    update) is a single pure function that jit can compile as one XLA program,
#    instead of a compiled gradient call surrounded by interpreted Python.
@jit
def train_step(params, m_state, v_state, input_ids, targets, step, lr):
    loss, grads = value_and_grad(loss_fn)(params, input_ids, targets)
    new_m = jax.tree.map(lambda m, g: beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g, m_state, grads)
    new_v = jax.tree.map(lambda v, g: beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2, v_state, grads)
    bias1 = 1 - beta1 ** (step + 1)
    bias2 = 1 - beta2 ** (step + 1)
    new_params = jax.tree.map(
        lambda p, m, v: p - lr * (m / bias1) / (jnp.sqrt(v / bias2) + eps_adam),
        params,
        new_m,
        new_v,
    )
    return loss, new_params, new_m, new_v


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training loop
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
num_steps = 1000
seen_lengths = set()  # every new sequence length costs one XLA compilation
compile_ms, cached_ms = [], []

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)

    input_ids = jnp.array(tokens[:n])
    targets = jnp.array(tokens[1 : n + 1])

    is_new_shape = n not in seen_lengths
    seen_lengths.add(n)

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    loss_val, params, m_state, v_state = train_step(
        params, m_state, v_state, input_ids, targets, step, learning_rate * (1 - step / num_steps)
    )
    # JAX dispatch is asynchronous: without blocking, we would be timing the
    # enqueue and not the work.
    jax.block_until_ready((loss_val, params))
    dt = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000

    if is_new_shape:
        compile_ms.append(dt)
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} | new sequence length n={n:2d} -> XLA trace #{len(seen_lengths)} | {dt:7.1f} ms")
    else:
        cached_ms.append(dt)

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss_val:.4f} | {dt:6.2f} ms")

# The point of the two numbers below: jit is not "slow once, then fast". It is
# "slow once per input shape", and the shapes here keep arriving throughout
# training because names have 14 different lengths.
print(f"\ndistinct sequence lengths: {len(seen_lengths)} -> {len(compile_ms)} traces of the same train_step")
print(f"  first-time-shape steps: {sum(compile_ms) / len(compile_ms):8.1f} ms mean (compilation included)")
print(f"  cached-shape steps:     {sum(cached_ms) / len(cached_ms):8.2f} ms mean")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high
print("\n--- inference (new, hallucinated names) ---")
rng_key = jax.random.key(0)
for sample_idx in range(20):
    tokens = [BOS]
    for _ in range(block_size):
        input_ids = jnp.array(tokens)
        logits = forward(params, input_ids)
        logits = logits[-1] / temperature
        rng_key, subkey = jax.random.split(rng_key)
        token_id = jax.random.categorical(subkey, logits).item()
        if token_id == BOS:
            break
        tokens.append(token_id)
    name = "".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:])
    print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {name}")

Using it instead of grad matters because the backward pass already computes the loss on its way through, so grad alone would cost a second forward pass just to have a number to print.

183.text: First moment update. What was a Python for k in params loop in lab 02 is now one jax.tree.map: same arithmetic per leaf, but expressed as a single traced operation that stops caring how many parameter tensors there are.

184.text: Second moment: the moving average of squared gradients, which is what gives Adam its per-parameter step size.

185.text: Bias correction for the first moment, which starts at zero and would otherwise drag the early steps toward nothing.

186.text: The same correction for the second moment. Both are scalars here, computed once and broadcast over every leaf below.

188.text: The parameter update itself. Nothing is mutated: the lambda returns fresh arrays and the old ones simply stop being referenced.

193.text: Hand back the complete new state, loss included. The caller rebinds params, m_state and v_state on the next line, which is what "functional optimizer" reduces to in practice.

199.text: Train for 1000 steps, one document per step. Each iteration: forward, loss, grad, Adam update.

200.text: The instrument for this lab's real lesson. jit specializes on input shapes, and one name per step means the sequence length keeps changing, so this set records how many distinct programs XLA has been asked to build.

201.text: Two buckets: steps that paid for a compilation and steps that got a cache hit. Keeping them apart is what turns "jit is slow the first time" into a measurement.

203.text: Iterate over training steps, processing one name per step to update model parameters.

204.text: Cycle through the dataset with modular indexing. After seeing all names, we loop back for another pass.

205.text: Convert the name into a sequence of integer token IDs with BOS markers at both ends.

206.text: Clip to the maximum context window. Most names fit easily, but this guard prevents overflow on unusually long entries.

208.text: Convert the Python token list to a JAX array so it can flow through the JIT-compiled forward pass.

209.text: Wrap the target tokens as a JAX array. These are the correct next characters the model should learn to predict.

211.text: Ask the question before adding to the set, so the step can be attributed to the right bucket. A first-time shape and a cached shape run the identical Python.

214.text: Time the step from here, not from the top of the loop: tokenizing a name in Python would otherwise be mixed into a number meant to be about XLA.

215.text: One call does the forward pass, the backward pass and the Adam update. Compare lab 03, where those are three separate lines and three separate dispatches.

216.text: The linearly decayed learning rate is passed in as an argument rather than closed over. A Python float baked into the trace would be a compile-time constant, and a new value every step would mean a new compilation every step.

220.text: JAX dispatch is asynchronous: the call above returns as soon as the work is queued. Without blocking here we would be timing the enqueue, and every step would look impossibly fast.

221.text: Elapsed milliseconds for the step. On a first-time shape this includes tracing and compiling train_step; on a repeat it is only the compiled program running.

223.text: Announce the compilations as they happen. They are not confined to the start of training: this run traced new shapes at step 1, again at step 156, again at step 481.

225.text: One line per trace, with the length that triggered it. The corpus allows 14 lengths and a 1000-step run reaches 12 of them, so the same function gets built a dozen times, scattered throughout training rather than bunched at the front.

227.text: Everything else is a cache hit, and cache hits are where the compiled program finally pays for itself.

229.text: Print the loss periodically so we can monitor whether the model is learning.

235.text: The count that makes the gotcha concrete: twelve traces of one function, because the input shape kept changing under it.

236.text: Steps that had to compile, averaged. Roughly three orders of magnitude slower than the rest, which is why an unnoticed shape change in a JAX pipeline shows up as a mysterious stall rather than a gentle slowdown.

237.text: Steps that reused a compiled program, averaged, and the reason people love jit. The fix for the gap between these two numbers is to make shapes static by padding to one fixed length, which is exactly what lab 06 does.

242.text: Temperature 0.5 makes generation more conservative: the model favors high-confidence predictions, producing more typical-sounding names.

244.text: Sampling needs randomness too, so inference gets its own key to thread through the loop. Nothing is ambient in JAX, not even at generation time.

245.text: Generate 20 brand-new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution.

246.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token as the initial prompt.

247.text: Generate one character at a time, up to the maximum sequence length. Each step feeds all generated tokens back through the model.

248.text: Convert growing token list to JAX array.

249.text: Forward pass, the same pure function, just called without gradient tracking.

250.text: Grab the logits for the last generated position and divide by temperature. Lower values make the distribution sharper and more predictable.

251.text: jax.random.split produces two new keys from one, JAX's way of consuming randomness without hidden state. Every random call needs a unique key.

252.text: categorical samples from log-probabilities (unnormalized logits). JAX's equivalent of PyTorch's multinomial.

253.text: When the model outputs the BOS token during generation, it signals the name is complete and we stop adding characters.

255.text: Append the newly sampled token to the growing list so it becomes part of the context for predicting the next character.

256.text: Map each token ID back to its character, skipping the leading BOS, to assemble the generated name as a readable string.

257.text: Print the finished name. The model assembled it from the 1000 names it saw during training, one per step, out of the 32K in the corpus.

units.title: JAX Batched
units.tagline: Use jax.vmap to automatically vectorize single-example code across a batch.
units.description:
jax.vmap is JAX's killer feature for batching: write code for a single example, and vmap automatically vectorizes it across a batch dimension.

Instead of manually reshaping tensors and adding batch dimensions everywhere (like in PyTorch batched), you write the clean single-example version and let the compiler figure out the batching. The result is identical to hand-batched code but with zero manual effort.

This lab shows the same padding and masking as PyTorch batched, but the core model code stays single-example clean.
learning_objectives: Apply jax.vmap to auto-vectorize single-example code across batches
Compare manual batching (PyTorch) with automatic vectorization (JAX)
Explain how function transformations compose in JAX

exercises.prompt: Replace jax.vmap with a manual Python loop over the batch dimension. Does the output change? How does the speed compare?
exercises.hint: Write a for loop that calls the single-example function for each item in the batch. Use jnp.stack to combine results. Compare timing with and without vmap.

exercises.prompt: Stack jax.vmap and jax.jit in different orders: jit(vmap(f)) vs. vmap(jit(f)). Is there a performance difference?
exercises.hint: Wrap the loss function both ways and time 100 training steps each. Check if JAX produces the same XLA computation graph for both.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: JAX batched edition.

Same architecture as 05_jax, but with mini-batch training via jax.vmap:
  - Write the forward pass for a single example
  - vmap automatically vectorizes it across a batch
  - Padding at the data level, but the model code stays single-example
  - Scaled-up model (2 layers, 64-dim embeddings, context 16)
  - Batches of 32, 1000 training steps

This is JAX's signature trick: "write for one, run for many."

It also fixes the problem 05_jax leaves you with. There, the sequence length
changed from step to step, so the jitted step recompiled a dozen times. Here
every batch is padded to the *static* block_size, so the shape never changes
and XLA compiles exactly once. The training loop counts both, so you can see
the recompilations disappear rather than take it on faith.

Reference: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017),
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
"""

import math
import os
import random
import time

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax import jit, value_and_grad, vmap

random.seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
PAD = vocab_size
vocab_size_with_pad = vocab_size + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size} (+1 pad = {vocab_size_with_pad})")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Hyperparameters (scaled up)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 64  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 2  # number of layers
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length
head_dim = n_embd // n_head  # dimension of each head
batch_size = 32
num_steps = 1000

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parameters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
key = jax.random.key(42)  # typed key, the modern jax.random API


def init_param(key, shape, std=0.08):
    return jax.random.normal(key, shape) * std


# One key per parameter tensor: wte, wpe, lm_head, plus six per layer.
num_param_tensors = 3 + 6 * n_layer
keys = jax.random.split(key, num_param_tensors)
ki = iter(keys)

params = {
    "wte": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size_with_pad, n_embd)),
}
# Zero the PAD embedding row so padding tokens contribute nothing
params["wte"] = params["wte"].at[PAD].set(jnp.zeros(n_embd))
params.update(
    {
        "wpe": init_param(next(ki), (block_size, n_embd)),
        "lm_head": init_param(next(ki), (vocab_size, n_embd)),
    }
)
for i in range(n_layer):
    params[f"l{i}.wq"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wk"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wv"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.wo"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc1"] = init_param(next(ki), (n_embd, 4 * n_embd))
    params[f"l{i}.fc2"] = init_param(next(ki), (4 * n_embd, n_embd))

num_params = sum(p.size for p in jax.tree.leaves(params))
print(f"num params: {num_params}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Forward pass (single example; vmap will handle the batch)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def rmsnorm(x):
    ms = jnp.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return x / jnp.sqrt(ms + 1e-5)


def forward_single(params, input_ids, pad_mask):
    """
    Forward pass for one sequence.
    input_ids: (T,) int array
    pad_mask: (T,) bool array, True where padded
    Returns: logits (T, vocab_size)
    """
    T = input_ids.shape[0]
    tok_emb = params["wte"][input_ids]  # (T, D)
    pos_emb = params["wpe"][jnp.arange(T)]  # (T, D)
    x = rmsnorm(tok_emb + pos_emb)

    for li in range(n_layer):
        x_res = x
        x_n = rmsnorm(x)

        Q = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wq"]
        K = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wk"]
        V = x_n @ params[f"l{li}.wv"]

        Q_h = Q.reshape(T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        K_h = K.reshape(T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)
        V_h = V.reshape(T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2)

        att = Q_h @ K_h.transpose(0, 2, 1) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        # Causal mask
        causal = jnp.triu(jnp.ones((T, T)), k=1).astype(bool)
        att = jnp.where(causal, -1e9, att)
        # Padding mask: block attention to PAD keys.
        #
        # Padding is always appended at the end of a sequence, never interleaved
        # with real tokens, and the causal mask already stops position t from
        # looking past t. So every key a real query can reach is a real token,
        # and this line only changes logits at pad *query* positions, which
        # target_mask then multiplies by zero. It is redundant here, and kept
        # because it stops being redundant with left-padding, bidirectional
        # attention, or several documents packed into one row.
        att = jnp.where(pad_mask[None, None, :], -1e9, att)
        # No nan_to_num guard needed: masking with -1e9 rather than -inf means
        # even a hypothetical fully masked row softmaxes to a uniform
        # distribution, not NaN. No row can be fully masked anyway, since row 0
        # always keeps position 0, which is BOS.
        att = jax.nn.softmax(att, axis=-1)

        attn_out = att @ V_h
        attn_cat = attn_out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(T, n_embd)
        x = attn_cat @ params[f"l{li}.wo"] + x_res

        # MLP
        x_res2 = x
        x_n2 = rmsnorm(x)
        h = x_n2 @ params[f"l{li}.fc1"]
        h = jax.nn.relu(h)
        x = h @ params[f"l{li}.fc2"] + x_res2

    logits = x @ params["lm_head"].T  # (T, V)
    return logits


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# vmap: the JAX way to batch
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# forward_single works on one sequence. vmap lifts it to work on a batch.
# in_axes=(None, 0, 0) means: shared params, batched input_ids, batched pad_mask.
forward_batch = vmap(forward_single, in_axes=(None, 0, 0))


def loss_fn(params, input_ids, targets, pad_mask, target_mask):
    """
    Batched cross-entropy loss.
    input_ids: (B, T), targets: (B, T), pad_mask: (B, T), target_mask: (B, T)
    """
    logits = forward_batch(params, input_ids, pad_mask)  # (B, T, V)
    log_probs = jax.nn.log_softmax(logits, axis=-1)
    B, T, V = log_probs.shape
    # Gather log-probs for target tokens
    target_log_probs = log_probs[jnp.arange(B)[:, None], jnp.arange(T)[None, :], targets]  # (B, T)
    # Mask out padding positions
    target_log_probs = target_log_probs * target_mask
    loss = -jnp.sum(target_log_probs) / jnp.sum(target_mask)
    return loss


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Adam optimizer (functional)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
learning_rate, beta1, beta2, eps_adam = 1e-2, 0.85, 0.99, 1e-8
m_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)
v_state = jax.tree.map(jnp.zeros_like, params)


# One jitted function for the whole step: loss, gradients and Adam together.
# value_and_grad gives the loss and the gradients from a single backward pass,
# and jax.tree.map applies the Adam arithmetic to every leaf of the parameter
# pytree without a Python loop.
@jit
def train_step(params, m_state, v_state, batch, step, lr):
    input_ids, targets, pad_mask, target_mask = batch
    loss, grads = value_and_grad(loss_fn)(params, input_ids, targets, pad_mask, target_mask)
    new_m = jax.tree.map(lambda m, g: beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g, m_state, grads)
    new_v = jax.tree.map(lambda v, g: beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2, v_state, grads)
    bias1 = 1 - beta1 ** (step + 1)
    bias2 = 1 - beta2 ** (step + 1)
    new_params = jax.tree.map(
        lambda p, m, v: p - lr * (m / bias1) / (jnp.sqrt(v / bias2) + eps_adam),
        params,
        new_m,
        new_v,
    )
    return loss, new_params, new_m, new_v


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Batching utility
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def make_batch(docs, step, batch_size):
    """
    Create a batch of token sequences, padded to the static block_size.

    Padding to block_size instead of to the longest sequence in the batch is the
    whole point. The obvious version pads to `max(len(s) for s in sequences)`,
    which changes from batch to batch, and every new value is a new input shape,
    and every new input shape makes jit trace and compile the step again. Padding
    to a constant means one compilation for the entire run.

    The price is arithmetic on padding: a batch whose longest name is 5
    characters still runs the full 16 columns. Static shapes are usually worth
    that, which is why real training pipelines bucket or pad to fixed lengths.

    Returns the batch plus the max_len that dynamic padding *would* have used,
    so the training loop can count the compilations this avoids.
    """
    batch_docs = [docs[(step * batch_size + i) % len(docs)] for i in range(batch_size)]
    sequences = []
    for doc in batch_docs:
        toks = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        # Safety bound, never hit by this corpus: the longest name is 15 chars,
        # so BOS + name + EOS is at most block_size + 1 tokens.
        toks = toks[: block_size + 1]
        sequences.append(toks)

    dynamic_len = max(len(s) for s in sequences) - 1  # what a max_len-padded batch would be
    T = block_size  # static, identical for every batch
    input_ids, target_ids, pad_masks, target_masks = [], [], [], []
    for s in sequences:
        n = len(s) - 1  # real input tokens; padding is appended after these
        inp = s[:n] + [PAD] * (T - n)
        tgt = s[1 : n + 1] + [0] * (T - n)  # 0 as dummy target for masked positions
        pmask = [False] * n + [True] * (T - n)
        tmask = [1.0] * n + [0.0] * (T - n)
        input_ids.append(inp)
        target_ids.append(tgt)
        pad_masks.append(pmask)
        target_masks.append(tmask)

    batch = (
        jnp.array(input_ids),
        jnp.array(target_ids),
        jnp.array(pad_masks),
        jnp.array(target_masks),
    )
    return batch, dynamic_len


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training loop
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
static_shapes = set()  # input shapes actually fed to train_step
dynamic_shapes = set()  # shapes a max_len-padded loop would have produced
step_ms = []

for step in range(num_steps):
    batch, dynamic_len = make_batch(docs, step, batch_size)
    dynamic_shapes.add((batch_size, dynamic_len))

    is_new_shape = batch[0].shape not in static_shapes
    static_shapes.add(batch[0].shape)

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    loss_val, params, m_state, v_state = train_step(
        params, m_state, v_state, batch, step, learning_rate * (1 - step / num_steps)
    )
    # JAX dispatch is asynchronous, so block before reading the clock.
    jax.block_until_ready((loss_val, params))
    step_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)

    if is_new_shape:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} | new input shape {batch[0].shape} -> XLA trace #{len(static_shapes)}")

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss_val:.4f} | {step_ms[-1]:7.2f} ms")

# The measurement that justifies padding to block_size. Every distinct shape
# costs one trace + compile of train_step (seconds); every repeat is free.
print(f"\ncompilations of train_step: {len(static_shapes)} (padding to the static block_size)")
print(f"  in-batch max_len values seen: {len(dynamic_shapes)} -> that many compilations if we padded dynamically")
print(f"  first step: {step_ms[0]:.1f} ms (trace + compile)")
print(f"  steps 2..{num_steps}: {sum(step_ms[1:]) / (num_steps - 1):.2f} ms mean, max {max(step_ms[1:]):.2f} ms")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference (single-example, no vmap needed)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high
print("\n--- inference (new, hallucinated names) ---")
rng_key = jax.random.key(0)
for sample_idx in range(20):
    tokens = [BOS]
    for _ in range(block_size):
        input_ids = jnp.array(tokens)
        pad_mask = jnp.zeros(len(tokens), dtype=bool)
        logits = forward_single(params, input_ids, pad_mask)
        logits = logits[-1] / temperature
        rng_key, subkey = jax.random.split(rng_key)
        token_id = jax.random.categorical(subkey, logits).item()
        if token_id == BOS:
            break
        tokens.append(token_id)
    name = "".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:])
    print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {name}")

23.text: This lab keeps the functional JAX style but adds the big batching idea: write the logic once for a single example, then lift it across a batch with transformation rather than manual rewiring.

24.text: Same corpus, so the teaching point is batching by transformation, not a new task.

25.text: The data pipeline stays ordinary. The interesting part is how little the model code has to change once vmap enters the picture.

28.text: Same JAX foundation as the previous lab, but now the focus shifts from explicit functional modeling to automatic vectorization.

29.text: The array API stays familiar while the execution story grows more powerful under the surface.

32.text: Fix the outer randomness so the benefit of vmap is visible as a code-structure improvement rather than as a different experiment.

37.text: Path to the shared dataset file used consistently across all labs.

38.text: Download the names dataset from the internet if it is not already present locally.

41.text: URL pointing to the raw names dataset hosted in Karpathy's repository.

44.text: Read the text file and split it into individual name strings, one per line.

45.text: Randomize the training order so the model does not memorize sequences of names.

48.text: The set of unique characters across all names forms our vocabulary. Each character gets a fixed integer ID.

49.text: The beginning-of-sequence token doubles as the end-of-sequence marker for name boundaries.

50.text: The real vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 letters plus the BOS/EOS marker. PAD is tracked separately.

51.text: PAD token for aligning variable-length sequences in a batch.

52.text: The embedding table needs 28 rows: 27 real tokens plus one for PAD. But the output head only predicts over the 27 real tokens.

58.text: 4x larger embeddings, same scale-up as lab 04.

60.text: Two transformer layers give the model more depth to build progressively richer representations of character patterns.

61.text: Names up to 16 characters fit in the context window. Longer names get truncated, but most fit easily.

62.text: Each attention head operates on 16 dimensions, giving finer-grained representations than lab 05.

63.text: 32 sequences processed in parallel per training step. Batching amortizes overhead and gives the optimizer a smoother gradient signal.

64.text: Train for 1000 steps, same as all previous labs. But each step now processes 32 names at once, so the model sees 32x more data overall.

69.text: One explicit key to seed everything. jax.random.key is the typed constructor current JAX expects; the older PRNGKey hands back a raw pair of uint32 instead.

72.text: Same initializer as lab 05.

77.text: Derive the number of keys from the model instead of hard-coding it, so adding a layer cannot silently exhaust the iterator below.

78.text: Pre-split one key per parameter tensor. JAX requires every random draw to name its source, which is what makes this initialization reproducible.

79.text: Iterate through the pre-split random keys, giving each parameter its own unique source of randomness.

81.text: Parameters dict, pytree structure.

82.text: The embedding table gets a row for PAD, so vocab_size_with_pad here and plain vocab_size for the output head. PAD needs a lookup; it is never a legal prediction.

85.text: Zero the PAD row after initialization. JAX arrays are immutable, so .at[i].set(...) returns a new array rather than writing in place, which is the functional counterpart of lab 04's with torch.no_grad() block.

86.text: Resume filling the parameter dict. It is split into two statements only because wte has to exist before its PAD row can be zeroed on the line above.

88.text: Position embeddings give the model a sense of order. Each position in the sequence has its own learned vector.

89.text: Output head, maps to real vocab only (27 tokens, no PAD).

92.text: Per-layer weight matrices, 2 layers now.

93.text: Weight matrix that projects the input into query vectors for the attention mechanism.

94.text: Weight matrix that produces key vectors for positions to be matched against queries.

95.text: Weight matrix that produces value vectors carrying content to be mixed by attention.

96.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output back into the embedding space.

97.text: First MLP weight matrix that expands the representation to 4x the embedding dimension for richer nonlinear transformations.

98.text: Second MLP weight matrix that compresses back to the original embedding dimension.

100.text: Sum up all array sizes in the parameter tree to report the total trainable parameter count.

107.text: RMSNorm, same function as lab 05.

108.text: Compute the mean of squared values along the last axis for RMS normalization.

109.text: Divide by the root-mean-square to normalize the input, keeping direction but stabilizing scale.

112.text: Forward pass for a single sequence. This is the key insight: you write the simplest possible code for one example and let vmap handle batching. Compare lab 04, where the entire forward pass was rewritten for (B, T, C) shapes.

119.text: Sequence length from the single example.

120.text: Token embeddings, single sequence, no batch dimension.

121.text: Position embeddings tell the model where each token sits. Without these, the model could not distinguish token order.

122.text: Combine token and position embeddings and normalize before entering the transformer.

124.text: Iterate through each transformer layer. With two layers now, the model builds progressively richer representations.

125.text: Save the current hidden state for the residual connection after attention.

126.text: Normalize the input before passing it to the attention sub-layer for stable training.

128.text: Q projection, operates on (T, D), not (B, T, D). No batch handling needed in the model code.

129.text: Project the normalized input into key vectors that other positions will query against.

130.text: Project the normalized input into value vectors carrying content to aggregate.

132.text: Multi-head reshape, for a single sequence.

133.text: Reshape keys into separate attention heads, matching the same multi-head pattern as queries.

134.text: Reshape values into separate attention heads for parallel processing across heads.

136.text: Compute scaled dot-product attention scores between all query-key pairs.

138.text: Build an upper-triangular boolean mask that blocks attention to future positions.

139.text: Set future positions to a large negative value so softmax gives them zero weight.

149.text: Blocking attention to PAD keys, and worth being honest: in this configuration it does nothing. Padding is appended, never interleaved, and the causal mask already stops position t from looking past t, so every key a real query can reach is real. The line only touches pad query rows, which target_mask later multiplies by zero. It becomes load-bearing with left-padding, bidirectional attention, or several documents packed into one row.

154.text: Softmax over the masked scores. There is no NaN guard here and none is needed: masking with -1e9 rather than -inf means even a hypothetical fully masked row would come out uniform instead of NaN, and no row can be fully masked anyway, since row 0 always keeps position 0, which is BOS.

156.text: Multiply attention weights by value vectors to produce the attention sub-layer output.

157.text: Transpose attention heads back and concatenate them into the full embedding dimension.

158.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output and add the residual connection in one expression. This completes the attention sub-layer.

161.text: Save the hidden state before the MLP for the second residual connection in this block.

162.text: Normalize before the feed-forward network, following the pre-norm transformer pattern.

163.text: Multiply by the expansion weights to widen the representation for richer transformations.

164.text: Apply ReLU activation to introduce nonlinearity between the two MLP linear layers.

165.text: Contract the MLP back to embedding dimension and add the residual. This completes the second sub-layer of the transformer block.

167.text: Final logits over the real vocabulary.

176.text: The line that does the batching. vmap(forward_single, in_axes=(None, 0, 0)) derives a batched version automatically, where None means params are shared rather than batched and 0 means batch along the first axis for inputs and masks. This one line replaces all of lab 04's manual batch reshaping.

179.text: Batched loss function. The forward pass is already batched thanks to vmap.

184.text: Call the vmap'd forward, returns (B, T, V) logits from (B, T) inputs.

185.text: Log-softmax is more numerically stable than computing softmax then taking the log separately, avoiding potential underflow issues.

186.text: Unpack batch, time, vocab dimensions.

188.text: Gather log-probs for target tokens using advanced indexing. Fancy indexing: for each batch and position, grab the log-prob of the correct target.

190.text: Zero out padding positions so they don't affect the loss.

191.text: Average only over real (non-padded) tokens. Dividing by sum(target_mask) ensures short sequences aren't penalized relative to long ones.

198.text: Same Adam hyperparameters as every other lab: lr=0.01, betas=(0.85, 0.99). Consistency makes it easy to compare across frameworks.

199.text: First moment state, zeros matching param shapes.

200.text: Second moment state tracks the magnitude of recent gradients per parameter, enabling Adam's adaptive learning rate behavior.

208.text: The whole step as one pure function: state in, state out. It is functionally identical to lab 05's train_step, which is the point, since vmap changed the model and left the training machinery alone.

209.text: Unpack the four arrays inside the jitted function. Passing the batch as one tuple keeps the call site short and lets jit treat the whole thing as a single pytree argument.

210.text: One call for the loss and every gradient. value_and_grad rather than grad because the backward pass computes the loss on its way through, so asking for both costs nothing extra, and it differentiates straight through the vmap.

211.text: First moment update via jax.tree.map, which replaces the for k in params loop earlier labs used. Same arithmetic per leaf, but now it lives inside the compiled program instead of between compiled calls.

212.text: Second moment: the moving average of squared gradients that gives Adam its per-parameter step size.

213.text: Bias correction for the first moment, which starts at zero and would otherwise hold the early steps back.

214.text: The same correction for the second moment. Both are scalars, computed once and broadcast across every leaf.

216.text: The update itself, mapped over three trees at once. Nothing is mutated; fresh arrays come out and the old ones stop being referenced.

221.text: Return the complete new state alongside the loss. The caller rebinds all four names, which is the whole of "functional optimizer" in practice.

227.text: Batch construction, and the one place this lab genuinely departs from lab 04: it pads to the static block_size rather than to whatever the longest sequence in this particular batch happens to be.

244.text: Gather batch_size documents from the dataset, cycling through with modular indexing to cover the full training set.

246.text: Convert each document's characters into integer token IDs that the model can process.

247.text: Wrap each name with beginning-of-sequence tokens to mark the start and end boundaries.

250.text: Truncate to the maximum context length. Most names are short enough, but this guard prevents overflow.

253.text: This records what dynamic padding would have chosen without padding anything, so the loop below can count the compilations this lab avoids.

254.text: The decision that makes the whole run compile once. A constant width means a constant input shape, and a constant input shape means jit traces train_step exactly one time.

255.text: For each sequence, create aligned input tokens, target tokens, padding masks, and target masks, all padded to the same length.

257.text: The actual number of real tokens in this sequence (before padding). Used to know where real data ends and padding begins.

258.text: Real tokens, then PAD out to the fixed width. A batch of five-character names still runs all 16 columns; wasted arithmetic is the price of a static shape, and it is usually the right trade.

259.text: Targets shifted by one, with 0 as a dummy filler. 0 is a real character, so it is target_mask below and not this array that keeps padding out of the loss.

260.text: The attention padding mask, True where padded. Redundant under right-padding plus causal masking, kept because the code shape is what you meet in real training scripts.

261.text: The mask that actually does the work: 1.0 on real positions, 0.0 on padding, multiplied into the per-token loss so padded positions contribute neither loss nor gradient.

267.text: Pack the four lists into JAX arrays, each of shape (B, block_size), the same shape on every single step of the run.

268.text: Input token IDs, real tokens followed by PAD.

269.text: Target tokens, shifted by one, with dummy values at padded positions that the target mask will zero out.

270.text: The boolean mask handed to attention to mark padded positions.

271.text: The float mask that weights the loss, so padded positions contribute zero to the gradient.

273.text: Return the batch plus the length dynamic padding would have used. The second value is purely instrumentation for the counter below.

279.text: Record the shapes actually fed to train_step. Because of the static padding above there will only ever be one.

280.text: And the shapes the obvious implementation would have produced, so the comparison is measured rather than argued.

281.text: Per-step wall-clock times, which is what makes the single compilation visible: one very slow step and then a flat line.

283.text: Iterate over training steps, processing a batch of 32 names per step.

284.text: Build the batch and collect the length dynamic padding would have used for it.

285.text: Book the counterfactual shape. Nine distinct in-batch maximum lengths turn up over the run, which is nine compilations avoided.

287.text: Ask whether this shape is new before recording it. The answer is only ever yes on the first step.

290.text: Start the clock. Step 1 will carry the trace-and-compile cost; nothing after it will.

291.text: One compiled program: forward pass over the batch, gradients, and the Adam update.

292.text: The decayed learning rate arrives as an argument, not as a captured Python float. A constant baked into the trace would change every step, and every change would be a fresh compilation.

295.text: JAX dispatch is asynchronous, so block before reading the clock. Otherwise the timing measures how fast work can be queued.

296.text: Store the step time. Comparing element 0 with the mean of the rest is the whole experiment.

298.text: This fires exactly once, at step 1. In lab 05 the same print fired twelve times, scattered through training.

301.text: Print the loss periodically so we can monitor whether the model is learning.

306.text: The payoff line: one compilation of train_step for the entire run, because the input shape never moved.

307.text: And the counterfactual: nine different in-batch maximum lengths, so padding to the longest sequence per batch would have meant nine traces of the same function. Lab 08 does exactly that, and prints the same nine.

308.text: The first step, carrying trace and compile. It costs seconds rather than milliseconds, a real price that is paid only once.

309.text: Every other step, with the maximum alongside the mean so a hidden recompilation could not hide inside an average.

314.text: Temperature 0.5 makes generation more conservative: the model favors high-confidence predictions, producing more typical-sounding names.

316.text: Generation needs randomness too, so inference threads its own key. Nothing is ambient in JAX, not even at sampling time.

317.text: Generate 20 brand-new names by sampling from the model's learned distribution.

318.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token as the initial prompt.

319.text: Generate one character at a time, up to the maximum sequence length. Each step feeds all generated tokens through the model.

320.text: Convert tokens to JAX array.

321.text: No padding during single-sequence inference, all False mask.

322.text: Use forward_single directly, no need for vmap when generating one sequence at a time.

323.text: Grab the logits for the last generated position and divide by temperature. Lower temperature makes the distribution sharper.

324.text: Split PRNG key for this sampling step.

325.text: Draw one token from the probability distribution to continue generating the name.

326.text: When the model predicts BOS, it signals the name is complete, so we stop generating.

328.text: Append the newly sampled token to the growing sequence for the next forward pass.

329.text: Map each token ID back to its character, skipping the leading BOS, to produce the generated name as a readable string.

330.text: Print the finished name. These names were invented by the model from statistical patterns it learned during training.
