units.title: KV Cache
units.tagline: The single most important inference optimization.
units.description:
During autoregressive generation, each new token attends to all previous tokens, so without caching every step recomputes K and V for the entire sequence. Two different quantities get called "the complexity of decoding" and they have different exponents. Over a T-token generation the attention scores go from O(T³) uncached to O(T²) cached; the projections and MLP go from O(T²) to O(T). Every cubic-to-quadratic claim in this lab, including the operation counter it prints, is about the attention term, the one that dominates at long context.

The KV cache stores previously computed key and value tensors and appends new ones incrementally. Each generation step only computes K and V for the new token, then concatenates with the cache. This reduces per-step work from O(n) to O(1) for the projection, though attention itself is still O(n).

Every production LLM serving system uses KV caching. It's the difference between seconds and minutes for long sequences.
learning_objectives: Implement incremental KV caching for autoregressive generation
Analyze the attention-score reduction from O(T^3) to O(T^2), and why projections and MLP go from O(T^2) to O(T)
Explain why KV caching is the most important inference optimization

exercises.prompt: Disable the KV cache and time generation both ways. The wall-clock ratio at name length will disappoint, so work out why before you look at the answer, then read the lab's per-step attention benchmark at T = 64, 256, 1024, 2048 to see where the speedup actually shows up.
exercises.hint: At T around 50 the projections, the MLP and the fixed per-call overhead dominate, and none of them shrink, so the stopwatch is measuring overhead rather than attention. The measured per-step ratio does grow with T, but it stays well short of the theoretical T for the same reason. That gap is why the operation counter, not the stopwatch, is this lab's headline.

exercises.prompt: Print the shape of the cached key and value tensors at each generation step. Verify they grow by exactly one position per step.
exercises.hint: After each step, print cache_k.shape and cache_v.shape. The sequence dimension should increment by 1 each time.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: KV Cache edition.

Same model as lab 03, but with a KV-cache-aware inference path that avoids
recomputing Key and Value tensors for already-processed positions. This is
THE fundamental optimization behind every fast LLM serving system.

Be precise about which cost is being counted, because two different quantities
get called "the complexity of decoding" and they have different exponents. Over
a T-token generation:

  attention scores    naive O(T^3)   cached O(T^2)
  projections + MLP   naive O(T^2)   cached O(T)

Every "cubic to quadratic" claim in this lab, including the operation counter it
prints, is about the attention term, the one that dominates at long context and
the only one the cache changes asymptotically.

KV caching is a standard inference optimization for autoregressive transformers,
implicit in the original "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017),
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 decoder design. The technique became essential
at scale as documented in "Efficient Transformers: A Survey" (Tay et al., 2022),
https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06732. This lab implements the basic form: cache K and
V tensors from previous positions, compute only the new position's Q/K/V, and
concatenate with the cache. Every production serving system (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM,
etc.) uses this as its foundation.
"""

import math
import os
import random
import time
from itertools import pairwise

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model config
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 16  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 1  # number of layers
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length
head_dim = n_embd // n_head  # dimension of each head

# ===========================================================================
# Unified model, supporting both standard and KV-cached inference
# ===========================================================================
# One model with two inference paths. When kv_cache=None, attention behaves like
# standard causal attention (same as lab 03). When kv_cache is provided,
# only the new positions compute Q/K/V and cached K/V are prepended.


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Attention with optional KV cache for efficient autoregressive decoding."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, kv_cache=None):
        B, T_new, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T_new, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T_new, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T_new, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

        if kv_cache is not None:
            cached_k, cached_v = kv_cache
            k = torch.cat([cached_k, k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([cached_v, v], dim=2)

        new_cache = (k, v)
        T_total = k.shape[2]

        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        # Causal mask: row i (absolute pos T_total-T_new+i) attends to cols 0..abs_pos
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T_new, T_total, device=x.device, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=T_total - T_new + 1)
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)

        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T_new, C)
        return self.wo(out), new_cache


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x, kv_cache=None):
        attn_out, new_cache = self.attn(self.norm1(x), kv_cache=kv_cache)
        x = x + attn_out
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x, new_cache


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx, past_caches=None, start_pos=0):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(start_pos, start_pos + T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        new_caches = []
        for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers):
            cache_i = past_caches[i] if past_caches is not None else None
            x, new_cache = layer(x, kv_cache=cache_i)
            new_caches.append(new_cache)
        return self.lm_head(x), new_caches


# ===========================================================================
# Training (identical to lab 03, ignoring caches during training)
# ===========================================================================
device = "cpu"
model = MicroGPT().to(device)
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 1000

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)

    input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device)
    targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)

    logits, _ = model(input_ids)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()

    if (step + 1) % 200 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ===========================================================================
# Inference comparison: naive (no cache) vs KV cache
# ===========================================================================
# Same model, same weights, two generation strategies.
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high
num_samples = 20
model.eval()


def sample_token(logits):
    probs = F.softmax(logits[0, -1] / temperature, dim=-1)
    return torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()


def generate_naive(num_samples=20):
    """Standard generation: re-run full sequence at every step. O(T^3) attention work."""
    total_attn_ops = 0
    total_steps = 0
    names = []
    for sample_idx in range(num_samples):
        torch.manual_seed(1000 + sample_idx)
        tokens = [BOS]
        for _ in range(block_size):
            idx = torch.tensor([tokens[-block_size:]], device=device)
            T = idx.shape[1]
            total_attn_ops += T * T * n_head
            total_steps += 1
            logits, _ = model(idx)  # no cache, so this recomputes everything
            token_id = sample_token(logits)
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        names.append("".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:]))
    return names, total_attn_ops, total_steps


def generate_with_cache(num_samples=20):
    """KV-cache generation: only process new token each step. O(T^2) attention work."""
    total_attn_ops = 0
    names = []
    for sample_idx in range(num_samples):
        torch.manual_seed(1000 + sample_idx)
        tokens = [BOS]
        past_caches = None
        for _ in range(block_size):
            if past_caches is None:
                idx = torch.tensor([tokens], device=device)
                T_new, start_pos = len(tokens), 0
            else:
                idx = torch.tensor([[tokens[-1]]], device=device)
                T_new, start_pos = 1, len(tokens) - 1
            total_attn_ops += T_new * len(tokens) * n_head
            logits, past_caches = model(idx, past_caches=past_caches, start_pos=start_pos)
            token_id = sample_token(logits)
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        names.append("".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:]))
    return names, total_attn_ops


print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("INFERENCE COMPARISON: Naive vs KV Cache")
print("=" * 60)

with torch.no_grad():
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    names_naive, ops_naive, steps_naive = generate_naive(num_samples)
    t_naive = time.perf_counter() - t0

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    names_cached, ops_cached = generate_with_cache(num_samples)
    t_cached = time.perf_counter() - t0

# Verify identical outputs
print("\n--- Generated names (both methods produce identical output) ---")
all_match = all(n1 == n2 for n1, n2 in zip(names_naive, names_cached))
for i, (n1, n2) in enumerate(zip(names_naive, names_cached)):
    match = "OK" if n1 == n2 else "MISMATCH!"
    print(f"  {i + 1:2d}: {n1:12s}  |  {n2:12s}  [{match}]")
print(f"\nAll outputs identical: {all_match}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The headline number: attention operations counted, not timed
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# This is a count of work actually performed, so it is exact and it is what the
# optimization is about. Wall clock comes later, with caveats.
print("\n--- Attention operation counts (Q*K multiply-adds, counted exactly) ---")
print(f"  Naive (full recompute):  {ops_naive:,} ops")
print(f"  KV cache (incremental):  {ops_cached:,} ops")
print(f"  Reduction:               {ops_naive / ops_cached:.1f}x fewer attention operations")

# Reconcile that measured reduction with the closed form, because they differ
# and the reason is worth one line: the formula is evaluated at T = block_size,
# but generation stops at BOS long before position 16.
T = block_size
avg_steps = steps_naive / num_samples
print("\n--- Reconciling with the closed form ---")
print(f"  For a full sequence of length T = {T}:")
print(f"  Naive total attention:   sum(t^2 for t=1..T) = T(T+1)(2T+1)/6 = {T * (T + 1) * (2 * T + 1) // 6} (per head)")
print(f"  Cached total attention:  sum(t   for t=1..T) = T(T+1)/2       = {T * (T + 1) // 2} (per head)")
print(f"  Ratio:                   (2T+1)/3 = {(2 * T + 1) / 3:.1f}x")
print(f"\n  The measured reduction is {ops_naive / ops_cached:.1f}x, not {(2 * T + 1) / 3:.1f}x, and nothing is wrong.")
print(f"  These names average {avg_steps:.1f} decode steps, not {T}: generation stops on BOS.")
print(
    f"  Evaluate the same formula at T = {avg_steps:.1f} and you get {(2 * avg_steps + 1) / 3:.1f}x. The saving grows"
)
print("  with sequence length, so a toy corpus of six-letter names sees the small end of it.")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Wall clock, end to end, and why it says the opposite
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("\n--- Wall-clock time, whole generation loop ---")
print(f"  Naive:    {t_naive * 1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"  KV cache: {t_cached * 1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"  Ratio:    {t_naive / t_cached:.2f}x  <- naive time / cached time, not a speedup figure")
print("\n  Do not read that ratio as the value of the KV cache. It is a measurement of")
print("  Python. One layer, 16 dimensions, six-token names: each forward pass is a few")
print("  dozen microseconds of tensor arithmetic wrapped in a few hundred microseconds of")
print("  interpreter and dispatch overhead. Both paths make the same NUMBER of forward")
print("  calls, so both pay that overhead the same number of times, and the arithmetic the")
print("  cache eliminates is too small to rise above the noise. Re-run this file and the")
print("  ratio moves; it has been seen below 1.00x on a loaded machine. That is a statement")
print("  about the benchmark, not about the optimization. The section below fixes the")
print("  benchmark instead of explaining away the number.")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Where the speedup actually lives: one decode step, at real context lengths
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# To see the effect, measure the thing the cache changes and nothing else: a
# single decode step, at a context length a serving system would actually reach.
# A fresh attention module on random activations is enough, since timing depends on
# tensor shapes, not on trained weights.
#
#   naive  = recompute Q,K,V for the whole prefix, run a T x T attention
#   cached = compute Q,K,V for one position, run a 1 x T attention
#
# Theory says the attention term shrinks by a factor of T. Reality falls short
# of that, and the gap is instructive.
#
# A microbenchmark is only worth printing if its numbers are stable, so this one
# is defended twice. Inside a timing run, take the minimum of many repetitions:
# anything else sharing the CPU can only ever make a call slower, so the mean
# measures the machine's mood while the minimum measures the code. Across runs,
# take the median, so one throttled run cannot set the reported number.
#
# The repetition count is not a fixed number, because no fixed number serves both
# ends of this table: a cached call is microseconds, where hundreds of reps cost
# nothing and five reps measure mostly noise, while a naive call at T = 2048 can
# take a large fraction of a second all by itself. So each run repeats until a
# time budget is spent, with a floor and a ceiling, and prints how many reps it
# actually got. A cell that lands on the floor did so because one call already
# costs more than the whole budget: fine when that call is tens of milliseconds,
# a reason to distrust the number when it is microseconds.
BENCH_ROUNDS = 5  # independent timing runs per cell; the median of these is reported
BENCH_BUDGET = 0.1  # seconds of repetitions inside one run
BENCH_MIN_REPS = 5  # never fewer, however slow the call
BENCH_MAX_REPS = 500  # never more, however fast the call


def best_of(module, x, kv_cache):
    """Fastest call to module(x, kv_cache=kv_cache), in seconds, and the rep count."""
    best, reps = float("inf"), 0
    deadline = time.perf_counter() + BENCH_BUDGET
    while reps < BENCH_MIN_REPS or (reps < BENCH_MAX_REPS and time.perf_counter() < deadline):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        module(x, kv_cache=kv_cache)
        best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - t0)
        reps += 1
    return best, reps


def bench_step(module, x, kv_cache):
    """Median over BENCH_ROUNDS runs of best_of, plus the total reps behind it."""
    module(x, kv_cache=kv_cache)  # warm up: first call pays allocator and cache misses
    runs = sorted(best_of(module, x, kv_cache) for _ in range(BENCH_ROUNDS))
    return runs[len(runs) // 2][0], sum(reps for _, reps in runs)


print("\n--- One decode step, attention module only, synthetic input ---")
print(f"  median of {BENCH_ROUNDS} runs, each the fastest of as many reps as fit in {BENCH_BUDGET:.2f}s")
print(f"  (floor {BENCH_MIN_REPS}, ceiling {BENCH_MAX_REPS} per run), after one warm-up call")
print(f"  {'T':>6} {'naive':>11} {'cached':>11} {'measured':>10} {'theory':>8} {'reps n/c':>12}")
bench_attn = CausalSelfAttention().eval()
rows = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for T_bench in (64, 256, 1024, 2048):
        x_full = torch.randn(1, T_bench, n_embd)
        x_one = torch.randn(1, 1, n_embd)
        bench_cache = (
            torch.randn(1, n_head, T_bench - 1, head_dim),
            torch.randn(1, n_head, T_bench - 1, head_dim),
        )
        t_step_naive, reps_naive = bench_step(bench_attn, x_full, None)
        t_step_cached, reps_cached = bench_step(bench_attn, x_one, bench_cache)
        rows.append((T_bench, t_step_naive, t_step_cached))
        print(
            f"  {T_bench:>6} {t_step_naive * 1e6:>9.1f}us {t_step_cached * 1e6:>9.1f}us "
            f"{t_step_naive / t_step_cached:>9.1f}x {T_bench:>7}x "
            f"{f'{reps_naive}/{reps_cached}':>11}"
        )
print("""
  The speedup grows with T, because naive attention is T x T against the cache's
  1 x T. It stays well short of the theoretical T because the projections and the
  fixed per-call overhead do not shrink at all, and at T = 64 that overhead still
  swamps everything, which is precisely what the 20-name wall clock above was
  measuring. This is the whole reason the operation counter, not the stopwatch, is
  this lab's headline.""")

# Both columns time work that grows with T, so both must grow with T. Check that
# rather than assert it: if this machine is too busy for the trend to survive,
# say so here instead of leaving the reader to trust an impossible table.
noisy = [name for name, col in (("naive", 1), ("cached", 2)) if not all(b[col] > a[col] for a, b in pairwise(rows))]
if noisy:
    print(f"""
  NOTE: on this run the {" and ".join(noisy)} column did not increase monotonically
  with T, which cannot be true of work that grows with T. Read that as contention
  on this machine, not as a property of the code, since something else had the CPU
  during the fast rows. Re-run on an idle machine, or raise BENCH_ROUNDS and
  BENCH_BUDGET above, before drawing any conclusion from the table.""")
else:
    print("  (Both timing columns increase monotonically with T on this run, as they must.)")

# ===========================================================================
# Summary
# ===========================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 60)
print("WHY KV CACHE MATTERS")
print("=" * 60)
print("""
  Cache stores K,V from previous positions. Each new token computes only its
  own Q,K,V and attends to all cached K,V, with no recomputation.

                  Without cache         With cache
  Step 1:         1 x 1  attention      1 x 1  attention
  Step 2:         2 x 2  attention      1 x 2  attention
  Step 3:         3 x 3  attention      1 x 3  attention
  ...
  Step T:         T x T  attention      1 x T  attention
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Total:          ~T^3/3 operations     ~T^2/2 operations

  At 2048 context the ratio (2T+1)/3 is 1366x FEWER ATTENTION OPERATIONS. That
  is not a 1366x speedup and the distinction matters: the projections, the MLP,
  and the memory traffic reading the cache back do not shrink by that factor,
  and past a few thousand tokens decode is memory-bound rather than compute-
  bound. The end-to-end win is large, large enough that no serving system ships
  without it, but it is smaller than the operation count, and it is bounded by
  whatever does not get cheaper.

  A 7B model (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128, fp16) needs 512 KB of cache per
  token, so ~1 GB for a 2048-token request. Prerequisite for speculative
  decoding, PagedAttention, and disaggregated serving.
""")

29.text: This lab is about wasted inference work, so even the imports hint at the story: same model, but now we can time the naive path against the cached one.

30.text: Same dataset, same task. That keeps the focus on the inference optimization rather than on model or data changes.

31.text: Randomness is only supporting cast here; the real experiment is how much repeated computation we can eliminate during generation.

32.text: Timing matters in this lab because the KV cache is the optimization that makes autoregressive decoding practical.

35.text: PyTorch gives us the same baseline model as before. The important difference is that attention can now remember yesterday's K and V instead of recomputing them.

36.text: Nothing dramatic changes in the layer stack. That is the point: the speedup comes from preserving history, not from inventing a new model.

37.text: Softmax and loss stay ordinary. What changes is how much of the prefix attention has to rebuild at each decoding step.

39.text: Benchmarks only mean something if the runs are comparable, so we lock the stochastic pieces down before measuring.

40.text: Set the PyTorch random seed for reproducible weight initialization and sampling.

45.text: Construct a portable file path to the shared dataset, relative to this script's location, so the code works regardless of where you clone the repo.

46.text: If the dataset file is missing, we download it automatically. This keeps the script self-contained with no manual setup required.

52.text: Read all names from the dataset file, one per line, stripping whitespace.

53.text: Randomize the training order so the model does not memorize sequences of names.

56.text: Gather every unique character from all names and sort them to build a deterministic character-to-integer vocabulary mapping.

57.text: Use the length of the character set as the beginning-of-sequence token ID.

58.text: The full vocabulary has 27 tokens: 26 lowercase letters plus the BOS marker.

64.text: Same tiny model config as lab 03, the model is identical, only inference changes.

65.text: Four parallel attention heads, each processing a different 4-dimensional slice.

66.text: A single transformer layer keeps the comparison focused on the caching optimization.

67.text: The longest sequence the model can process at once. Names are short, so 16 tokens is more than enough for this dataset.

68.text: Each attention head operates on a 4-dimensional slice of the 16-dimensional embedding.

78.text: RMSNorm, same as previous labs.

84.text: Divide by the root-mean-square of the activation vector. Simpler than LayerNorm since it skips mean subtraction, but equally effective for stabilizing training.

87.text: The critical change: attention now accepts an optional KV cache. Same weights, two inference paths.

90.text: Constructor is unchanged from lab 03.

92.text: Q, K, V, and output projections, identical to the uncached version.

93.text: Linear projection that transforms embeddings into key vectors for attention.

94.text: Linear projection that transforms embeddings into value vectors for attention.

95.text: Project the concatenated multi-head output back to the model dimension.

97.text: Forward now takes an optional kv_cache, this is the entire innovation of this lab.

98.text: T_new is 1 during cached inference (just the new token) vs. full sequence length without cache.

99.text: Project queries for the new positions only. During cached inference, this is a single token.

100.text: Project keys for the new positions only.

101.text: Project values for the new positions only.

103.text: If we have a cache from previous steps, prepend it.

104.text: Unpack the cached K and V tensors from previous positions.

105.text: This is the crucial reuse step: old keys stay alive, and only the new key is appended. The history grows without being recomputed.

106.text: Values follow the same pattern as keys, completing the cached prefix. The new token now sees the full past through reused K/V rather than rebuilt K/V.

108.text: Save the updated cache for the next step, it grows by one position each time.

109.text: T_total = total sequence length including cached positions.

111.text: Attention: Q is (B, heads, T_new, hd), K is (B, heads, T_total, hd). The result is (B, heads, T_new, T_total).

113.text: Build the causal mask with torch.triu: each new query at absolute position T_total-T_new+i can attend to all positions up to and including itself, but not beyond.

114.text: Replace scores for future positions with negative infinity. After softmax, these become exactly zero, enforcing the causal constraint that tokens cannot peek ahead.

115.text: Softmax to get attention weights.

117.text: Weighted sum of values and reshape.

118.text: Return both the output and the updated cache, which is passed on to the next step.

121.text: The two-layer feed-forward network, unchanged from previous labs. The MLP operates per-position and does not need any caching since it has no cross-position state.

124.text: Project each token's representation into a 4x wider hidden space for richer computation.

125.text: Compress the expanded hidden representation back down to the original embedding dimension.

127.text: Run the input through the two-layer feed-forward network with ReLU activation.

128.text: Two linear layers with ReLU in between. The expansion to 4x width gives the network more room to learn nonlinear transformations before compressing back down.

131.text: Transformer block, now threads the KV cache through.

134.text: Normalize activations before the attention sublayer. Pre-norm keeps gradients well-behaved and is the standard in modern transformers like LLaMA.

135.text: The attention sublayer, now accepting an optional KV cache. When a cache is provided, it only processes new positions and prepends cached keys and values.

139.text: Forward now accepts and returns a cache.

140.text: Attention: receives cache, returns updated cache.

141.text: Add the attention output back to the input via a residual connection. The MLP and attention each contribute refinements without overwriting the original representation.

142.text: MLP with residual (MLP doesn't need a cache).

143.text: Return both the block's output and the updated KV cache. The caller collects caches from all layers and passes them back on the next generation step.

146.text: Full model, threads caches through all layers.

149.text: Look up a learned embedding vector for each input token to represent its identity.

150.text: Positional embeddings, start_pos will offset these during cached inference.

151.text: Normalize the combined embeddings before feeding them into the transformer layers.

152.text: A stack of transformer blocks, each with its own attention and MLP. During cached inference, each layer maintains its own independent KV cache.

153.text: Map the final hidden states to vocabulary-sized logits for next-token prediction.

154.text: Apply the custom weight initialization function to every module in the model.

157.text: Static method that initializes weights with a small Gaussian for stable early training.

159.text: Draw initial weights from a narrow Gaussian so activations stay reasonably scaled.

161.text: Forward now takes past_caches and start_pos, the KV cache interface.

162.text: Extract the batch size and sequence length from the input tensor shape.

163.text: Look up a learned embedding vector for each input token to represent its identity.

164.text: Position embeddings offset by start_pos. During cached inference, this is the position of the new token, not 0. Without this offset, the model would think every new token is at position 0.

165.text: Combine token and position embeddings, normalize.

166.text: Collect updated caches from each layer.

167.text: Thread caches through each layer.

168.text: Grab the cache for this layer (or None on the first pass).

169.text: Forward through the layer, receiving the updated cache.

170.text: Save this layer's updated cache into the collection. On the next generation step, it will be passed back so the layer can skip recomputing past keys and values.

171.text: Return the logits and the full cache stack for the next generation step.

177.text: Use CPU for this tiny model since it trains in seconds without a GPU.

178.text: Instantiate the model with the same architecture as lab 03. The only difference is that the forward pass now supports an optional KV cache for efficient generation.

179.text: Same parameter count as lab 03.

181.text: Set up the Adam optimizer with momentum and epsilon tuned for this small model.

182.text: Train for 1000 steps, which is enough for this tiny model to learn basic name patterns.

184.text: Training loop, caches are ignored during training (standard teacher-forced training).

185.text: Pick the next training document by cycling through the shuffled name list.

186.text: Encode each character in the name as a token ID, bookended by BOS markers.

187.text: Limit the sequence length to block_size so it fits the model's positional embeddings.

189.text: Convert the token IDs into a tensor the model can consume as its input sequence.

190.text: Build the target sequence by shifting the input one position to the right for next-token prediction.

192.text: Forward pass. The _ discards caches, training doesn't need them.

193.text: Measure how far the model's predictions are from the true next tokens using cross-entropy.

195.text: Clear out any leftover gradients from the previous step so they do not accumulate.

196.text: Compute gradients for every parameter by propagating the loss backward through the graph.

197.text: Linearly reduce the learning rate from its initial value down to zero over the course of training.

198.text: Write the decayed learning rate into every parameter group so the optimizer uses it.

200.text: Apply the optimizer step, adjusting every parameter in the direction that reduces the loss.

209.text: Temperature controls the sampling distribution's sharpness. At 0.5, high-probability tokens become even more dominant, producing more conservative but coherent names.

211.text: Switch to eval mode for inference.

214.text: Shared sampling helper: take logits, apply temperature, sample one token.

215.text: Temperature-scaled softmax on the last position's logits.

216.text: Multinomial sampling, stochastic generation.

219.text: Naive generation: re-run the full sequence through the model at every step, which costs O(n^3) total attention.

221.text: Track attention operations to quantify the difference.

224.text: Fixed seed per sample so naive and cached produce identical outputs.

225.text: Same seed as the cached generation, so the outputs must match.

226.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token so the model starts fresh.

227.text: Generate up to block_size tokens.

228.text: Feed the entire sequence so far. This is the waste, since Q/K/V are recomputed for every previous token.

229.text: Count attention operations: T*T per head, for all heads.

230.text: O(T^2) per step, and T grows each step, giving O(T^3) total.

232.text: No cache, everything is recomputed from scratch every step.

233.text: Randomly draw one token from the probability distribution for stochastic generation.

234.text: If the model predicts BOS, treat it as an end-of-name signal and stop generating.

236.text: Add the newly sampled token to the growing sequence and continue generating.

237.text: Convert the list of generated token IDs back into a readable name string.

241.text: KV-cached generation: process only the new token each step, which costs O(n^2) total attention.

243.text: Count the attention operations (Q times K multiply-adds) at each step so we can precisely measure how much computation the KV cache saves.

246.text: Same seed, outputs will be identical.

247.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token so the model starts fresh.

248.text: Initialize the cache as empty since no tokens have been processed yet on the first pass.

250.text: First step: no cache yet, process the full initial sequence (just BOS).

252.text: Position zero for the very first token. The positional embedding needs this offset to assign the correct position encoding to the BOS token.

254.text: Subsequent steps feed only the last token. This is the key optimization, one token instead of the full sequence.

255.text: Start position = where this token sits in the sequence.

256.text: Attention ops: T_new * T_total per head. With T_new=1, this is just T_total, linear, not quadratic.

257.text: This is the entire payoff of the lab in one line: feed one fresh token in, get one larger cache out. The old prefix survives as state instead of being rebuilt from scratch.

258.text: Randomly draw one token from the probability distribution for stochastic generation.

259.text: If the model predicts BOS, treat it as an end-of-name signal and stop generating.

261.text: Add the newly sampled token to the growing sequence and continue generating.

262.text: Convert the list of generated token IDs back into a readable name string.

270.text: Disable gradient tracking for both generation methods so the comparison is fair and neither wastes time computing gradients during inference.

271.text: Start the wall clock for the naive path. Read the number it produces with suspicion: at one layer and 16 dimensions the arithmetic the cache removes is smaller than Python's per-call overhead, so this timer is mostly measuring the interpreter.

272.text: Generate 20 names with no cache, recomputing the whole prefix at every step, and return the exact attention-operation count alongside the names. The count is the measurement that matters here; the stopwatch is along for the ride.

275.text: Time the cached path the same way, over the same 20 names and the same seeds. Both loops make the same number of forward calls, so the fixed overhead cancels and only the shrunken attention term is left to show up, and at this scale it does not.

281.text: Verify the outputs are identical, since the cache is an optimization rather than an approximation. Same model, same weights and same random seed give the same output.

282.text: Side-by-side comparison of every generated name.

283.text: Flag any mismatch (there shouldn't be any).

285.text: All outputs should match perfectly.

292.text: The headline is a count of work actually performed, so it is exact and reproducible on any machine. Wall clock comes later, with caveats.

295.text: 4.3x fewer attention operations over these 20 names. An operation reduction is not a speedup: the projections, the MLP, and the Python around them are unchanged, so this bounds the win rather than reporting it.

300.text: Evaluate the closed form at T = block_size so it can be reconciled with the measured count. The two disagree, and the reason is worth a line rather than a hand-wave.

301.text: Average decode steps per name, measured rather than assumed. These names stop on BOS after about 5.8 steps, so generation never reaches position 16 and the formula's T = 16 was never the right input.

304.text: Naive: sum of t^2 for t=1..T = T(T+1)(2T+1)/6. Cubic growth.

305.text: Cached: sum of t for t=1..T = T(T+1)/2. Quadratic growth.

306.text: The ratio grows linearly with sequence length, longer sequences benefit more from caching.

307.text: Print measured against theoretical and then explain the gap, instead of quietly reporting whichever is more flattering. 4.3x versus 11.0x is not an error in either number.

310.text: Re-evaluate the same (2T+1)/3 at the observed 5.8 steps and it lands on 4.2x, right where the counter did. The saving grows with sequence length, so a corpus of six-letter names sees the very small end of it.

317.text: End-to-end wall clock, reported because the reader will want it and then immediately qualified. This ratio has been seen anywhere from below 1.00x to a few x on the same code, because it moves with machine load, which is a fact about the benchmark rather than about the cache.

320.text: Labelled 'not a speedup figure' in the output itself. Twenty six-letter names on a 16-dimensional model is a measurement of dispatch overhead with a little attention arithmetic hidden inside it.

321.text: Rather than explaining away an unhelpful number, the lab says what the number is measuring and then fixes the benchmark below. That is the more useful lesson: the optimization was fine, the experiment was wrong.

360.text: A time budget rather than a repetition count. No single count serves this table: a cached call is microseconds, where five reps measure mostly noise, while a naive call at T = 2048 can take a large fraction of a second by itself.

365.text: Take the fastest of many runs, not the mean. Anything else sharing the CPU can only ever make a call slower, so the mean measures the machine's mood while the minimum measures the code.

367.text: Seed the running minimum at infinity so the first iteration always wins, and count the reps so the table can show how much evidence is behind each cell.

369.text: Repeat until the budget is spent, subject to a floor and a ceiling. A cell that lands on the floor did so because one call already costs more than the whole budget: fine when that call is tens of milliseconds, a reason to distrust the number when it is microseconds.

372.text: One timer around one call, then keep the smallest. Loop overhead sits outside the measured region, so it cannot contaminate the number the way an outer average would.

377.text: The second defence: median across independent runs, so one throttled run cannot set the reported number. Minimum within a run, median across runs.

379.text: One untimed call per path first. The first allocation of a large tensor and the first pass through cold caches are one-time costs, and whichever path is measured first would otherwise absorb them.

384.text: The section that finally demonstrates the effect: measure the one thing that actually shrinks — the attention module for a single decode step — on synthetic tensors, so nothing about training or weights is in the way.

388.text: A fresh attention module on random activations is enough, because timing depends on tensor shapes rather than on trained weights. Reusing the trained model would have tied this benchmark to block_size = 16, which is precisely the length where the effect is invisible.

391.text: T = 64, 256, 1024, 2048. Sweeping the context length is what turns a single ambiguous ratio into a curve, and a curve you can see the shape of is worth more than any one timing.

392.text: The naive input: the whole prefix, re-projected and re-attended from scratch, giving a T x T score matrix.

393.text: The cached input is exactly one position. This is the asymmetry the whole lab is about, one row of queries against the full history instead of T of them.

394.text: A synthetic cache of the right shape stands in for a real one. What is being timed is the 1 x T attention and the cache concatenation, and neither cares whether the stored keys are meaningful.

398.text: Best-of-N for the naive step: recompute Q, K, V for the whole prefix and run a T x T attention.

399.text: Best-of-N for the cached step: one position's Q, K, V against the cached prefix, a 1 x T attention.

402.text: Print the measured ratio next to the theoretical T. On this box it climbs from under 2x at T = 64 to several hundred times at T = 2048, the right shape and comfortably short of theory.

406.text: The curve grows with T because naive attention is T x T against the cache's 1 x T. It stays under the theoretical T because the projections and the fixed per-call overhead do not shrink at all.

414.text: Both columns time work that grows with T, so both must grow with T. The lab checks that instead of asserting it — an earlier version of this benchmark reported a cached time that fell from 342.9 us at T = 1024 to 259.1 us at T = 2048, which is impossible, and nothing in the output flagged it.

447.text: At 2048 context (2T+1)/3 is 1366x fewer attention operations, and the next sentence exists to stop that being read as a 1366x speedup. Projections, MLP, and the memory traffic reading the cache back do not shrink by that factor.

451.text: The end-to-end win is large enough that no serving system ships without the cache, and it stays smaller than the operation count, bounded by whatever does not get cheaper. Past a few thousand tokens decode is memory-bound rather than compute-bound, so the bound is real rather than pedantic.
