"""
microGPT: PyTorch quantized edition.

Same architecture as 03_pytorch, but with INT8 quantization for inference.
Trains in FP32, quantizes Linear layers to INT8, then measures size, speed,
weight error and held-out loss. Only the Linear layers are quantized, so the
size reduction lands near 3.5x rather than the ideal 4x. This dequantize-to-FP32
path is SLOWER than FP32, not faster; production INT8 kernels are what buy speed.

Post-training quantization follows the principles in "Quantization and Training
of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference" (Jacob et al.,
2018), https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.05877. For LLM-specific quantization, see
"LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale" (Dettmers
et al., 2022), https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339. Note that this lab implements
simulated per-tensor symmetric quantization for educational purposes -- the
forward pass dequantizes INT8 weights back to float, so it demonstrates model
SIZE savings, not the speed improvements that real INT8 GEMM kernels provide.
Production systems use per-channel quantization and also quantize activations.
"""

import copy
import math
import os
import random
import time

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model (larger than 03 to show quantization benefits)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 64  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 2  # number of layers
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length
head_dim = n_embd // n_head  # dimension of each head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)

        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
model = MicroGPT().to(device)
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 1000

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)

    input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device)
    targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)

    logits = model(input_ids)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Quantization
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("\n--- quantization ---")


# NOTE: This is a *simulated* quantization for educational purposes.
# The forward pass dequantizes INT8 weights back to the activation dtype,
# so it does not use actual INT8 GEMM kernels. The benchmark below
# demonstrates model size savings rather than speed improvements.
class QuantizedLinear(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, fp32_linear):
        super().__init__()
        w = fp32_linear.weight.data
        scale = w.abs().max() / 127.0
        self.register_buffer("weight_int8", torch.round(w / scale).to(torch.int8))
        self.register_buffer("scale", scale.detach().clone())
        self.bias = fp32_linear.bias

    def forward(self, x):
        return F.linear(x, self.weight_int8.to(x.dtype) * self.scale, self.bias)


def quantize_model(model):
    # deepcopy gives an independent model without re-running __init__ (and so
    # without throwing away a fresh random init), and materializing the module
    # list up front means we are not mutating the module tree while walking it.
    model_q = copy.deepcopy(model)
    for _, module in list(model_q.named_modules()):
        for name, child in list(module.named_children()):
            if isinstance(child, nn.Linear):
                setattr(module, name, QuantizedLinear(child))
    return model_q


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference & Benchmark
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high


@torch.no_grad()
def generate(model, n=1):
    model.eval()
    samples = []
    for _ in range(n):
        tokens = [BOS]
        for _ in range(block_size):
            idx = torch.tensor([tokens[-block_size:]], device=device)
            probs = F.softmax(model(idx)[0, -1] / temperature, dim=-1)
            token_id = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        samples.append(tokens[1:])
    return samples


# NOTE: Speed comparison is included for completeness, but this simulated
# quantization path is expected to be similar or slower than FP32 because
# we dequantize on every forward pass. The key takeaway is model size reduction.
n_bench = 100  # samples per timing run


def benchmark(model):
    import tempfile

    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
        path = os.path.join(d, "model.pt")
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), path)
        size_mb = os.path.getsize(path) / (1024 * 1024)
    # Warm up before timing. Whichever arm runs first otherwise absorbs the
    # one-time setup cost (thread pool, kernel selection, cold caches), and on a
    # cold machine that is large enough to reverse the comparison entirely.
    generate(model, 5)
    # Seed immediately before generating so both models draw the same sampling
    # decisions. Without this the two timings run different numbers of forward
    # passes on different-length sequences, and the "comparison" compares nothing.
    torch.manual_seed(1234)
    # perf_counter, not time(): this is a monotonic high-resolution clock, and
    # a wall clock that can be stepped by NTP has no business timing a benchmark.
    start = time.perf_counter()
    generate(model, n_bench)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    return size_mb, elapsed / n_bench * 1000


fp32_size, fp32_time = benchmark(model)
print(f"FP32: {fp32_size:.3f} MB, {fp32_time:.2f} ms/sample")

model_int8 = quantize_model(model)
int8_size, int8_time = benchmark(model_int8)
print(
    f"INT8: {int8_size:.3f} MB ({int8_size / fp32_size:.1%}), {int8_time:.2f} ms/sample ({int8_time / fp32_time:.1%})"
)
print(
    f"size: {fp32_size / int8_size:.2f}x smaller | speed: {int8_time / fp32_time - 1:+.1%} vs FP32 (dequantizing on every forward costs time; the exact figure is machine-dependent)"
)
print("\nNote: This implementation prioritizes memory savings.")
print("Production systems use INT8 kernels for both size and speed benefits.")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Quantization error: what precision actually costs
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Size and speed are the easy numbers. The one that matters for deployment is
# how much the weights moved, and whether that moves the model's predictions.
print("\n--- quantization error per layer ---\n")
print(f"  {'layer':<22s} {'max|W|':>9s} {'scale':>10s} {'max abs err':>11s} {'as % of max|W|':>15s}")

fp32_weights = {name: mod.weight.data for name, mod in model.named_modules() if isinstance(mod, nn.Linear)}
worst_err = 0.0
for name, mod in model_int8.named_modules():
    if isinstance(mod, QuantizedLinear):
        w = fp32_weights[name]
        # Round-trip the INT8 weights back to float and compare with the original.
        dequant = mod.weight_int8.to(torch.float32) * mod.scale
        err = (w - dequant).abs().max().item()
        worst_err = max(worst_err, err)
        wmax = w.abs().max().item()
        print(f"  {name:<22s} {wmax:>9.5f} {mod.scale.item():>10.2e} {err:>11.2e} {100 * err / wmax:>14.3f}%")
print(f"\n  worst layer error: {worst_err:.2e}")
print("  Symmetric per-tensor INT8 rounds to a grid of step `scale`, so the error is")
print("  bounded by scale/2 = max|W|/254, about 0.4% of the largest weight, per layer.")


# Weight error is only interesting if it shows up in the model's predictions.
# Measure per-token cross-entropy on names the model never trained on.
@torch.no_grad()
def eval_loss(m, names):
    m.eval()
    total, count = 0.0, 0
    for doc in names:
        tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
        logits = m(torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device))
        targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)
        total += F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1), reduction="sum").item()
        count += n
    return total / count


# Training walked docs[0:num_steps], so anything after that is unseen.
heldout = docs[num_steps : num_steps + 2000]
fp32_loss = eval_loss(model, heldout)
int8_loss = eval_loss(model_int8, heldout)
print(f"\n  held-out loss on {len(heldout)} unseen names:")
print(f"    FP32: {fp32_loss:.4f}")
print(f"    INT8: {int8_loss:.4f}  ({int8_loss - fp32_loss:+.4f}, {100 * (int8_loss - fp32_loss) / fp32_loss:+.3f}%)")
print("  The sample lists below come out identical, which is a nice result but not")
print("  evidence of zero error, since the perturbation is just too small to flip any of")
print("  these sampling decisions. The loss delta above is the honest measure.")

for label, m in [("FP32", model), ("INT8", model_int8)]:
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    print(f"\n--- {label} samples ---")
    for i, s in enumerate(generate(m, 10)):
        print(f"  {i + 1:2d}: {''.join(uchars[t] for t in s)}")

141.text: Map the final hidden states to vocabulary-sized logits for predicting the next token.

147.text: Use CPU for this tiny model since it trains in seconds without a GPU.

148.text: Instantiate the model and move it to the target device for training.

151.text: Set up the Adam optimizer with momentum and epsilon tuned for this small model.

152.text: Train for 1000 steps, enough for this model to learn basic character-level name patterns.

154.text: Standard training loop, identical to other labs.

155.text: Pick the next training document by cycling through the shuffled name list.

156.text: Encode each character in the name as a token ID, bookended by BOS markers.

157.text: Limit the sequence length to block_size so it fits the model's positional embedding table.

159.text: Convert the first n token IDs into a tensor the model can consume as input.

160.text: Build the target sequence by shifting the input one position to the right for next-token prediction.

162.text: Run the full model on the current input batch to get next-token predictions.

163.text: Measure how far the model's predictions are from the true next tokens using cross-entropy loss.

165.text: Clear out any leftover gradients from the previous step so they do not accumulate.

166.text: Compute gradients for every parameter by propagating the loss backward through the graph.

167.text: Linearly reduce the learning rate from its initial value down to zero over the course of training.

168.text: Write the decayed learning rate into every parameter group so the optimizer uses it on the next step.

170.text: Apply the optimizer step, adjusting every parameter in the direction that reduces the loss.

185.text: The quantized linear layer: stores weights as INT8 integers (1 byte each) instead of FP32 floats (4 bytes each). A single scale factor maps between the two representations.

186.text: Takes a trained FP32 linear layer and quantizes its weights.

188.text: Detach the FP32 weight tensor from the computation graph since we only need the raw numbers for the quantization math.

189.text: Compute the scale factor: map the weight range [-max, +max] to [-127, +127]. This single scalar is the key, it determines the precision of the quantization.

190.text: Round to nearest integer and cast to INT8. Each weight now fits in 1 byte instead of 4. The register_buffer saves it as a non-parameter tensor (no gradients).

191.text: Keep the scale factor as a buffer so we can undo the quantization during inference by multiplying INT8 values back to float.

192.text: Carry over bias if the original layer had one (ours don't).

194.text: Forward: dequantize on-the-fly by casting back to float and multiplying by scale. In production, INT8 matmul kernels avoid this cast entirely, they compute directly in integer arithmetic.

195.text: Cast INT8 to float, multiply by scale, then do the matrix multiply. Mathematically: x @ (W_int8 * scale)^T. The approximation error is small because neural network weights are typically well-distributed.

198.text: Quantize the entire model: create a fresh copy and replace all Linear layers with QuantizedLinear.

202.text: deepcopy gives an independent model that keeps the trained weights. Building a fresh type(model)() and loading a state dict would work too, but it re-runs __init__ and throws away a random initialization for nothing.

203.text: Walk every module, and materialize the list first: swapping children while iterating the live module tree is the kind of bug that shows up as a silently half-quantized model.

204.text: Look for nn.Linear children to replace. Embeddings are left in FP32, which is why the size reduction lands near 3.5x rather than the ideal 4x.

205.text: Found one, replace with quantized version.

213.text: Controls how peaked the sampling distribution is. Lower temperature means more deterministic output; higher means more creative variety.

216.text: Decorator: no gradient tracking needed for inference.

217.text: Generate names, same function for both FP32 and INT8 models.

218.text: Switch to evaluation mode so the model produces consistent outputs during generation.

220.text: Loop through each sample, generating one name at a time from the model.

221.text: Begin each generated name with the beginning-of-sequence token so the model starts fresh.

223.text: Feed the current token sequence through the model to get next-token logits, keeping only the last block_size tokens.

224.text: Temperature-scaled softmax and sample in one line.

225.text: Randomly draw one token from the probability distribution for stochastic generation.

226.text: If the model predicts BOS, treat it as an end-of-name signal and stop generating.

228.text: Add the newly sampled token to the growing sequence and continue generating the next one.

239.text: Benchmark: measure model size on disk and generation speed.

240.text: Temp file import for saving the model.

242.text: Write the model's state dict to a temporary file on disk so we can measure its serialized size in bytes.

244.text: Serialize the state dict, this is what you'd ship to production.

245.text: File size in MB. The run measures 3.48x smaller rather than the naive 4x, because only the nn.Linear weights become INT8, while the two embedding tables, the RMSNorm gains and the per-layer scales all stay FP32.

253.text: Seed immediately before generating so both models make the same sampling decisions. Without it the two timings run different numbers of forward passes over different-length names, and the comparison compares nothing.

256.text: perf_counter, not time: a monotonic high-resolution clock. A wall clock that NTP can step backwards has no business timing a benchmark.

257.text: Generate 100 names in one timed block. One name is a few milliseconds of interpreter noise; a hundred is enough for the per-sample average to mean something.

259.text: Return size on disk and milliseconds per sample together, so every row of the comparison reports both halves of the tradeoff. The size figure is the honest win here; the timing is the one that goes the wrong way.

262.text: Benchmark the original FP32 model.

265.text: Quantize the trained model to INT8.

266.text: Run the same benchmark suite on the INT8 model to compare size and speed against the original FP32 baseline.

281.text: Size and speed are the easy numbers. The one that decides whether you can ship a quantized model is how far the weights moved, so measure it per layer instead of asserting that INT8 is 'close enough'.

282.text: Report max|W|, the scale, the worst absolute error, and that error as a percentage of the layer's largest weight. The percentage is the portable column: it should come out the same for every layer, and if it does not, something is wrong with the scale.

284.text: Grab the FP32 weights by module name before quantizing, so each quantized layer can be compared against the exact tensor it came from. Names line up because quantize_model replaces children in place.

290.text: Round-trip the INT8 weights back through the scale and compare with the original. This is the error the model actually sees at inference rather than a theoretical bound, since the forward pass performs this same dequantization on every call.

291.text: Take the worst element, not the mean. An average error would be reassuring and useless: what breaks a quantized model is the outlier weight, which is exactly why production schemes go per-channel.

294.text: Every layer prints at about 0.394% of its own max|W|. The constancy is the point: symmetric per-tensor quantization has a fixed relative cost, and the differences between layers are entirely differences in weight range.

296.text: The measured numbers match the closed form: rounding to a grid of step scale bounds the error at scale/2 = max|W|/254, which is where the 0.4% comes from. Theory and measurement agreeing is the cheapest sanity check available.

303.text: Weight error is only interesting if it reaches the predictions. Per-token cross-entropy on names the model never trained on is the standard way to ask that, and it is the comparison this lab previously promised without making.

311.text: reduction="sum" with an explicit token count, rather than averaging per name. Otherwise short names would count as much as long ones and the figure would drift with the length distribution instead of the weights.

317.text: Training walked docs[0:num_steps], so everything past that index is genuinely unseen. A held-out set carved out of the same shuffle costs nothing and is the difference between a loss number and a memorization check.

319.text: The same names scored under the INT8 model. Both models see identical inputs in identical order, so the delta is attributable to the rounded weights and nothing else.

322.text: The delta comes out around +0.0001 nats, roughly six thousandths of a percent. That answers 'does INT8 hurt this model' with a number and a sign rather than a shrug.

323.text: The sample lists below match exactly, and the lab declines to treat that as evidence of zero error: the perturbation is simply too small to flip any of these sampling decisions. The loss delta is the measurement; identical samples are a coincidence of temperature and vocabulary size.

327.text: Side-by-side comparison loop for FP32 and INT8 samples. Each model will be sampled under the same random seed so differences come from the weights, not different random draws.

328.text: Reset the RNG before sampling each model so FP32 and INT8 draw the same random numbers; otherwise the two sample lists would differ for reasons unrelated to quantization.

330.text: Generate 10 samples from the current model under that fixed seed.

331.text: Decode and print each generated name.

units.title: Text Diffusion
units.tagline: Names emerge from pure noise through iterative unmasking.
units.description:
Instead of generating left-to-right, masked diffusion starts from a sequence of all [MASK] tokens and iteratively reveals them. At each step, the model predicts what's behind every mask, and the most confident predictions are unmasked.

This is the text equivalent of image diffusion models like Stable Diffusion. The key difference from autoregressive models: the generation order is determined by model confidence, not left-to-right position. The model might unmask the middle of a name before the beginning.

The lab uses PyTorch for tensors and autograd, but with a fundamentally different training objective (predict masked tokens) and generation process (iterative unmasking with confidence-based remasking). Because the step count is a dial that left-to-right decoding does not have, the run generates names at 16, 8 and 4 denoising steps from the same trained model and prints the forward passes each costs: at 16 steps the names are clean, at 8 they start to fray, at 4 they are mostly mush. How few steps you can get away with is the question production diffusion LMs are actually trying to answer.
learning_objectives: Implement masked diffusion for non-autoregressive text generation
Compare confidence-based unmasking with left-to-right generation
Analyze the tradeoffs between diffusion and autoregressive approaches

exercises.prompt: The lab already sweeps 16, 8 and 4 denoising steps. Push it further: add 32 and 2 to the sweep. Where does extra compute stop buying quality, and where does the output fall apart?
exercises.hint: Edit the tuple in the `for num_steps_denoise in (16, 8, 4):` loop. Watch the printed forward-pass count as well as the names, since the question is what you get per pass, not just how good the names are.

exercises.prompt: Modify the unmasking schedule to always unmask from left to right instead of by confidence. Does this make the output better or worse?
exercises.hint: Replace the confidence-based selection with positional ordering. This makes it behave more like autoregressive generation but within the diffusion framework.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: Masked Diffusion Language Model (PyTorch).

Instead of generating names left-to-right like a GPT, names emerge from pure
noise -- all [MASK] tokens -- through iterative unmasking. Same transformer
architecture, fundamentally different generative paradigm.

Built on the image-domain foundation of "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic
Models" (Ho et al., 2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239. The discrete-text
diffusion framework follows "Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language
Models" (Sahoo et al., 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07524, and "Large
Language Diffusion Models" (Nie et al., 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992.
The denoising schedule and confidence-based unmasking in this lab are
illustrative simplifications -- the original MDLM uses a continuous-time ELBO
with an absorbing-state forward process.
"""

import math
import os
import random

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

# MASK replaces BOS, PAD handles fixed-length sequences
uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
MASK = len(uchars)  # [MASK], the "noise" state that the model learns to denoise
PAD = len(uchars) + 1  # [PAD], which fills unused positions in fixed-length sequences
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 2
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model: bidirectional transformer (no causal mask)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 16  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 2  # number of layers (diffusion needs depth to gather scattered clues)
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length (names are padded/truncated to this)
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class BidirectionalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Every position attends to every other, with no causal mask."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

        # Bidirectional: no causal mask, every position sees every other
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)

        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = BidirectionalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class MicroDiffusion(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        # Weight tying: same matrix for input embeddings and output projection
        self.lm_head.weight = self.wte.weight
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
model = MicroDiffusion().to(device)
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 3000
batch_size = 32  # diffusion needs batching, since single-sample gradients are too noisy
print(f"batch size: {batch_size} (diffusion needs batching, since single-sample gradients are too noisy)")

for step in range(num_steps):
    # Build a batch of (clean, noisy) pairs, each with its own random masking
    clean_batch = []
    noisy_batch = []
    mask_batch = []  # True where masked

    for b in range(batch_size):
        doc = docs[(step * batch_size + b) % len(docs)]
        clean = [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [PAD] * (block_size - len(doc))
        clean = clean[:block_size]

        # Forward process: corrupt by masking each token with probability t
        # Log-uniform t sampling: t ∝ 1/t, cancels the 1/t ELBO weight
        t = math.exp(random.uniform(math.log(0.2), 0))
        noisy = [MASK if random.random() < t else c for c in clean]
        is_masked = [n == MASK for n in noisy]

        if not any(is_masked):
            # Ensure at least one masked token for a training signal
            pos = random.randrange(block_size)
            noisy[pos] = MASK
            is_masked[pos] = True

        clean_batch.append(clean)
        noisy_batch.append(noisy)
        mask_batch.append(is_masked)

    # Forward pass: predict clean tokens from noisy input
    input_ids = torch.tensor(noisy_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)
    targets = torch.tensor(clean_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)
    mask = torch.tensor(mask_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)

    logits = model(input_ids)  # (B, block_size, vocab_size)
    logits[:, :, MASK] = logits[:, :, MASK] - 1e6  # never predict MASK

    # Loss only on masked positions, averaged across the batch
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[mask], targets[mask])

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference: iterative denoising from all-MASK to clean names
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The step count is a dial, not a constant, and it is the whole reason to care
# about diffusion: with fewer steps than tokens, several positions commit in the
# same forward pass. Left-to-right decoding has no such dial, and it always costs
# one forward pass per token. Note that the first arm below (16 steps for 16
# positions) is not that saving: it cannot commit more than one position per
# step on average, and the run reports that it does not.


def denoise(num_denoise_steps):
    """Generate one name by iterative unmasking. Returns (name, passes, commits)."""
    seq = [MASK] * block_size  # start from pure noise
    passes = 0
    commits = []  # positions committed per step, the schedule as measured

    for step_i in range(num_denoise_steps, 0, -1):
        # Cosine schedule: `t` is the fraction of positions masked going into
        # this step, `s` the fraction the schedule wants masked after it.
        t = math.cos(math.pi / 2 * (1 - step_i / num_denoise_steps))
        s = math.cos(math.pi / 2 * (1 - (step_i - 1) / num_denoise_steps))
        temperature = 0.3 + 0.5 * t  # explore early, commit late

        logits = model(torch.tensor([seq], device=device))[0]  # (block_size, vocab_size)
        passes += 1

        predicted = list(seq)
        confidences = []
        for i in range(block_size):
            if seq[i] == MASK:
                logits_i = logits[i].clone()
                logits_i[MASK] = logits_i[MASK] - 1e6  # never predict MASK
                probs = F.softmax(logits_i / temperature, dim=-1)
                predicted[i] = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
                confidences.append((probs.max().item(), i))

        # Commit the most confident predictions and re-mask the rest, so the
        # number left masked is what the schedule asked for. Anchoring on
        # block_size, rather than on how many happen to be masked right now, is what
        # lets the schedule set the pace; the `- 1` floor guarantees every step
        # commits at least one position. Which of the two binds depends on the
        # step count: with as many steps as positions the floor wins every time,
        # and the per-step commit counts printed below say which happened.
        n_to_remask = 0
        if confidences:
            n_to_remask = min(int(block_size * s), len(confidences) - 1)
            confidences.sort()
            for _, i in confidences[:n_to_remask]:
                predicted[i] = MASK
        commits.append(len(confidences) - n_to_remask)
        seq = predicted

    return "".join(uchars[c] for c in seq if c < len(uchars)), passes, commits


model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    for num_steps_denoise in (16, 8, 4):
        torch.manual_seed(1234)  # same noise every time, so only the schedule differs
        print(f"\n--- inference: {num_steps_denoise} denoising steps ---")
        total_passes = 0
        commits = []
        for sample_idx in range(10):
            name, passes, commits = denoise(num_steps_denoise)
            total_passes += passes
            print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {name}")
        print(f"  {total_passes / 10:.1f} forward passes per name (left-to-right needs up to {block_size})")
        # The commit counts depend only on block_size and the schedule, not on
        # sampling, so one sample's pattern is every sample's pattern.
        print(f"  positions committed per step: {','.join(str(c) for c in commits)}")
        if max(commits) == 1:
            print("  Every step committed exactly one position: with as many steps as")
            print("  positions the `- 1` floor is what sets the pace, not the cosine")
            print("  schedule, and this arm costs the same as left-to-right decoding.")

print(
    "\nFewer steps means more positions committed per pass, so generation gets cheaper"
    "\nand, at this scale, visibly worse. How few steps you can get away with is the"
    "\ncentral question in diffusion language models."
)

1.text: This lab implements a masked diffusion language model, the text equivalent of image diffusion. Instead of adding Gaussian noise to pixels, we replace characters with MASK tokens.

2.text: The model name says it all: instead of predicting the next token, this model starts from an all-MASK sequence and iteratively reveals tokens.

8.text: Two key papers: MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) introduced the masked diffusion framework; LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) scaled it to large language models and showed competitive results.

18.text: Diffusion replaces left-to-right generation with a denoising process, so the math here supports both ordinary attention scaling and the noise schedule that drives unmasking.

19.text: Same names corpus as the autoregressive labs. That makes the paradigm shift easier to feel: the data is familiar, the generation process is not.

20.text: Randomness is part of the model here, not just setup noise. Diffusion repeatedly corrupts and reveals tokens, so stochasticity is part of the teaching story.

22.text: PyTorch gives us the same transformer machinery, but this lab asks it to solve a different problem: predict masked positions everywhere at once instead of next-token only.

23.text: The building blocks look familiar, which is useful because it shows how much of the transformer survives even when the generation paradigm changes completely.

24.text: The loss and softmax are ordinary; the unusual part is that the model keeps revisiting uncertain positions instead of committing left to right.

26.text: Even a stochastic denoising process should be inspectable, so we seed the run to make the unmasking trajectory reproducible.

27.text: PyTorch's RNG also needs to be pinned so the diffusion behavior you see comes from the algorithm, not a different initialization.

29.text: The setup is still standard PyTorch. The diffusion-specific behavior shows up in the masking objective and the iterative unmasking loop, not in the imports.

32.text: Builds the path to the dataset file relative to this script, one directory up in data/.

33.text: Auto-downloads the dataset if missing.

34.text: Lazy import: only load urllib if we actually need to download.

39.text: Each line becomes one document, and stripping whitespace prevents ghost tokens.

40.text: Shuffling prevents the model from memorizing alphabetical order.

41.text: Quick sanity check: we should see ~32K names.

43.text: In autoregressive models we needed BOS to start generation. In diffusion, MASK serves that role, since the model starts from all-MASK and denoises. PAD is still needed for fixed-length batching.

44.text: Sorted unique characters become our vocabulary. Each character gets a deterministic token ID from 0 to n-1.

45.text: MASK is the "noise" token. In diffusion, we corrupt data by replacing real tokens with MASK, then train the model to reverse that corruption. This replaces the BOS token used in autoregressive models.

46.text: PAD fills unused positions in fixed-length sequences. Diffusion processes every position simultaneously, so all sequences must be the same length.

47.text: Two extra tokens beyond the character set: MASK and PAD.

48.text: 28 tokens: 26 lowercase letters + MASK + PAD. The small vocabulary makes it easy to see diffusion dynamics without complexity.

51.text: The model section. The transformer architecture is nearly identical to the autoregressive labs, with one key difference: attention is bidirectional, so there is no causal mask.

53.text: 16-dimensional embeddings, small but enough for character-level patterns.

54.text: 4 attention heads, each seeing 4 dimensions of the 16-dim embedding.

55.text: Two layers instead of one, because diffusion needs more depth to gather clues from scattered unmasked positions, where autoregressive models always have full left context.

56.text: Fixed sequence length of 16. All names are padded or truncated to fit. Diffusion processes every position in parallel.

57.text: Each head operates on a 4-dimensional slice: 16 / 4 = 4.

60.text: RMSNorm: simpler than LayerNorm, just scales by inverse root-mean-square. No learnable parameters.

65.text: The forward method normalizes by root-mean-square: simpler than LayerNorm because there is no mean subtraction or learned bias.

66.text: Compute root-mean-square and scale so vectors have roughly unit magnitude. The rsqrt fuses the division and square root for efficiency.

69.text: The key difference from GPT is bidirectional attention. Every position can see every other position, with no causal mask, which lets the model gather clues from all unmasked tokens in any direction to fill in the blanks.

72.text: Constructor sets up the same Q/K/V/O projections as the autoregressive attention. The difference is purely in the forward pass: no causal mask.

74.text: Query projection: "what am I looking for?"

75.text: Key projection: "what do I contain?"

76.text: Value projection: the actual content that attention retrieves.

77.text: Output projection recombines heads.

79.text: The forward pass computes multi-head attention. B=batch, T=sequence length, C=embedding dimension.

81.text: Reshape Q into (batch, heads, seq_len, head_dim) so each head attends independently.

82.text: Keys and values get the same (B, heads, T, head_dim) reshape so all three tensors align for batched attention.

86.text: Scaled dot-product attention, with no causal mask. That is the key difference from GPT: every position sees every other.

87.text: Softmax over all positions gives attention weights. In GPT, future positions would be masked to -inf here.

89.text: Weighted sum of values, then reshape back to (batch, seq_len, n_embd).

93.text: Standard two-layer feed-forward network, identical to the autoregressive labs. The MLP processes each position independently after attention has mixed information across positions.

96.text: Expand to 4x width, the "thinking space" of the MLP.

100.text: ReLU between the two linear layers creates the nonlinearity that lets the network learn complex patterns.

103.text: Transformer block: attention then MLP, each with pre-norm and residual connections. Same architecture as the autoregressive labs, with only the attention mask changed.

106.text: Pre-norm: normalize before each sublayer for stable training.

107.text: Bidirectional attention instead of the causal attention used in GPT.

108.text: Second pre-norm before the MLP sublayer.

"""
microGPT: Masked Diffusion Language Model (PyTorch).

Instead of generating names left-to-right like a GPT, names emerge from pure
noise -- all [MASK] tokens -- through iterative unmasking. Same transformer
architecture, fundamentally different generative paradigm.

Built on the image-domain foundation of "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic
Models" (Ho et al., 2020), https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239. The discrete-text
diffusion framework follows "Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language
Models" (Sahoo et al., 2024), https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07524, and "Large
Language Diffusion Models" (Nie et al., 2025), https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09992.
The denoising schedule and confidence-based unmasking in this lab are
illustrative simplifications -- the original MDLM uses a continuous-time ELBO
with an absorbing-state forward process.
"""

import math
import os
import random

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

# MASK replaces BOS, PAD handles fixed-length sequences
uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
MASK = len(uchars)  # [MASK], the "noise" state that the model learns to denoise
PAD = len(uchars) + 1  # [PAD], which fills unused positions in fixed-length sequences
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 2
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model: bidirectional transformer (no causal mask)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 16  # embedding dimension
n_head = 4  # number of attention heads
n_layer = 2  # number of layers (diffusion needs depth to gather scattered clues)
block_size = 16  # maximum sequence length (names are padded/truncated to this)
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class BidirectionalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Every position attends to every other, with no causal mask."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

        # Bidirectional: no causal mask, every position sees every other
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)

        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = BidirectionalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class MicroDiffusion(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        # Weight tying: same matrix for input embeddings and output projection
        self.lm_head.weight = self.wte.weight
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
model = MicroDiffusion().to(device)
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 3000
batch_size = 32  # diffusion needs batching, since single-sample gradients are too noisy
print(f"batch size: {batch_size} (diffusion needs batching, since single-sample gradients are too noisy)")

for step in range(num_steps):
    # Build a batch of (clean, noisy) pairs, each with its own random masking
    clean_batch = []
    noisy_batch = []
    mask_batch = []  # True where masked

    for b in range(batch_size):
        doc = docs[(step * batch_size + b) % len(docs)]
        clean = [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [PAD] * (block_size - len(doc))
        clean = clean[:block_size]

        # Forward process: corrupt by masking each token with probability t
        # Log-uniform t sampling: t ∝ 1/t, cancels the 1/t ELBO weight
        t = math.exp(random.uniform(math.log(0.2), 0))
        noisy = [MASK if random.random() < t else c for c in clean]
        is_masked = [n == MASK for n in noisy]

        if not any(is_masked):
            # Ensure at least one masked token for a training signal
            pos = random.randrange(block_size)
            noisy[pos] = MASK
            is_masked[pos] = True

        clean_batch.append(clean)
        noisy_batch.append(noisy)
        mask_batch.append(is_masked)

    # Forward pass: predict clean tokens from noisy input
    input_ids = torch.tensor(noisy_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)
    targets = torch.tensor(clean_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)
    mask = torch.tensor(mask_batch, device=device)  # (B, block_size)

    logits = model(input_ids)  # (B, block_size, vocab_size)
    logits[:, :, MASK] = logits[:, :, MASK] - 1e6  # never predict MASK

    # Loss only on masked positions, averaged across the batch
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits[mask], targets[mask])

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()

    if (step + 1) % 10 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference: iterative denoising from all-MASK to clean names
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The step count is a dial, not a constant, and it is the whole reason to care
# about diffusion: with fewer steps than tokens, several positions commit in the
# same forward pass. Left-to-right decoding has no such dial, and it always costs
# one forward pass per token. Note that the first arm below (16 steps for 16
# positions) is not that saving: it cannot commit more than one position per
# step on average, and the run reports that it does not.


def denoise(num_denoise_steps):
    """Generate one name by iterative unmasking. Returns (name, passes, commits)."""
    seq = [MASK] * block_size  # start from pure noise
    passes = 0
    commits = []  # positions committed per step, the schedule as measured

    for step_i in range(num_denoise_steps, 0, -1):
        # Cosine schedule: `t` is the fraction of positions masked going into
        # this step, `s` the fraction the schedule wants masked after it.
        t = math.cos(math.pi / 2 * (1 - step_i / num_denoise_steps))
        s = math.cos(math.pi / 2 * (1 - (step_i - 1) / num_denoise_steps))
        temperature = 0.3 + 0.5 * t  # explore early, commit late

        logits = model(torch.tensor([seq], device=device))[0]  # (block_size, vocab_size)
        passes += 1

        predicted = list(seq)
        confidences = []
        for i in range(block_size):
            if seq[i] == MASK:
                logits_i = logits[i].clone()
                logits_i[MASK] = logits_i[MASK] - 1e6  # never predict MASK
                probs = F.softmax(logits_i / temperature, dim=-1)
                predicted[i] = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
                confidences.append((probs.max().item(), i))

        # Commit the most confident predictions and re-mask the rest, so the
        # number left masked is what the schedule asked for. Anchoring on
        # block_size, rather than on how many happen to be masked right now, is what
        # lets the schedule set the pace; the `- 1` floor guarantees every step
        # commits at least one position. Which of the two binds depends on the
        # step count: with as many steps as positions the floor wins every time,
        # and the per-step commit counts printed below say which happened.
        n_to_remask = 0
        if confidences:
            n_to_remask = min(int(block_size * s), len(confidences) - 1)
            confidences.sort()
            for _, i in confidences[:n_to_remask]:
                predicted[i] = MASK
        commits.append(len(confidences) - n_to_remask)
        seq = predicted

    return "".join(uchars[c] for c in seq if c < len(uchars)), passes, commits


model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    for num_steps_denoise in (16, 8, 4):
        torch.manual_seed(1234)  # same noise every time, so only the schedule differs
        print(f"\n--- inference: {num_steps_denoise} denoising steps ---")
        total_passes = 0
        commits = []
        for sample_idx in range(10):
            name, passes, commits = denoise(num_steps_denoise)
            total_passes += passes
            print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {name}")
        print(f"  {total_passes / 10:.1f} forward passes per name (left-to-right needs up to {block_size})")
        # The commit counts depend only on block_size and the schedule, not on
        # sampling, so one sample's pattern is every sample's pattern.
        print(f"  positions committed per step: {','.join(str(c) for c in commits)}")
        if max(commits) == 1:
            print("  Every step committed exactly one position: with as many steps as")
            print("  positions the `- 1` floor is what sets the pace, not the cosine")
            print("  schedule, and this arm costs the same as left-to-right decoding.")

print(
    "\nFewer steps means more positions committed per pass, so generation gets cheaper"
    "\nand, at this scale, visibly worse. How few steps you can get away with is the"
    "\ncentral question in diffusion language models."
)
