184.text: Softmax converts logits to probabilities. Returns (T, V), one distribution per position.

190.text: Standard autoregressive generation: one token, one forward pass, repeat. This is the baseline we want to beat.

192.text: Start with just the BOS token.

193.text: No gradients needed for generation.

194.text: Generate up to max_len tokens.

195.text: Run the model on the full token sequence and return only the last position's probability distribution for next-token prediction.

196.text: Sample one token from the distribution.

197.text: The BOS token doubles as an end-of-sequence marker. When sampled, it signals that the name is complete.

198.text: End-of-sequence detected, so stop generating further tokens for this name.

199.text: Append the new token and continue.

200.text: Hand back the generated token sequence with the leading BOS removed, since it was just a start signal, not part of the name.

206.text: The heart of the lab: speculative decoding with draft model draft and target model target. K=4 means the draft model guesses 4 tokens ahead.

240.text: Five counters, and the interesting part is that drafted and evaluated are different numbers. Every proposal increments drafted; only proposals the target actually ruled on increment evaluated, because after the first rejection the rest of the window is discarded unexamined. Three different acceptance figures come out of these five counters.

242.text: Disable PyTorch's gradient tracking during inference since we don't need backpropagation, saving memory and compute.

245.text: Copy current tokens, the draft model will extend this speculatively.

246.text: Track each drafted token and its probability under the draft model.

247.text: Speculatively generate K tokens using the cheap draft model. These guesses will be verified against the target in one batch.

248.text: Stop if we've hit the length limit.

249.text: Break out of the draft loop.

250.text: Get draft model's next-token probabilities. This is cheap because the draft model is small.

251.text: Keep a running count of how many forward passes the draft model has executed, for the efficiency comparison later.

252.text: Sample a token from the draft distribution.

253.text: Record the token and its draft probability q(x), we'll need q(x) for the acceptance ratio.

254.text: Append the newly sampled token to the draft sequence so the next draft step can condition on it.

256.text: Edge case: no tokens were drafted.

257.text: Edge case: if no tokens were drafted (e.g., length limit hit immediately), skip the verification step entirely.

259.text: Record how many tokens the draft model proposed.

263.text: The key efficiency win: the target model scores every drafted position in a single forward pass, where autoregressive decoding would need K separate ones. Since inference is memory-bound, with reading weights dominating, one pass costs almost the same as K.

264.text: Count target forward passes, should be much fewer than autoregressive.

267.text: Track how many consecutive drafts get accepted in this round.

271.text: Snapshot the prefix length before the accept loop. tokens grows every time we accept, so reading len(tokens) inside the loop would drift by +i and verify each drafted token against the wrong row of the target's output.

277.text: Verify each drafted token against the target model's distribution.

281.text: Map draft position i to a row of the target's output. The target scored the whole drafted sequence in one pass, so the row we want is at absolute position base_len - 1 + i — minus whatever fell off the front of the context window, which is what row_offset carries.

282.text: Make sure the draft position maps to a valid index in the target's output tensor.

283.text: The position is beyond what the target model computed, so exit the verification loop.

284.text: Get the target model's probability p(x) for the exact token the draft proposed.

287.text: Zero draft probability means the draft model would never have picked this token, reject.

291.text: The denominator of alpha. Counting here rather than at the top of the loop is what keeps alpha the literature's per-token acceptance rate: tokens that were never examined never dilute it.

292.text: The acceptance probability: min(1, p(x)/q(x)). If the target likes this token at least as much as the draft, always accept. If the target likes it less, accept proportionally. This ratio is what guarantees the output distribution matches the target exactly.

294.text: Coin flip: accept with the computed probability.

296.text: Token accepted, add to the final sequence.

297.text: Bump the accepted token counter, so accepted and drafted can be compared to compute the acceptance rate.

298.text: Special case: accepted token is BOS (end of sequence).

299.text: Remove BOS from the output and stop generating.

304.text: The BOS was verified and accepted, so it counts in accepted even though it is popped off and never emitted. accepted measures verification outcomes, not output length, which is why the earlier "don't count BOS" behaviour was wrong for alpha.

305.text: Bundle the final token sequence with the draft/target statistics so the caller can analyze both quality and efficiency.

308.text: Retrieve the target model's full probability distribution at the rejected position, needed for the correction sampling step.

309.text: The residual distribution, and the most subtle line in the lab. Clamping p - q at zero keeps only the mass the target wants that the draft under-supplied; resampling from that (normalized) exactly compensates for the tokens the accept test rejected. This clamp plus the min(1, p/q) test above is the whole losslessness proof of Leviathan et al.

310.text: Sum the corrected distribution to check if it has positive mass. If it's all zeros, we'll fall back to the raw target distribution.

311.text: If there's positive mass in the adjusted distribution...

312.text: Normalize to a proper probability distribution.

314.text: Fallback: if adjustment zeroes everything out, use the target's raw distribution.

316.text: If the sampled token is BOS (end-of-sequence marker), the name is done and we should stop generating further tokens.

317.text: Record the final counts and return early since the name ended with the corrected token.

318.text: Package the completed sequence and return it to the caller along with the generation statistics.

319.text: Add the corrected token to the output sequence. This token was sampled from the adjusted distribution to match the target's behavior.

320.text: After rejection, restart the draft loop from the new position. Don't try to reuse remaining drafts.

322.text: Python for-else: this runs if the loop completed without break, meaning every one of the K tokens was accepted.

324.text: When all K drafts are accepted, we get a bonus: the target already computed the probability distribution for the position after the last draft. Same window correction applies.

325.text: Bounds check on the bonus position.

326.text: Look up what the target model would predict at the bonus position, which we get for free since the target already computed it.

327.text: Sample a bonus token, a free extra token from the target with no additional cost.

328.text: A bonus token of BOS is the target's own stop decision, so this path returns rather than falling through. Falling through would discard the stop, redraft from the same prefix and quietly bias generated names longer, a losslessness bug hiding in the happy path.

334.text: Fold this round's accepted run into the totals before the early return, so a sequence that ends on a bonus token still contributes to the acceptance statistics.

336.text: Add this free bonus token to the sequence. It cost zero extra forward passes since it came from the target's existing computation.

338.text: Update accepted count at end of round.

340.text: Package the completed token sequence together with the acceptance statistics for the final benchmark comparison.

348.text: Switch draft model to evaluation mode (disables dropout if any).

349.text: Switch target model to evaluation mode.

353.text: Utility: time a generation function over n_samples runs.

354.text: Print a label identifying which generation method is about to be timed, so the benchmark output is easy to read.

358.text: perf_counter, not time(): monotonic and high resolution. A lab whose whole output is a timing measurement should not be reading a clock that NTP is allowed to step underneath it.

359.text: Run the generation function for all samples, collecting both the outputs and the total wall-clock time.

360.text: Stop the clock and hand the elapsed time back with the samples, so the caller can divide by whatever it wants (per sample, per token, per forward pass).

362.text: Bundle the generated samples together with the elapsed time so the caller can analyze both output quality and speed.

365.text: The draft/target cost ratio is the premise of speculative decoding, so measure it rather than inferring it from parameter counts. Everything the lab claims about why the wall clock disappoints rests on this one number.

371.text: Random token ids at a fixed length: we are timing the forward pass, not the model's opinion of the input.

373.text: One untimed call first. The first forward pass pays for lazy allocation and kernel selection, and folding that into the mean would inflate the smaller model more than the larger one, which is exactly the comparison we are trying to make.

380.text: Benchmark 1: standard autoregressive decoding with the target model (the baseline).

381.text: One forward pass per token, the slowest approach.

388.text: Accumulators for the per-sample stats dicts. Summing across all 50 samples rather than averaging per-sample ratios matters: alpha is a ratio of totals, not a mean of ratios.

389.text: List to collect results with stats.

392.text: A named function instead of a lambda, because timed_generate only wants the token list back while we also want the stats. The previous version was a lambda exploiting the fact that list.append returns None; this says what it does.

393.text: K=4: the draft proposes four tokens per round, so at best one target forward pass replaces five.

398.text: Benchmark 2: speculative decoding, timed under exactly the same harness as the autoregressive baseline so the comparison is like for like.

400.text: Add up each statistic category (drafted, accepted, target passes, draft passes) across all generated samples.

401.text: Add this sample's individual stat values into the running totals for the final summary.

403.text: Benchmark 3: draft-only autoregressive (for reference, fast but lower quality).

404.text: Uses the small draft model alone.

410.text: Alpha, the per-token acceptance rate from the literature: of the proposals the target actually ruled on, what fraction survived. This is the K-independent number, and it is the one to quote.

411.text: Draft window utilization: accepted over all proposals, including the ones thrown away after the first rejection. It falls as K grows even with an unchanged draft model, which is why it is not a property of the draft model and not a substitute for alpha.

412.text: Mean accepted run per round, meaning accepted tokens divided by target forward passes. This is the figure that actually determines speedup, because it is how many tokens each expensive target pass buys.

413.text: Average target forward passes per sample, should be much less than the average token count.

414.text: Average draft forward passes per sample.

416.text: Average tokens generated speculatively (should match autoregressive closely).

418.text: Time one draft forward pass in isolation, away from the sampling loop.

419.text: And one target forward pass. The ratio of these two is what decides whether the algorithm can pay for itself on this machine.

421.text: Print the statistics section header before showing acceptance rates and forward pass counts.

427.text: Lead with the forward-pass count, because that is the metric that transfers. On a GPU with a real model the target forward dominates everything, so cutting target forwards per name is the win.

429.text: The other side of the ledger: the draft forwards are extra work that did not exist in the baseline. Speculative decoding is a trade, not a free lunch.

431.text: Three acceptance figures from the same run, printed together on purpose. Papers quote whichever one flatters the method, and they can differ by tens of points on identical data.

432.text: Alpha: accepted over evaluated. Independent of K, so this is the number you can compare across papers.

433.text: Mean accepted run of a K=4 window. Compare it against K to see how much of the speculation budget the draft model is actually earning.

434.text: Window utilization: accepted over all K proposals. Lower than alpha by construction, because everything after the first rejection is counted as proposed and never evaluated.

439.text: The measured per-forward-pass costs, not an estimate from parameter counts. This is the line that explains the wall clock below.

440.text: The arbitrage the whole technique depends on. At this scale the cost ratio and the parameter ratio have come apart completely, because both models are dominated by per-call Python and dispatch overhead rather than arithmetic. In production that ratio is 10-100x, which is where the reported 2-3x speedups come from.

445.text: The wall clock, reported as a ratio rather than a "speedup" because on this box it comes out below 1.00. Printing an unflattering measurement is the point: the forward-pass reduction is real and transfers, the wall clock is a property of this CPU and this interpreter.

449.text: Token counts should be similar, the distribution is mathematically identical.

463.text: The headline claim of this lab is that the output distribution is unchanged. A speedup number does not test that at all, so test it directly.

464.text: 500 samples per arm. Enough that the noise floor below is a stable reference, small enough to run on a CPU in the same script.

467.text: A 27-bin character histogram is a crude summary of a distribution over strings, but it is a statistic both arms must agree on if the accept/reject math is right.

476.text: Total variation distance: the largest disagreement any event can show between two distributions. Zero means identical, one means disjoint support.

481.text: Autoregressive run A, the reference sample from the target model alone.

482.text: Autoregressive run B, from the same model with the same settings. This second run is the essential part: two finite samples from one distribution already differ, and without that reference "the distributions match" is unfalsifiable, since any small difference can be waved away.

483.text: And the speculative sample, drawn the same way and at the same size, so the only difference between it and A is the decoding algorithm.

493.text: Three histograms from the three runs, ready to be compared pairwise.

494.text: AR versus AR: the noise floor. This is how far apart two samples from the same distribution land at this sample size, and it is the yardstick everything else is measured against.

495.text: AR versus speculative: the number under test. On its own it means nothing, and it becomes evidence only when divided by the floor above.

497.text: Print the floor first and label it, so the reader cannot mistake the measured distance for an absolute error.

499.text: The ratio is the actual verdict. Around 1x means the speculative sample is no further from an autoregressive sample than another autoregressive sample would be.

501.text: Two noise floors is a deliberately loose threshold, and both branches print. A check whose failure branch is unreachable is not a check, so the failure text is written out in full and left in the file.

511.text: State the limits of the test in the output rather than in a comment. Two summary statistics at n=500 can fail to detect a real difference; they cannot prove there is none. The proof lives in Leviathan et al. (2023), and this is a sanity check on the implementation of it.

549.text: Show actual generated names from each method.

551.text: The names generated by standard autoregressive decoding with the full target model, our quality baseline.

552.text: The names generated by speculative decoding, which should match the target's distribution exactly despite being faster.

553.text: Names from the small draft model alone. Faster but lower quality, included to show the quality gap that speculative decoding bridges.

555.text: Print which generation method produced the following names so we can compare quality across approaches.

556.text: Show the first 10 samples from each method.

557.text: Decode token IDs back to characters and print.

558.text: Visual separator between the three methods' output blocks for cleaner readability in the terminal.

units.title: Tiled Attention (FlashAttention)
units.tagline: Three attention implementations producing identical outputs. The difference is memory trips.
units.description:
FlashAttention restructures the attention computation to minimize memory transfers between fast SRAM and slow HBM (main GPU memory).

Standard attention materializes the full N×N attention matrix in HBM, which is O(N²) memory. FlashAttention processes attention in tiles that fit in SRAM, accumulating results with online softmax (the log-sum-exp trick). The output is mathematically identical, but memory usage drops from O(N²) to O(N).

This lab implements three versions, standard, online softmax and tiled, so you can verify they produce the same output while understanding why the tiled version is faster on real hardware. The online-softmax variant is the instructive middle step: it never materializes the N×N matrix either, but it re-reads all of K and V once per query row, so it does more memory traffic than standard attention. Tiling is what amortizes that re-reading across a whole block of queries, and the lab counts the HBM reads and writes for all three.
learning_objectives: Implement standard, online-softmax, and tiled (FlashAttention) attention
Explain the online softmax trick using log-sum-exp
Analyze why tiled attention reduces memory from O(N^2) to O(N)

exercises.prompt: Every tile size gives identical output, down to 1, so asking for the smallest correct tile answers itself. Ask what tile size does change instead: run the N=2048, d=128 projection at tile widths 32, 64, 256 and 512 and find where the tiled/standard ratio stops improving. Why is there an optimum rather than bigger always being better?
exercises.hint: The closed form is tiled_ops(n, dim, tile). K/V traffic is amortized across the tile, so it falls as the tile grows, but the score tile is tile × tile and has to fit in SRAM, which is the real cap on hardware. Read the max_intermediate figure the lab prints next to the counts to see that second curve going the other way.

exercises.prompt: The HBM counters already exist, so read them instead of adding them. At N=2048, d=128 the online-softmax variant does more memory operations than standard attention. Derive its closed form, online_ops = 2*N*d + d*N*(N+1), from the loop that produces it and name the line that costs.
exercises.hint: The stats['hbm_reads'] += 2 * d inside the inner loop of online_softmax_attention runs once per (query row, key) pair, which is where the N² term comes from. Compare it with the tiled version's 2 * block_cols * d, charged once per block of queries rather than once per query, and the amortization factor is the tile width.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: Tiled attention edition.

Same architecture as the PyTorch version (03), but demonstrating three
attention implementations for inference: standard, online-softmax, and
tiled (FlashAttention algorithm). All three produce identical outputs;
the difference is how many "slow memory" (HBM) operations they need.

Training uses PyTorch; the attention implementations are in explicit NumPy
to make every memory access visible and countable.

The tiled algorithm implements the core idea from "FlashAttention: Fast and
Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness" (Dao et al., 2022),
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135. The online softmax technique used within
tiles is from "Online normalizer calculation for softmax" (Milakov &
Gimelshein, 2018), https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867. Also see
"FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work
Partitioning" (Dao, 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691. Note that this
is a pedagogical NumPy implementation of the algorithmic idea -- the real
FlashAttention is a fused CUDA kernel that exploits GPU SRAM directly. The
math is identical; the performance difference comes from hardware-level
memory management.
"""

import math
import os
import random

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)
torch.set_default_dtype(
    torch.float64
)  # Intentional for this standalone lab (float64 needed for numerical accuracy demos)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    urllib.request.urlretrieve(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt", input_path
    )

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS, vocab_size = len(uchars), len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model (PyTorch, identical architecture to Lab 03)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd, n_head, n_layer, block_size = 16, 4, 1, 16
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        out = (F.softmax(att, dim=-1) @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(self.norm2(x))))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        x = self.norm_in(self.wte(idx) + self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)))
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model = MicroGPT()
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 1000

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
    input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]])
    targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]])
    logits = model(input_ids)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()
    if (step + 1) % 200 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Extract trained weights to NumPy for attention experiments
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training used PyTorch for convenience. The attention implementations below
# are in explicit NumPy so every memory access is visible and countable.
sd = {k: v.detach().numpy() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
P = {"wte": sd["wte.weight"], "wpe": sd["wpe.weight"], "lm_head": sd["lm_head.weight"]}
for i in range(n_layer):
    for w in ("wq", "wk", "wv", "wo"):
        P[f"l{i}.{w}"] = sd[f"layers.{i}.attn.{w}.weight"].T
    for w in ("fc1", "fc2"):
        P[f"l{i}.{w}"] = sd[f"layers.{i}.{w}.weight"].T


def softmax_np(logits):
    exps = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return exps / exps.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)


def rmsnorm_np(x):
    return x / np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-5)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three attention implementations, the core of this lab
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("\n--- comparing attention implementations ---\n")


def inference_forward(token_ids, attn_fn):
    """Forward pass using a pluggable attention function (all NumPy)."""
    n = len(token_ids)
    last_stats = {}
    x = rmsnorm_np(P["wte"][token_ids] + P["wpe"][np.arange(n)])
    for li in range(n_layer):
        x_res = x.copy()
        x_n = rmsnorm_np(x)
        Q_h, K_h, V_h = (
            (x_n @ P[f"l{li}.{w}"]).reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2) for w in ("wq", "wk", "wv")
        )
        attn_out, last_stats = attn_fn(Q_h, K_h, V_h, n)
        x = attn_out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, n_embd) @ P[f"l{li}.wo"] + x_res
        x_res = x.copy()
        x_n = rmsnorm_np(x)
        h = x_n @ P[f"l{li}.fc1"]
        x = np.maximum(h, 0) @ P[f"l{li}.fc2"] + x_res
    return x @ P["lm_head"].T, last_stats


# --- 1) Standard attention: materialize the full NxN matrix ---


def standard_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len):
    """
    Classic attention: compute the full attention matrix, write it to memory.
    On a real GPU this writes the NxN matrix to HBM (slow main memory).

    Shapes are read off Q (n_head, seq_len, head_dim) rather than the module
    globals, so the same function can be called at the model's tiny dimensions
    and at production dimensions in the scaling sweep further down.
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0}
    stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * nh * seq_len * d
    att = Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1) / math.sqrt(d)
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    causal = np.triu(np.ones((seq_len, seq_len)), k=1).astype(bool)
    att = np.where(causal, -1e9, att)
    stats["hbm_reads"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    att_probs = softmax_np(att)
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    stats["hbm_reads"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len + nh * seq_len * d
    out = att_probs @ V
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * d
    # Largest single intermediate that has to be allocated: the NxN score
    # matrix, for every head. This is the array FlashAttention refuses to build.
    stats["max_intermediate"] = att.nbytes
    return out, stats


# --- 2) Online softmax attention: never store the full NxN matrix ---


def online_softmax_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len):
    """
    Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018): compute attention row by row
    without ever materializing the full NxN attention matrix.

    This is the algorithmic *stepping stone* to FlashAttention, not an optimum.
    It fixes the memory footprint (no NxN array anywhere), but it pays for that
    by re-reading all of K and V once per query row: O(N^2 * d) element reads
    instead of standard attention's O(N^2 + N*d). At the tiny head_dim of this
    model that trade looks free; at head_dim=128 it is dramatically worse than
    standard attention. The scaling sweep below measures exactly that.

    Tiling (next function) is what turns this idea into a win: same running
    softmax, but K/V are read once per *block* of queries instead of once per
    query row.
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0}
    out = np.zeros_like(Q)

    for h in range(nh):
        for i in range(seq_len):
            q_i = Q[h, i]
            stats["hbm_reads"] += d

            running_max = -np.inf
            running_sum = 0.0
            running_out = np.zeros(d)

            for j in range(i + 1):  # causal: only attend to positions <= i
                k_j = K[h, j]
                v_j = V[h, j]
                stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * d

                score = np.dot(q_i, k_j) / math.sqrt(d)
                new_max = max(running_max, score)
                # On the first key running_max is -inf, so this is exp(-inf) = 0
                # and the accumulators start from scratch. No special case needed.
                correction = math.exp(running_max - new_max)
                running_sum = running_sum * correction + math.exp(score - new_max)
                running_out = running_out * correction + math.exp(score - new_max) * v_j
                running_max = new_max

            out[h, i] = running_out / running_sum
            stats["hbm_writes"] += d

    # Largest intermediate: a single head_dim accumulator. Nothing NxN, and
    # nothing that grows with N at all, which is the one thing this buys us.
    stats["max_intermediate"] = d * Q.itemsize
    return out, stats


# --- 3) Tiled attention (FlashAttention algorithm) ---


def tiled_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len, block_size_tile=4):
    """
    FlashAttention: tile the computation into blocks.

    Instead of processing one key at a time (online softmax) or the full
    matrix (standard), process BLOCKS of keys at once. Each block fits in
    fast on-chip memory (SRAM).
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0, "max_intermediate": 0}
    Bc = block_size_tile
    Br = block_size_tile
    out = np.zeros_like(Q)

    for h in range(nh):
        for i_start in range(0, seq_len, Br):
            i_end = min(i_start + Br, seq_len)
            Qi = Q[h, i_start:i_end]
            block_rows = i_end - i_start
            stats["hbm_reads"] += block_rows * d

            row_max = np.full(block_rows, -np.inf)
            row_sum = np.zeros(block_rows)
            row_out = np.zeros((block_rows, d))

            max_j = i_end  # causal: only attend up to current position
            for j_start in range(0, max_j, Bc):
                j_end = min(j_start + Bc, max_j)
                Kj = K[h, j_start:j_end]
                Vj = V[h, j_start:j_end]
                block_cols = j_end - j_start
                stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * block_cols * d

                scores = Qi @ Kj.T / math.sqrt(d)
                # Biggest thing this algorithm ever allocates: one Br x Bc score
                # tile (plus the Br x d output accumulator). Both are chosen to
                # fit in SRAM, and neither depends on N.
                stats["max_intermediate"] = max(stats["max_intermediate"], scores.nbytes + row_out.nbytes)

                # Apply causal mask within this block
                for bi in range(block_rows):
                    for bj in range(block_cols):
                        if (j_start + bj) > (i_start + bi):
                            scores[bi, bj] = -1e9

                # Online softmax update across blocks
                block_max = scores.max(axis=-1)
                new_max = np.maximum(row_max, block_max)
                old_correction = np.exp(row_max - new_max)
                exp_scores = np.exp(scores - new_max[:, None])

                row_sum = row_sum * old_correction + exp_scores.sum(axis=-1)
                row_out = row_out * old_correction[:, None] + exp_scores @ Vj
                row_max = new_max

            out[h, i_start:i_end] = row_out / row_sum[:, None]
            stats["hbm_writes"] += block_rows * d

    return out, stats

def tiled_ops(n, dim, tile):
    n_blocks = n // tile
    return n_blocks * 2 * tile * dim + dim * tile * n_blocks * (n_blocks + 1)

--- GPU memory hierarchy (why this matters) ---

  Level         Size        Bandwidth       What lives here
  ──────────    ────────    ────────────    ───────────────────────────
  Registers     ~few KB     fastest         Current computation
  SRAM (L1)     ~20 MB      ~19 TB/s       FlashAttention keeps Q,K,V blocks here
  HBM (VRAM)    ~80 GB      ~2 TB/s        Standard attention writes N*N matrix here
  CPU DRAM      ~TBs        ~50 GB/s        Model doesn't fit in GPU? Swap here

Standard attention writes the full N*N attention matrix to HBM, 10x slower

339.text: If the key position is after the query position, mask it out.

340.text: Replace causally invalid scores with a large negative value so softmax gives them zero weight, matching the standard attention mask.

343.text: Online softmax update across blocks, same math as Algorithm 2, but operating on entire blocks at once.

348.text: Update running sum: rescale old sum, add new block's contribution.

349.text: Update running output: rescale old output, add new weighted values. This is the block version of the online softmax accumulation.

350.text: Update the running max for the next block.

352.text: Normalize by the final sum, completes the softmax computation for this query block.

353.text: Write out the finished output block. The N x N matrix never existed, so there is nothing else to flush.

At head_dim=4 re-reading K and V costs almost nothing, so online softmax looks cheap and the ranking above is an artefact of the toy model's width. The sweep below re-runs the same counters at a realistic head_dim and the ranking changes.

"""
microGPT: Tiled attention edition.

Same architecture as the PyTorch version (03), but demonstrating three
attention implementations for inference: standard, online-softmax, and
tiled (FlashAttention algorithm). All three produce identical outputs;
the difference is how many "slow memory" (HBM) operations they need.

Training uses PyTorch; the attention implementations are in explicit NumPy
to make every memory access visible and countable.

The tiled algorithm implements the core idea from "FlashAttention: Fast and
Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness" (Dao et al., 2022),
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135. The online softmax technique used within
tiles is from "Online normalizer calculation for softmax" (Milakov &
Gimelshein, 2018), https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.02867. Also see
"FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work
Partitioning" (Dao, 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691. Note that this
is a pedagogical NumPy implementation of the algorithmic idea -- the real
FlashAttention is a fused CUDA kernel that exploits GPU SRAM directly. The
math is identical; the performance difference comes from hardware-level
memory management.
"""

import math
import os
import random

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)
torch.set_default_dtype(
    torch.float64
)  # Intentional for this standalone lab (float64 needed for numerical accuracy demos)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    urllib.request.urlretrieve(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt", input_path
    )

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
BOS, vocab_size = len(uchars), len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model (PyTorch, identical architecture to Lab 03)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd, n_head, n_layer, block_size = 16, 4, 1, 16
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        out = (F.softmax(att, dim=-1) @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(self.norm2(x))))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        x = self.norm_in(self.wte(idx) + self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)))
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
model = MicroGPT()
print(f"num params: {sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())}")
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
num_steps = 1000

for step in range(num_steps):
    doc = docs[step % len(docs)]
    tokens = [BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in doc] + [BOS]
    n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
    input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]])
    targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]])
    logits = model(input_ids)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    lr_t = 1e-2 * (1 - step / num_steps)
    for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
        pg["lr"] = lr_t
    optimizer.step()
    if (step + 1) % 200 == 0 or step == 0:
        print(f"step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps:4d} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Extract trained weights to NumPy for attention experiments
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training used PyTorch for convenience. The attention implementations below
# are in explicit NumPy so every memory access is visible and countable.
sd = {k: v.detach().numpy() for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}
P = {"wte": sd["wte.weight"], "wpe": sd["wpe.weight"], "lm_head": sd["lm_head.weight"]}
for i in range(n_layer):
    for w in ("wq", "wk", "wv", "wo"):
        P[f"l{i}.{w}"] = sd[f"layers.{i}.attn.{w}.weight"].T
    for w in ("fc1", "fc2"):
        P[f"l{i}.{w}"] = sd[f"layers.{i}.{w}.weight"].T


def softmax_np(logits):
    exps = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return exps / exps.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)


def rmsnorm_np(x):
    return x / np.sqrt(np.mean(x**2, axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-5)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three attention implementations, the core of this lab
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("\n--- comparing attention implementations ---\n")


def inference_forward(token_ids, attn_fn):
    """Forward pass using a pluggable attention function (all NumPy)."""
    n = len(token_ids)
    last_stats = {}
    x = rmsnorm_np(P["wte"][token_ids] + P["wpe"][np.arange(n)])
    for li in range(n_layer):
        x_res = x.copy()
        x_n = rmsnorm_np(x)
        Q_h, K_h, V_h = (
            (x_n @ P[f"l{li}.{w}"]).reshape(n, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 0, 2) for w in ("wq", "wk", "wv")
        )
        attn_out, last_stats = attn_fn(Q_h, K_h, V_h, n)
        x = attn_out.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, n_embd) @ P[f"l{li}.wo"] + x_res
        x_res = x.copy()
        x_n = rmsnorm_np(x)
        h = x_n @ P[f"l{li}.fc1"]
        x = np.maximum(h, 0) @ P[f"l{li}.fc2"] + x_res
    return x @ P["lm_head"].T, last_stats


# --- 1) Standard attention: materialize the full NxN matrix ---


def standard_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len):
    """
    Classic attention: compute the full attention matrix, write it to memory.
    On a real GPU this writes the NxN matrix to HBM (slow main memory).

    Shapes are read off Q (n_head, seq_len, head_dim) rather than the module
    globals, so the same function can be called at the model's tiny dimensions
    and at production dimensions in the scaling sweep further down.
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0}
    stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * nh * seq_len * d
    att = Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1) / math.sqrt(d)
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    causal = np.triu(np.ones((seq_len, seq_len)), k=1).astype(bool)
    att = np.where(causal, -1e9, att)
    stats["hbm_reads"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    att_probs = softmax_np(att)
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len
    stats["hbm_reads"] += nh * seq_len * seq_len + nh * seq_len * d
    out = att_probs @ V
    stats["hbm_writes"] += nh * seq_len * d
    # Largest single intermediate that has to be allocated: the NxN score
    # matrix, for every head. This is the array FlashAttention refuses to build.
    stats["max_intermediate"] = att.nbytes
    return out, stats


# --- 2) Online softmax attention: never store the full NxN matrix ---


def online_softmax_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len):
    """
    Online softmax (Milakov & Gimelshein, 2018): compute attention row by row
    without ever materializing the full NxN attention matrix.

    This is the algorithmic *stepping stone* to FlashAttention, not an optimum.
    It fixes the memory footprint (no NxN array anywhere), but it pays for that
    by re-reading all of K and V once per query row: O(N^2 * d) element reads
    instead of standard attention's O(N^2 + N*d). At the tiny head_dim of this
    model that trade looks free; at head_dim=128 it is dramatically worse than
    standard attention. The scaling sweep below measures exactly that.

    Tiling (next function) is what turns this idea into a win: same running
    softmax, but K/V are read once per *block* of queries instead of once per
    query row.
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0}
    out = np.zeros_like(Q)

    for h in range(nh):
        for i in range(seq_len):
            q_i = Q[h, i]
            stats["hbm_reads"] += d

            running_max = -np.inf
            running_sum = 0.0
            running_out = np.zeros(d)

            for j in range(i + 1):  # causal: only attend to positions <= i
                k_j = K[h, j]
                v_j = V[h, j]
                stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * d

                score = np.dot(q_i, k_j) / math.sqrt(d)
                new_max = max(running_max, score)
                # On the first key running_max is -inf, so this is exp(-inf) = 0
                # and the accumulators start from scratch. No special case needed.
                correction = math.exp(running_max - new_max)
                running_sum = running_sum * correction + math.exp(score - new_max)
                running_out = running_out * correction + math.exp(score - new_max) * v_j
                running_max = new_max

            out[h, i] = running_out / running_sum
            stats["hbm_writes"] += d

    # Largest intermediate: a single head_dim accumulator. Nothing NxN, and
    # nothing that grows with N at all, which is the one thing this buys us.
    stats["max_intermediate"] = d * Q.itemsize
    return out, stats


# --- 3) Tiled attention (FlashAttention algorithm) ---


def tiled_attention(Q, K, V, seq_len, block_size_tile=4):
    """
    FlashAttention: tile the computation into blocks.

    Instead of processing one key at a time (online softmax) or the full
    matrix (standard), process BLOCKS of keys at once. Each block fits in
    fast on-chip memory (SRAM).
    """
    nh, _, d = Q.shape
    stats = {"hbm_reads": 0, "hbm_writes": 0, "max_intermediate": 0}
    Bc = block_size_tile
    Br = block_size_tile
    out = np.zeros_like(Q)

    for h in range(nh):
        for i_start in range(0, seq_len, Br):
            i_end = min(i_start + Br, seq_len)
            Qi = Q[h, i_start:i_end]
            block_rows = i_end - i_start
            stats["hbm_reads"] += block_rows * d

            row_max = np.full(block_rows, -np.inf)
            row_sum = np.zeros(block_rows)
            row_out = np.zeros((block_rows, d))

            max_j = i_end  # causal: only attend up to current position
            for j_start in range(0, max_j, Bc):
                j_end = min(j_start + Bc, max_j)
                Kj = K[h, j_start:j_end]
                Vj = V[h, j_start:j_end]
                block_cols = j_end - j_start
                stats["hbm_reads"] += 2 * block_cols * d

                scores = Qi @ Kj.T / math.sqrt(d)
                # Biggest thing this algorithm ever allocates: one Br x Bc score
                # tile (plus the Br x d output accumulator). Both are chosen to
                # fit in SRAM, and neither depends on N.
                stats["max_intermediate"] = max(stats["max_intermediate"], scores.nbytes + row_out.nbytes)

                # Apply causal mask within this block
                for bi in range(block_rows):
                    for bj in range(block_cols):
                        if (j_start + bj) > (i_start + bi):
                            scores[bi, bj] = -1e9

                # Online softmax update across blocks
                block_max = scores.max(axis=-1)
                new_max = np.maximum(row_max, block_max)
                old_correction = np.exp(row_max - new_max)
                exp_scores = np.exp(scores - new_max[:, None])

                row_sum = row_sum * old_correction + exp_scores.sum(axis=-1)
                row_out = row_out * old_correction[:, None] + exp_scores @ Vj
                row_max = new_max

            out[h, i_start:i_end] = row_out / row_sum[:, None]
            stats["hbm_writes"] += block_rows * d

    return out, stats


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Compare all three on the same input
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
sample_tokens = np.array([BOS] + [uchars.index(ch) for ch in docs[0]])[:block_size]
seq_len = len(sample_tokens)

logits_std, stats_std = inference_forward(sample_tokens, standard_attention)
logits_online, stats_online = inference_forward(sample_tokens, online_softmax_attention)
logits_tiled, stats_tiled = inference_forward(sample_tokens, tiled_attention)

diffs = [
    ("online softmax", np.max(np.abs(logits_std - logits_online)), 1e-10),
    ("tiled", np.max(np.abs(logits_std - logits_tiled)), 1e-6),
]
print(f"sequence length: {seq_len}")
for label, diff, tol in diffs:
    print(f"max diff (standard vs {label + '):':<16s} {diff:.2e}")
    assert diff < tol, f"{label} diverged: {diff}"
print("All three produce identical output (within floating-point tolerance).\n")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Memory operation comparison
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("--- memory operation counts (HBM reads + writes) ---\n")

for name, stats, note in [
    ("Standard attention", stats_std, "writes N*N attention matrix to HBM, reads it back for softmax"),
    ("Online softmax", stats_online, "never stores N*N matrix, but re-reads all of K/V for every query row"),
    (
        "Tiled (FlashAttention, block_size=4)",
        stats_tiled,
        "reads K/V once per block of queries, so the K/V traffic is amortized by Bc",
    ),
]:
    r, w = stats["hbm_reads"], stats["hbm_writes"]
    print(f"{name}:\n  HBM reads: {r:>6d}  writes: {w:>6d}  total: {r + w:>6d}")
    print(f"  largest intermediate array: {stats['max_intermediate']:>6d} bytes")
    print(f"  Key insight: {note}\n")

print(
    f"Careful: this ranking is an artefact of head_dim={head_dim}. Online softmax looks\n"
    f"cheap here only because head_dim is tiny, so re-reading K/V costs almost nothing.\n"
    f"The sweep below shows what happens at a realistic head_dim.\n"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Scaling sweep: the quadratic-vs-linear story needs more than 7 tokens
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The comparison above runs on one short name (seq_len=7) at head_dim=4. That is
# far too small to show anything about scaling: at head_dim=4 the N*N score
# matrix is barely larger than the N*d inputs. Sweep N on synthetic Q/K/V at a
# realistic head_dim so the crossover is actually visible.
sweep_d = 64  # a realistic per-head dimension (the model above uses 4)
sweep_tile = 64  # a realistic FlashAttention block size (the demo above uses 4)
print(f"--- scaling sweep: synthetic Q/K/V, n_head=1, head_dim={sweep_d}, tile={sweep_tile} ---\n")


def hbm_total(stats):
    return stats["hbm_reads"] + stats["hbm_writes"]


hdr = f"  {'N':>4}  {'standard':>10}  {'online':>10}  {'tiled':>10}  {'tiled/std':>9}  {'online/std':>10}"
print(hdr)
print("  " + "-" * (len(hdr) - 2))
for N_sweep in (64, 128, 256, 512):
    Qs, Ks, Vs = (rng.standard_normal((1, N_sweep, sweep_d)) for _ in range(3))
    o_std, s_std = standard_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, N_sweep)
    o_on, s_on = online_softmax_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, N_sweep)
    o_ti, s_ti = tiled_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, N_sweep, block_size_tile=sweep_tile)
    # Same algebra at a real head_dim: all three still agree to float64 precision.
    assert np.max(np.abs(o_std - o_on)) < 1e-12, "online softmax diverged in sweep"
    assert np.max(np.abs(o_std - o_ti)) < 1e-12, "tiled diverged in sweep"
    t_std, t_on, t_ti = hbm_total(s_std), hbm_total(s_on), hbm_total(s_ti)
    print(f"  {N_sweep:>4}  {t_std:>10d}  {t_on:>10d}  {t_ti:>10d}  {t_ti / t_std:>8.2f}x  {t_on / t_std:>9.2f}x")

# The counters above are proxies for traffic. This is the thing you can actually
# run out of: the largest single array each algorithm has to hold at once.
print(f"\n  largest intermediate array actually allocated, N=512, head_dim={sweep_d}:")
Qs, Ks, Vs = (rng.standard_normal((1, 512, sweep_d)) for _ in range(3))
for label, stats in [
    ("standard: the N x N score matrix", standard_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, 512)[1]),
    ("online:   one head_dim accumulator", online_softmax_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, 512)[1]),
    (f"tiled:    one {sweep_tile}x{sweep_tile} tile + output block", tiled_attention(Qs, Ks, Vs, 512, sweep_tile)[1]),
]:
    print(f"    {label:<40s} {stats['max_intermediate']:>9,d} bytes")
print(
    "  Standard grows as N^2. The other two are set by head_dim and tile size and do\n"
    "  not grow with N at all, which is why FlashAttention can run context lengths\n"
    "  that standard attention cannot fit in memory, whatever the traffic counts say.\n"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Projection to a production shape (same counting formulas, closed form)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# These are the closed forms of the counters above, not new measurements, so the
# numbers are directly comparable with the sweep.
N, d = 2048, 128
std_ops = 4 * N * N + 4 * N * d
online_ops = 2 * N * d + d * N * (N + 1)


def tiled_ops(n, dim, tile):
    n_blocks = n // tile
    return n_blocks * 2 * tile * dim + dim * tile * n_blocks * (n_blocks + 1)


print(f"--- same counters projected to N={N}, d={d}, one head ---\n")
print(f"  standard          {std_ops:>12,d}")
print(f"  online softmax    {online_ops:>12,d}   {online_ops / std_ops:>6.1f}x MORE than standard")
for tile in (64, 256, 512):
    ops = tiled_ops(N, d, tile)
    print(f"  tiled, Bc={tile:<4d}    {ops:>12,d}   {std_ops / ops:>6.2f}x fewer than standard")
print(
    "\n  Two things to read off this table. First, online softmax is a memory-footprint\n"
    "  fix, not a memory-traffic fix: it is 30x WORSE than standard on total HBM ops at\n"
    "  d=128, because it streams all of K and V once per query row. Second, tiling's\n"
    "  advantage is tile-size dependent, so there is no single 'Nx fewer' number.\n"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# GPU memory hierarchy context
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
print("""
--- GPU memory hierarchy (why this matters) ---

  Level         Size        Bandwidth       What lives here
  ──────────    ────────    ────────────    ───────────────────────────
  Registers     ~few KB     fastest         Current computation
  SRAM (L1)     ~20 MB      ~19 TB/s       FlashAttention keeps Q,K,V blocks here
  HBM (VRAM)    ~80 GB      ~2 TB/s        Standard attention writes N*N matrix here
  CPU DRAM      ~TBs        ~50 GB/s        Model doesn't fit in GPU? Swap here

Standard attention writes the full N*N attention matrix to HBM, 10x slower
memory. FlashAttention tiles the computation so it stays in SRAM, never
materializing the full matrix. Same math, same forward-pass FLOPs, ~2-4x faster
on real hardware. (The often-quoted "FlashAttention does extra FLOPs" applies to
the BACKWARD pass, which recomputes the score tiles instead of storing them.
The forward pass implemented above does not do any extra arithmetic.)""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Inference: generate names using tiled attention
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
temperature = 0.5  # in (0, 1], control the "creativity" of generated text, low to high
print("\n--- inference (tiled attention) ---")
for sample_idx in range(20):
    generated = [BOS]
    sample = []
    for _ in range(block_size):
        logits, _ = inference_forward(np.array(generated), tiled_attention)
        logits = logits[-1] / temperature
        probs = softmax_np(logits.reshape(1, -1))[0]
        token_id = rng.choice(vocab_size, p=probs)
        if token_id == BOS:
            break
        generated.append(token_id)
        sample.append(uchars[token_id])
    print(f"sample {sample_idx + 1:2d}: {''.join(sample)}")
