Reading the total alone hides both effects.

303.text: How much the wall clock grew across the sweep, to be compared against the FLOP growth on the next line.

304.text: And how much the FLOP count grew. The two numbers are wildly different, and the gap is the amount of the short-prompt measurement that was never arithmetic in the first place.

305.text: Attention's share of prefill FLOPs at the short end, where the dense terms dominate.

306.text: And at the long end. Watching this share climb is the honest version of "prefill is compute-bound": true at production context lengths, not at the length of a name.

339.text: Controls how peaked the sampling distribution is. Lower temperature means more deterministic output; higher means more variety.

344.text: Simulated prefill cost per prompt token. Deliberately in the milliseconds: on a loaded host time.sleep() overshoots by around a millisecond, so a simulation built on 0.3 ms sleeps would measure OS scheduling noise instead of its own cost model. Only the ratios between these three constants matter.

345.text: Simulated decode cost per step, lower than prefill's per-token cost. Decode does less arithmetic per token; on real hardware it is memory-bound instead.

353.text: The one cost disaggregation adds and colocated serving never pays. In this lab the handoff is a tuple of the same tensors on a queue, with no copy at all, so without an explicit charge the simulation would report the transfer as free while the closing text says it costs a millisecond. Charge it, then print the break-even value.

357.text: A serving request: prompt, timing metadata, and generated tokens.

358.text: A numeric ID that uniquely identifies this request in the serving system.

360.text: When this request arrives in the system.

361.text: Upper limit on how many tokens to generate per request, bounding the decode phase for this simulation.

362.text: Time-to-first-token: the key latency metric for user experience.

364.text: List that collects the tokens generated for this request during the decode phase.

371.text: Each request carries its own sampling RNG. The global torch RNG is unusable here: the disaggregated arm samples from two threads, so thread interleaving decides who draws which number and the generated names changed from run to run. Per-request generators make both strategies draw the same numbers in the same order for the same request, so the text is identical by construction and only latency differs.

374.text: Create a realistic workload: mix of short prompts (fast prefill) and long prompts (slow prefill). The long prompts are the problem, they block everything in colocated serving.

377.text: Loop through the specified number of requests, creating each with a random prompt and staggered arrival time.

378.text: 30% chance of a long prompt (8-12 tokens), these are the "heavy" requests that cause head-of-line blocking.

379.text: Fill the prompt with random token IDs drawn from the vocabulary to simulate a realistic request payload.

384.text: Stagger arrivals by 0.3 ms so requests do not all appear at t=0. Head-of-line blocking needs a queue to form.

386.text: One torch.Generator per request, seeded from its id. This is the mechanism that makes the two strategies byte-identical: the seed travels with the request rather than with the worker that happens to process it.

392.text: Simulate a prefill operation: run the actual model, and sleep to stand in for GPU time.

393.text: Real forward pass to get logits and KV caches.

394.text: Sleep proportional to prompt length, longer prompts take longer to prefill.

398.text: The prefill-to-decode handoff, modelled as a delay proportional to prompt length, which is how the real thing scales, since the KV cache is per token. In production this is NVLink or RDMA; here it is the only honest way to make a zero-copy tuple pass cost something.

400.text: Sleep for the transfer, then return the charge in milliseconds so the results section can total it and compute a break-even.

404.text: Simulate a decode step: real model computation + simulated GPU time.

405.text: Real single-token forward pass with KV cache.

410.text: Sample one token, from a generator passed in rather than from the global RNG. That extra parameter is the whole fix for the cross-thread nondeterminism.

411.text: Temperature-scaled softmax, then one multinomial draw against this request's generator. Same request, same draws, whichever worker and whichever thread executes it.

421.text: Colocated serving: one worker does both prefill and decode. Requests are handled FIFO, so a long prefill blocks every request behind it.

423.text: Handle one request at a time in FIFO order: prefill its prompt, then decode all tokens before moving to the next.

424.text: Wait until the request's arrival time.

425.text: Sleep if the request hasn't arrived yet.

427.text: Prefill the prompt. If this one is long, every subsequent request waits.

428.text: Record time-to-first-token, this is terrible for requests stuck behind long prefills.

429.text: Sample the first token and start decoding. In this arm the same worker just did the prefill, so the first token lands immediately after it.

430.text: Decode loop: generate tokens one at a time.

431.text: Stop on BOS (end token) or context limit.

433.text: Append each newly generated token to this request's output list, building the name character by character.

434.text: One decode step with KV cache.

435.text: Sample the next token from this request's generator and advance the position.

442.text: Disaggregated serving: separate prefill and decode workers connected by a queue, so prefill does not block decode. The key insight is that while one worker prefills a long prompt, the other keeps decoding in-flight requests.

443.text: Thread-safe queue connects prefill worker to decode worker.

444.text: Results collection with lock for thread safety.

445.text: Signal when prefill is done; wall-clock baseline.

448.text: The prefill worker owns the wide prompt-processing phase, then hands finished KV state across the queue instead of hanging around to decode tokens itself.

450.text: Wait for each request's arrival time.

453.text: Prefill the prompt, runs independently of any ongoing decoding.

458.text: Ship the KV cache before recording the first-token time. The first token is not useful until the request can actually continue on the decode worker, so the transfer belongs inside TTFT rather than outside it.

459.text: Record time-to-first-token, which now depends only on this request's prefill rather than on the requests before it.

460.text: Push the prefilled request state onto the thread-safe queue so the decode worker can pick it up without data races.

461.text: Hand off the prefilled state over the queue: request, KV caches, first sampled token and position. This tuple is the whole interface between the two workers.

462.text: Signal that all prefills are done.

464.text: The decode worker lives on the other side of that handoff, interleaving many in-flight requests while the prefill worker keeps chewing through new prompts.

466.text: A dict mapping request id to that request's in-flight decode state. This is what continuous batching looks like structurally: many requests advance one step each per pass, rather than one request running to completion.

467.text: Keep running until prefill is done and all decodes finish.

473.text: Sample the completion flag before draining the queue. Read afterwards, prefill could append its last request and set the flag in the window between drain and check, and the loop would exit having silently dropped that request, which then makes the paired comparison misalign every row after it. A one-line reordering, and the reason the result table can be trusted.

474.text: Poll the queue for any newly prefilled requests that the prefill worker has handed off for decoding.

475.text: Drain the queue, grab all available prefilled requests.

476.text: Unpack the handoff: request, KV caches, first sampled token, position.

477.text: Admit each newly prefilled request into the active set, keyed by id, with an empty output list.

478.text: Record the drained-queue state while still holding the lock, so the exit test below reasons about a consistent snapshot rather than re-reading the queue unlocked.

479.text: If nothing active and prefill not done, briefly wait.

480.text: Exit only when prefill has finished, the queue is empty, and nothing is in flight. All three conditions, evaluated against the same snapshot.

484.text: Rebuild the active set each pass rather than mutating it while iterating. Requests that finished this step simply do not get carried over.

485.text: One decode step for every in-flight request per pass. This interleaving is what the colocated arm does not do, and it is the actual mechanism behind the latency difference.

486.text: Evaluate stopping conditions for each active request: did it generate BOS (end token) or hit the maximum length?

487.text: Request finished: record timing and results.

488.text: Acquire the results lock before writing, since the main thread reads results after both workers finish.

491.text: Continue generating: append token, decode one step, sample next.

492.text: One decode step with KV cache.

493.text: Carry the request forward with its next sampled token, again from its own generator. Which thread ran this step does not affect what was drawn.

494.text: Filter out finished requests so we only continue decoding the ones that still have tokens left to generate.

496.text: Spin up one thread for the prefill worker and one for the decode worker, which will run concurrently.

497.text: Start both workers, they run in parallel.

498.text: Launch both threads to begin parallel execution of the prefill and decode workers.

499.text: Block until both worker threads complete, ensuring all requests have finished processing before returning results.

500.text: Join the second worker thread. After this returns, all generation work is done and results are ready.

501.text: Sort by request id so the two strategies can be zipped row by row, and return the total transfer charge alongside, since it feeds the break-even calculation in the results.

505.text: Show the workload configuration: how many requests, their prompt lengths, and arrival pattern for context.

506.text: Generate the test workload of requests with mixed prompt lengths and staggered arrival times.

508.text: Label long vs short prompts, long ones are the troublemakers.

511.text: The colocated arm. There is no seed being set here on purpose: each request built its own generator in make_workload, so reproducibility travels with the request rather than depending on the order the workers happen to run in.

514.text: The disaggregated arm on a freshly built but identically seeded workload. Same per-request generators, so both arms produce the same names for the same request and the only thing that differs is when those names arrive.

515.text: Assert nothing was dropped before comparing. The termination race this guards against used to silently lose the last request, and a dropped row would shift every pair in the table below.

524.text: Count text mismatches instead of trusting that the RNG plumbing works. The claim "only latency differs" is checked, not asserted.

525.text: Compare each request between the two strategies.

526.text: Extract how many tokens were in this request's prompt for the comparison table.

527.text: TTFT speedup: how much faster was disaggregated for this request?

528.text: Decode generated tokens back to characters.

529.text: Decode the disaggregated-generated tokens back to characters for the side-by-side name comparison.

530.text: Compare the two arms' output for this request. Any difference here means the per-request generator plumbing has a hole in it.

545.text: Report the mismatch count explicitly. When this was sampling from the global RNG across two threads it was never zero, and the resulting diffs were easy to mistake for a bug in the scheduling.

546.text: And make it fatal. Per-request generators are supposed to make the two strategies produce identical text; if that ever stops being true the latency comparison is comparing two different workloads.

548.text: Average TTFT across all requests, the headline metric.

549.text: Compute the average time-to-first-token across all requests in the disaggregated strategy.

550.text: Average time-to-first-token, both arms. This is the headline metric, and the caveats printed below are what keep it from being read as more than it is.

551.text: Total wall-clock time for all requests to complete.

552.text: Compute the total wall-clock time for the disaggregated strategy to complete all requests.

553.text: Show the total completion time for both strategies side by side to quantify the end-to-end throughput difference.

557.text: Average prompt length, needed to convert a per-token transfer cost into a per-request one.

558.text: The average TTFT advantage in milliseconds, the quantity the transfer cost has to eat before disaggregation stops paying.

567.text: The mean of the cumulative prompt length — on average, how many prompt tokens are queued ahead of a request plus its own. Because the handoff runs inline on the prefill worker, that is the number of tokens whose transfer cost each request waits behind.

568.text: Break-even: the per-token transfer cost at which the whole TTFT gain is eaten. Using the mean prompt length here instead would overstate it by roughly the queue depth, because it would charge each request only for its own tokens.

569.text: The transfer bill, totalled across the workload and already included in the disaggregated TTFT above. Not a footnote about production hardware: a charge this run actually paid.

571.text: The break-even transfer cost: the per-token price at which the advantage disappears entirely. This is the number that makes the KV handoff an engineering constraint rather than a caveat in prose.

573.text: And an invitation to falsify it — raise KV_TRANSFER_COST_MS past this value and re-run. A break-even you can cross is worth more than a claim you cannot.

576.text: The caveats, printed with the result rather than left to the reader. One worker against two, a strict-FIFO baseline with no continuous batching, and sleeps standing in for GPU time — what is being demonstrated is the scheduling structure, not a benchmark.

units.title: Self-Improving Model
units.tagline: The model generates data, scores it, and retrains on its own best outputs.
units.description:
A model that improves itself through iterative self-training. Each round: generate candidate names, score them with a verifiable quality function, keep only the best, and retrain on the mix of real data plus self-generated data.

This is the core pattern behind STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner), self-rewarding language models, and Karpathy's autoresearch project. A bigram-statistics scorer acts as the verifier, making the lab fully self-contained, with no external LLM needed.

The measured result is the opposite of the folklore, which is why the lab runs three arms from identical weights and identical seeds: filtered (keep the top 20%), unfiltered (keep everything), and a real-data control. The filtered arm is the one that collapses. Quality rises by +0.3955 while the unique fraction falls from 96.0% to 46.5%, with one name accounting for 97 of 200 samples, because top-k selection is itself a distribution-narrowing operator, and at a 15% mix ratio the unfiltered arm keeps its diversity. That is Goodhart's law in 400 lines: the metric improves while the model dies, so read quality and diversity together or you will not see it happen.
learning_objectives: Implement the generate-score-filter-retrain self-improvement loop
Explain why top-k filtering is itself a distribution-narrowing operator that can drive collapse
Compare self-improved output quality against the baseline

exercises.prompt: The lab already runs the unfiltered arm (keep_fraction=1.0), and at the default 15% mix ratio it holds its diversity better than the filtered arm. Reproduce that, then predict and check what happens as you tighten KEEP_TOP_FRACTION to 0.05.
exercises.hint: Read the unique-fraction table, not the quality table: the quality column rises in the arm that collapses. Tighter filtering means a narrower kept set, so expect the filtered arm to concentrate faster. The per-round count of distinct names among the self-generated retraining slots is the earliest signal.

exercises.prompt: MIX_RATIO is 0.15, not 30%. Raise it to 0.5 and then to 1.0 and watch which arm collapses at each setting. At what mix ratio does the unfiltered arm become the dangerous one, as the folklore expects?
exercises.hint: MIX_RATIO decides how many of the 300 retraining steps see a self-generated name, 45 of 300 by default. At 0.15 the filtered arm is the one that concentrates, because selection deliberately throws away the tails. As the ratio rises, the unfiltered arm's own errors get enough weight to dominate. Compare the unique-fraction column across all three arms, not the quality column.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: Self-improving model edition.

A tiny character-level GPT that iteratively improves itself by generating
candidate outputs, scoring them with a verifiable quality function, and
retraining on its own best generations alongside the original data.

This implements a simplified form of filtered self-training, closest in spirit
to "STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning" (Zelikman et al., 2022,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465), which keeps only verified-correct
self-generated rationales. Karpathy's autoresearch project
(https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch) applies the same
generate-evaluate-keep loop to hyperparameter optimization. Broader related
work includes "Self-Rewarding Language Models" (Yuan et al., 2024,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020), which uses a learned self-judge rather
than a fixed scorer, and "SPIN" (Chen et al., 2024,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335), which uses distribution-matching self-play.

This lab uses a fixed handcrafted scorer (bigram statistics) as the verifier,
which is simpler than the learned judges in Self-Rewarding LMs or the
distribution-matching in SPIN. No external LLM is needed. The verifier is
built from a held-out split of the corpus, so it scores names the model has
never trained on.

The interesting result here is a failure, and the lab is built to show it.
The loop runs three arms from identical starting weights and identical seeds:
filtered (keep the top 20%), unfiltered (keep everything), and a control that
retrains on real data only with the same step budget. Every round prints the
quality score AND two things the quality score cannot see: the fraction of
unique names and the most-repeated name with its count. Watch the quality
metric rise while diversity falls. That is Goodhart's law, on screen, in a
loop small enough to read in one sitting.
"""

import copy
import itertools
import math
import os
import random
from collections import Counter

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
char_to_id = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(uchars)}
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Held-out split: the verifier must not read the model's training data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The original version of this lab built the bigram verifier from the same
# corpus the model trained on, so a high "quality" score could simply mean the
# model had memorized the training set. Splitting the corpus fixes that: the
# model only ever sees train_docs, the verifier only ever sees heldout_docs.
# A generated name now has to look like names the verifier has seen and the
# model has not.
HELDOUT_SIZE = 3000
heldout_docs = docs[:HELDOUT_SIZE]
train_docs = docs[HELDOUT_SIZE:]
train_set = set(train_docs)  # used to measure novelty (is the name actually new?)
print(f"train docs: {len(train_docs)}, held-out docs (verifier only): {len(heldout_docs)}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Quality scorer: the "verifier" that decides which self-generations to keep
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We build a bigram model from real names the model never trains on (the
# held-out split). This serves as a ground-truth quality signal: generated
# names that match real-name statistics score higher. In STaR, the verifier
# checks logical correctness; here it checks "does this look like a real name?"
#
# Important limitation to keep in mind while reading the results: this verifier
# scores each name in isolation. It has no opinion about the *distribution* of
# names, so a model that emits one very high-scoring name over and over gets a
# great score. Phase 2 measures exactly that failure.


def build_bigram_scorer(names):
    """Build a log-probability scorer from bigram statistics of real names."""
    counts = {}
    for name in names:
        seq = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in name] + [BOS]
        for a, b in itertools.pairwise(seq):
            counts[(a, b)] = counts.get((a, b), 0) + 1
    # Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing: P(b|a) = (count(a,b) + 1) / (count(a) + V)
    total_per_context = {}
    for (a, _), c in counts.items():
        total_per_context[a] = total_per_context.get(a, 0) + c
    log_probs = {}
    for (a, b), c in counts.items():
        log_probs[(a, b)] = math.log((c + 1) / (total_per_context[a] + vocab_size))
    # Default for unseen bigrams: use per-context denominator when available
    default_lp_per_context = {a: math.log(1 / (t + vocab_size)) for a, t in total_per_context.items()}
    # Fallback for completely unseen contexts
    default_lp_unknown = math.log(1 / vocab_size)
    return log_probs, default_lp_per_context, default_lp_unknown


def score_name(name, log_probs, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk):
    """Score a generated name by average bigram log-probability with length penalty."""
    if len(name) < 3 or len(name) > 15:
        return -10.0  # reject too-short or too-long names
    seq = [BOS] + [char_to_id.get(ch, 0) for ch in name if ch in char_to_id] + [BOS]
    total = 0.0
    for a, b in itertools.pairwise(seq):
        total += log_probs.get((a, b), default_lp_ctx.get(a, default_lp_unk))
    # A sequence of N tokens contains N-1 bigrams, so that is what we average
    # over. Dividing by len(seq) (the token count) would quietly shrink every
    # score toward zero, more so for short names.
    avg_lp = total / (len(seq) - 1)
    # Penalize names far from the typical length (mean ~6 chars in the dataset)
    length_penalty = -0.1 * abs(len(name) - 6)
    return avg_lp + length_penalty


bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk = build_bigram_scorer(heldout_docs)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model (same architecture as lab 03)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 32
n_head = 4
n_layer = 1
block_size = 16
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training and generation helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
temperature = 0.5


def train_on_data(model, data, num_steps, base_lr=1e-2, verbose=True):
    """Train the model on a list of name strings."""
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=base_lr, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
    total_loss = 0
    for step in range(num_steps):
        doc = data[step % len(data)]
        tokens = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
        input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device)
        targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)
        logits = model(input_ids)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        lr_t = base_lr * (1 - step / num_steps)
        for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
            pg["lr"] = lr_t
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
        if verbose and ((step + 1) % 200 == 0 or step == 0):
            print(f"  step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")
    return total_loss / num_steps


@torch.no_grad()
def generate_names(model, n_samples=100):
    """Generate n_samples names from the model."""
    model.eval()
    names = []
    for _ in range(n_samples):
        tokens = [BOS]
        for _ in range(block_size):
            idx = torch.tensor([tokens[-block_size:]], device=device)
            logits = model(idx)
            logits = logits[0, -1] / temperature
            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
            token_id = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        name = "".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:])
        if name:
            names.append(name)
    model.train()
    return names


def evaluate_quality(names):
    """Compute average quality score for a list of names."""
    scores = [score_name(n, bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk) for n in names]
    return sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else -10.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The metrics the quality score cannot see
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Average quality is a per-name statistic, so it is blind to two failure modes
# that matter more than the score itself:
#   diversity: a collapsed model emits the same high-scoring string forever
#   novelty:   a model can score well by parroting its training corpus
# Both are one line of Python each. Printing them next to the quality score is
# the difference between "the loop worked" and "the loop found a shortcut".


def diversity_stats(names):
    """Return (unique fraction, most-repeated name, its count)."""
    if not names:
        return 0.0, "", 0
    counts = Counter(names)
    top_name, top_count = counts.most_common(1)[0]
    return len(counts) / len(names), top_name, top_count


def novelty(names):
    """Fraction of generated names that do not appear verbatim in the training corpus."""
    if not names:
        return 0.0
    return sum(1 for n in names if n not in train_set) / len(names)

NUM_ROUNDS = 6
SAMPLES_PER_ROUND = 300
KEEP_TOP_FRACTION = 0.2  # filtered arm: keep the top 20% of self-generated names
RETRAIN_STEPS = 300
MIX_RATIO = 0.15  # 15% self-generated, 85% real data in retraining


def run_arm(keep_fraction, mix_ratio, label):
    """
    Run the generate -> score -> filter -> retrain loop for NUM_ROUNDS and
    measure quality, diversity and novelty after every round.

    Three settings of the two knobs give us three arms of one experiment:
      keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.15 -> the filtered loop this lab teaches
      keep_fraction=1.0, mix_ratio=0.15 -> the naive loop (keep everything)
      keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.0  -> control: real data only, same budget
    The control matters. Without it, we cannot tell whether the self-generated
    data helped or whether 1800 extra training steps would have done the same.
    """
    # Same seeds and the same starting weights for every arm, so the arms
    # differ only in what data they retrain on.
    random.seed(4242)
    torch.manual_seed(4242)
    arm_model = MicroGPT().to(device)
    arm_model.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(initial_state))

    stats = []
    for round_idx in range(NUM_ROUNDS):
        # Step 1: Generate candidates
        candidates = generate_names(arm_model, SAMPLES_PER_ROUND)

        # Step 2: Score and filter, keeping the best `keep_fraction` of them
        scored = [(name, score_name(name, bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk)) for name in candidates]
        scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
        n_keep = max(1, int(len(scored) * keep_fraction))
        kept = [name for name, _ in scored[:n_keep]]
        all_quality = evaluate_quality(candidates)

        # Step 3: Mix self-generated data with real data for retraining.
        # mix_ratio sets how many retraining steps see a self-generated name
        # (45 of 300 with the defaults), and that is usually fewer than the
        # number of names we kept (60). So we sample the self-generated slots
        # uniformly from the whole kept set. Walking `kept` in score order
        # instead would silently use only the top 15% and discard the rest.
        n_self = int(RETRAIN_STEPS * mix_ratio)
        if n_self <= len(kept):
            self_slots = random.sample(kept, n_self)
        else:
            # More slots than kept names: reuse them, so a few names influence
            # many steps. This is what happens if you raise MIX_RATIO.
            self_slots = [random.choice(kept) for _ in range(n_self)]
        mixed_data = self_slots + [random.choice(train_docs) for _ in range(RETRAIN_STEPS - n_self)]
        random.shuffle(mixed_data)

        # Step 4: Retrain on mixed data
        avg_loss = train_on_data(arm_model, mixed_data, RETRAIN_STEPS, base_lr=5e-3, verbose=False)

        # Step 5: Evaluate quality, plus the two things quality cannot see
        post_names = generate_names(arm_model, EVAL_SAMPLES)
        post_quality = evaluate_quality(post_names)
        unique_frac, top_name, top_count = diversity_stats(post_names)
        novel_frac = novelty(post_names)

        stats.append(
            {
                "round": round_idx + 1,
                "candidates": len(candidates),
                "kept": n_keep,
                "slots": n_self,
                "distinct_fed": len(set(self_slots)),
                "all_quality": all_quality,
                "post_quality": post_quality,
                "unique": unique_frac,
                "top_name": top_name,
                "top_count": top_count,
                "novel": novel_frac,
                "avg_loss": avg_loss,
            }
        )

        # The "slots" figure is how many of the RETRAIN_STEPS steps see a
        # self-generated name, and "distinct" is how many different names those
        # slots contain. When the kept set itself fills up with copies of one
        # high-scoring name, "distinct" drops even though "slots" does not.
        print(
            f"  {label} round {round_idx + 1}: "
            f"kept {n_keep:3d}/{len(candidates)}, self slots {n_self:3d} ({len(set(self_slots)):2d} distinct), "
            f"quality {all_quality:.4f} -> {post_quality:.4f}, "
            f"unique {unique_frac:5.1%}, top '{top_name}' x{top_count:<3d} "
            f"novel {novel_frac:5.1%}, loss {avg_loss:.4f}"
        )

    return arm_model, stats

print(f"""
The filtered loop moved the quality metric by {total_improvement:+.4f} and the
unique fraction by {final_unique - baseline_unique:+.1%} ({baseline_unique:.1%} -> {final_unique:.1%}).
One name, '{final_top_name}', accounts for {final_top_count} of {EVAL_SAMPLES} samples ({top_share:.1%}).

That is Goodhart's law in 400 lines: the metric can improve while the model
dies. The verifier scores names one at a time, so a model that discovers a
single high-scoring string and emits it over and over gets a better average
score than a model that produces many plausible different names. The loop
optimized what we measured, and we measured the wrong thing.

Note which arm ended up least diverse in this run: {least_diverse}. The
folklore says the UNFILTERED loop is the dangerous one, and at large mix ratios
it is. But filtering is itself a distribution-narrowing operation: taking the
top {KEEP_TOP_FRACTION:.0%} by a per-name score deliberately throws away the tails, so with
only {MIX_RATIO:.0%} of the retraining stream coming from the model, the filtered arm is the
one that concentrates. Selection pressure toward a narrow optimum is not a bug
in the filter, it is what the filter does.

The control arm (real data only, same seeds, same step budget) reached
{control_quality:.4f} vs the filtered arm's {final_quality:.4f}, so the
self-generated data is doing real work on the metric, and the problem is not that
the loop does nothing, it is that the metric it improves is incomplete.

The per-round quality trajectory is also not monotonic. Do not expect a clean
staircase: each round retrains on a fresh random sample, and the loop has no
revert-on-regression rule, so rounds can and do go backwards.

Fixes that would make this loop trustworthy, none of them implemented here:
  - score the distribution, not just each name (penalize repeats)
  - deduplicate the kept set before retraining
  - keep a diversity floor as a hard constraint, not a hope
  - revert a round when any tracked metric regresses
""")
