print(f"""
{"=" * 60}
HOW SELF-IMPROVEMENT WORKS
{"=" * 60}

The self-improvement loop has four steps per round:

  1. GENERATE: Model produces {SAMPLES_PER_ROUND} candidate names
  2. SCORE:    Bigram quality function + length penalty rates each candidate
     (the verifier is built from {len(heldout_docs)} held-out names the model never trains on)
  3. FILTER:   Keep only the top {KEEP_TOP_FRACTION:.0%} (verified good outputs)
  4. RETRAIN:  Mix {MIX_RATIO:.0%} self-generated + {1 - MIX_RATIO:.0%} real data, train {RETRAIN_STEPS} steps

Keeping only VERIFIED good outputs reduces the risk of collapse. Naive
self-training (keeping all outputs) lets the model amplify its own errors.
The quality filter mitigates this, though it does not fully prevent mode
collapse, and the numbers above show it did not prevent it here either.
Diversity controls, quality thresholds, and revert-on-regression would
strengthen the loop further.

Measured in this run:
  filtered    quality {final_quality:.4f}, unique {final_unique:.1%}
  unfiltered  quality {unfiltered_quality:.4f}, unique {unfiltered_unique:.1%}
  control     quality {control_quality:.4f}, unique {control_unique:.1%}

Do not memorize the ordering of those three numbers: it depends on the seed,
the scorer, and how many rounds you run. Memorize the habit of printing all
three columns, because "quality went up" on its own cannot tell you whether
the loop learned or narrowed.

This is a simplified version of the pattern behind:
  - STaR: keep self-generated rationales only if the answer is correct
  - Karpathy's autoresearch: keep code changes only if loss improves
  - Self-Rewarding LMs use a learned judge (not a fixed scorer like here)
  - SPIN uses distribution-matching self-play (a different mechanism)
""")

2.text: The title marks this as a self-improvement lab: the base model architecture stays familiar, but the training loop starts consuming its own filtered outputs.

4.text: The core idea: the model generates outputs, scores them for quality, keeps only the best, and retrains on those. This is the generate-evaluate-retrain loop.

5.text: Verification is explicit here. The model does not automatically trust its own samples; each candidate must pass an external quality check first.

6.text: Retraining mixes accepted self-generated names back with the original corpus so the loop can improve without fully drifting off-distribution.

8.text: Filtered self-training is the central mechanism: generate candidates, verify them, then feed only the survivors back into training.

9.text: STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner) showed that keeping only verified-correct self-generations prevents the model from amplifying its own mistakes.

10.text: STaR is the closest ancestor here because its core safeguard is exactly the same one this lab uses: keep only verified-good self-generated data.

11.text: Karpathy’s autoresearch is relevant because it uses the same keep-or-discard feedback loop, just over code and hyperparameters instead of text samples.

14.text: Self-Rewarding LMs extend the idea: the model itself acts as both generator and judge, creating a self-reinforcing improvement cycle.

19.text: The verifier is handcrafted rather than learned, which keeps the self-improvement loop transparent enough to inspect line by line.

20.text: That simplification matters pedagogically: the verifier here is cheap, explicit, and stable enough to understand without adding another model.

22.text: A fixed handcrafted scorer keeps the lab self-contained, with no external LLM and no learned judge to debug, and it is built from a held-out split, so a high score cannot just mean the model memorized its own training set.

25.text: The result this lab is built around is a failure, and it is the filtered arm that fails. Read the diversity column next to the quality column throughout: the metric improves while the model dies.

37.text: Math is only needed for the verifier. The model itself is standard PyTorch; the self-improvement novelty lives in the scoring loop.

38.text: The lab still uses the shared local dataset so the verifier and the model judge the same distribution.

42.text: PyTorch handles the model and optimizer. The interesting part is how its outputs get recycled back into training.

43.text: Module definitions let this lab reuse the same small GPT skeleton as the earlier PyTorch labs.

44.text: Functional helpers like softmax and cross-entropy stay in `F`, keeping the training loop compact.

46.text: Fixing both RNGs is important because the whole point is to compare the model before and after self-improvement under repeatable sampling.

47.text: Fixed seeds ensure reproducibility so you can compare results across runs and verify the self-improvement trend is real.

52.text: Resolve the shared corpus path relative to this lab so the script can run from its own directory.

53.text: If the dataset is missing, fetch it once. That keeps the lab self-contained without bundling a large text file.

56.text: The verifier should be grounded in real data, so the downloaded corpus is the same names dataset used everywhere else in the series.

59.text: The training corpus is still the anchor dataset. Self-improvement starts from real examples rather than replacing them.

60.text: Shuffle before the split, not after. The held-out slice is taken off the front of this list, so an unshuffled corpus would hand the verifier an alphabetical prefix and the model everything else.

63.text: Build the vocabulary once from the real corpus so both training and verification speak the same token language.

64.text: Building the character vocabulary from the actual data. The sorted set ensures a deterministic mapping from characters to token IDs.

65.text: The BOS token doubles as both start and stop marker, which keeps sampling and scoring aligned on where names begin and end.

66.text: BOS (beginning/end of sequence) token is placed after all real characters. It signals where names start and end during generation.

78.text: 3000 names withheld from training, reserved for the verifier alone. The earlier version of this lab built the verifier from the same corpus the model trained on, which meant a rising "quality" score could simply mean the model had memorized the training set.

79.text: The verifier's corpus. The model never sees these names, so scoring well on them requires generalizing rather than reciting.

80.text: The model's corpus. The split is the only thing that makes the quality number mean anything: a generated name now has to look like names the verifier has seen and the model has not.

81.text: A set of the training names, so novelty can be checked in O(1) per generated name. Without this the loop could score beautifully by parroting its own training data back.

86.text: This section builds the verifier. The model will not trust its own generations blindly; every candidate has to clear this external score.

87.text: The verifier, and a deliberately simple stand-in for a judge model: bigram statistics of real names the model never trains on. In STaR the verifier checks logical correctness; here it checks the narrower question "does this look like a real name?", which is answerable exactly and cheaply.

92.text: The limitation that ends up dominating the whole experiment: this verifier scores each name in isolation. It has no opinion about the distribution of names, so a model that emits one very high-scoring string forever earns a great average score. Everything the loop does downstream is a consequence of this one blind spot.

98.text: This function is the external judge. It compresses the real-name distribution into a cheap statistical model that can score every generated sample.

99.text: Docstring: build a log-probability scorer from bigram statistics. It is called with heldout_docs, never the training split, so the character pairs it learns come from names the model has never been shown.

100.text: Counts store how often each ordered character pair appears in the real dataset. That becomes the backbone of the quality score.

101.text: Iterate over real names only. The verifier must be anchored in genuine data before any self-generated samples enter the loop.

102.text: Wrap each name with BOS on both sides so the scorer learns realistic starts and stops, not just interior letter transitions.

103.text: Walk the name as overlapping character pairs. itertools.pairwise yields (a,b), (b,c), (c,d) and so on, and these adjacent pairs are the bigrams whose counts become the verifier.

104.text: Counting all adjacent character pairs (bigrams). These counts form the basis of the quality scorer.

105.text: Laplace smoothing ensures the verifier can still assign a finite score to rare or unseen bigrams instead of collapsing to negative infinity.

106.text: Collapse pair counts down to per-context totals so each transition can be normalized into a conditional probability.

107.text: Summing counts per context character to compute conditional probabilities: P(next_char | current_char).

108.text: Aggregate counts by left context so each bigram can later be normalized into a conditional probability.

109.text: Store verifier scores in log-space because self-generated names may be long enough for raw probability products to underflow.

110.text: Convert raw counts into log-probabilities so long sequences can be scored without underflow.

111.text: This is the smoothed conditional probability `P(next | current)` for every bigram actually seen in the real corpus.

112.text: Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing prevents zero probabilities for unseen bigrams. Log-space avoids floating-point underflow when multiplying many small probabilities.

113.text: Per-context fallback probabilities let the scorer degrade gracefully when a start character is known but a specific transition was never observed.

114.text: Keep a fallback for contexts that exist but whose particular continuation never appeared in the data.

116.text: The scorer returns both explicit seen-transition log-probs and fallbacks, which is what makes it usable as a robust filter instead of a brittle lookup table.

119.text: The scoring function is the heart of the self-improvement loop -- it decides which generated names are 'good enough' to retrain on.

121.text: The one hard constraint in the scorer. Everything else here is a smooth preference, but a name outside 3 to 15 characters is rejected outright rather than scored, which is why a degenerate one-character string cannot win on a flattering per-bigram average.

122.text: A fixed floor, far below anything the bigram term produces for a plausible name, so a rejected candidate sorts to the bottom and the top-fraction filter can never select it. The same value is the fallback in evaluate_quality when a batch is empty.

123.text: Unknown characters are dropped before scoring so the verifier judges only over the vocabulary it actually knows how to score.

124.text: Accumulate bigram scores across the whole name. Better names are the ones whose local transitions keep matching the real corpus.

125.text: Walk the name as overlapping character pairs. itertools.pairwise yields (a,b), (b,c), (c,d) and so on, and these adjacent pairs are the bigrams whose counts become the verifier.

126.text: Sum of bigram log-probabilities measures how well the generated name matches the statistical patterns of real names.

130.text: A sequence of N tokens contains N-1 bigrams, so that is what we average over. Dividing by the token count instead would quietly shrink every score toward zero, and shrink short names most, a length bias hiding inside the normalizer.

131.text: Length penalty keeps the filter from rewarding degenerate very short or very long strings that happen to get decent local bigram scores.

132.text: A soft preference for the dataset's typical length (about 6 characters), which stops the filter rewarding degenerate very short or very long strings that happen to score well per bigram.

133.text: Final score = language-model plausibility plus a soft preference for the dataset’s typical length.

136.text: Build the verifier once, from the held-out split, before any training happens. Fixed for the whole run: a moving scorer would make the round-over-round quality numbers incomparable, and a scorer fitted on the model's own training data would make them meaningless.

138.text: From here on the code is a plain small GPT. The lab's novelty lies in what happens after generation.

141.text: Use a slightly wider embedding than the earlier toy models so the self-improvement loop has enough capacity to move.

142.text: Four heads keep the attention shape conventional and make the comparison to the PyTorch baseline easier.

143.text: One transformer block is enough here because the experiment is about the data loop, not model scale.

144.text: The context window stays tiny because names are short. That keeps repeated retraining rounds cheap.

145.text: Head width is derived from the chosen embedding size and head count, just like the earlier transformer labs.

148.text: RMSNorm stays identical to the earlier labs so the reader is not juggling a second architectural change.

157.text: Attention also stays standard causal self-attention. The self-improvement experiment should isolate the training-data feedback loop.

167.text: Queries are split into attention heads here, but unlike the verifier logic this is just the standard transformer machinery reused from earlier labs.

170.text: Scale attention scores by head width just as in the baseline transformer; otherwise the logits would get too sharp.

178.text: The MLP block is unchanged. Again, the point is to keep the core model familiar while the outer loop changes.

188.text: Each transformer block is residual attention plus residual MLP, same template as the earlier autoregressive labs.

197.text: Residual connections are unchanged. The model backbone stays conventional so the experiment isolates the effect of the outer self-improvement loop.

202.text: The top-level model is intentionally boring here. That makes it easier to attribute changes in output quality to the self-improvement loop itself.

205.text: Token embeddings map integer ids into vectors. These are the same embeddings later sampled through autoregressive generation.

206.text: Position embeddings keep order information explicit so the model can tell early letters from later ones.

207.text: Normalize the summed token and position embeddings before they enter the transformer stack.

213.text: All linear layers and embeddings get the same small Gaussian init so the loop starts from a stable baseline.

217.text: Forward is standard next-token prediction: embed, add position, run the transformer, project back to vocabulary logits.

218.text: The batch and sequence dimensions are unpacked for readability. This lab never hides tensor shapes from the reader.

220.text: Position ids are generated on the fly from sequence length, just like in the earlier PyTorch labs.

230.text: Everything runs on CPU. The model is small enough that the cost of this lab is the number of generate-score-retrain rounds, not the arithmetic inside any one of them.

231.text: Temperature 0.5 for every generation call in the loop. It stays fixed across arms and rounds, so any change in output diversity is the model's doing rather than the sampler's.

234.text: This helper trains the model on any list of strings -- real data, self-generated data, or a mix. The flexibility is key for the self-improvement loop.

236.text: Each retraining phase creates a fresh optimizer, so self-improvement is happening through new data exposure rather than optimizer-state carryover.

237.text: Track average loss over the mini-run so each phase can report a comparable training signal.

239.text: Cycling through the training docs with modulo ensures every sample gets used even if num_steps exceeds the dataset size.

240.text: Teacher forcing stays unchanged. The self-improvement idea lives entirely in how the training examples are chosen, not in a different objective.

241.text: Clip the example to the context window, leaving one token over for the shifted target. Names are short so this rarely bites, but it is what stops a long name indexing past the position embedding table.

242.text: Pack one short name into a batch of size 1. The lab stays simple on batching so the outer generate-filter-retrain logic remains easy to follow.

244.text: One forward pass produces next-token logits at every position at once. That is what makes teacher forcing cheap: a name of n tokens yields n training signals from a single pass.

245.text: Cross-entropy is still the learning signal. What changes across rounds is the curation of the data feeding into that same loss.

248.text: Linear decay remains in place during retraining so later self-improvement rounds make smaller, more conservative parameter updates.

249.text: Write the decayed rate into every parameter group so the optimizer picks it up on this step.

254.text: Periodic loss prints let you see whether each retraining phase is still learning from the mixed data rather than destabilizing.

255.text: Returning average loss lets us track whether the model is actually learning from the mixed data in each self-improvement round.

258.text: No gradients anywhere in generation. Candidates are treated as data, not as a differentiable path back into the model, which is exactly what separates this loop from ordinary training.

259.text: Generation is kept separate from training because the model alternates between acting as a teacher and acting as a student.

264.text: Each name starts from the BOS token, just like during training. The model then predicts characters one at a time.

265.text: Generation is capped at block size so the model proposes full candidate names but cannot wander into arbitrarily long degenerate strings.

266.text: Only the most recent context window is fed back in. The generation routine is standard autoregressive sampling.

268.text: Temperature scaling controls randomness: dividing logits by temperature < 1 sharpens the distribution, making high-probability characters more likely.

270.text: Sampling rather than argmax keeps candidate diversity high enough for filtering to matter.

274.text: Convert token IDs back to characters, skipping the initial BOS. This is the raw generated name that will be scored.

275.text: Drop empty strings. A sample whose very first token is BOS decodes to nothing, and letting those through would pad the candidate pool with names that score the rejection floor by definition.

277.text: Put the model back in training mode before returning, since the same object goes straight into train_on_data for the next round.

281.text: Aggregate quality is the loop-level metric. The lab judges improvement by whether batches of sampled names look more like the real corpus over time.

284.text: Average score across all names gives one number to compare: baseline quality vs. post-self-improvement quality.

298.text: Diversity, in three lines. Average quality is a per-name statistic and cannot see repetition at all, so the unique fraction and the most-repeated name are printed alongside it every round.

304.text: Return the unique fraction plus the single most-repeated name and its count. The count is what makes collapse legible: "46% unique" is abstract, "one name 97 times out of 200" is not.

307.text: Novelty: the other thing quality cannot see. A model can score well by reciting its training corpus verbatim, which is memorization dressed up as improvement.

311.text: One line, using the training-set membership check built earlier. Cheap enough that there is no excuse for not printing it every round.

321.text: Train one ordinary supervised model first. Self-improvement should start from a competent baseline, not random noise.

324.text: The initial fit, longer than any single retraining round below. Every arm starts from the weights this produces, so the loop is only ever asked to improve a model that already works.

325.text: Phase 1 trains on real data only. This gives the model a reasonable starting point before self-improvement begins.

335.text: A baseline sample taken before any self-improvement, so every later round has something to be compared against on all three metrics, quality, diversity and novelty, rather than only the first.

336.text: Baseline quality is the number to beat. If self-improvement works, post-loop quality should be measurably higher than this.

348.text: Phase 2 is the actual experiment: three arms from identical weights and identical seeds, differing only in what data they retrain on. The aim is to show what the quality metric hides while it rises, which takes more than showing the loop working.

351.text: Six rounds. Enough for a trend to appear, few enough that the whole three-arm experiment runs in about a minute.

352.text: 300 candidates per round: enough for a top-20% filter to have real selection pressure, cheap enough to re-run.

353.text: The filtered arm keeps the top 20% by verifier score. Read that as what it is: a distribution-narrowing operator. Top-k selection deliberately throws away the tails, and in this run it is the filtered arm that collapses while the unfiltered arm holds its diversity, the opposite of the folklore.

354.text: Retraining is intentionally short and local. The lab is modeling iterative improvement, not a full second training run.

355.text: 15% of retraining steps see a self-generated name and the rest stay real. That real-data majority is why the naive arm survives here, and at higher mix ratios the unfiltered loop does become the dangerous one. Which arm collapses is a function of this knob rather than a law.

358.text: One function, three arms. keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.15 is the filtered loop this lab teaches; 1.0, 0.15 is the naive loop that keeps everything; 0.2, 0.0 is the control that retrains on real data only at the same step budget. The control is what makes the other two interpretable, since without it there is no way to tell whether the self-generated data helped or whether 1800 extra training steps would have done the same.

372.text: Reseed to the same value at the top of every arm, and load the same snapshot weights below. The arms have to differ in exactly one thing or the comparison is worthless.

378.text: One round: generate, score, filter, mix, retrain, measure. Six of these per arm, with quality, diversity and novelty recorded after every one so the trajectory is visible rather than just the endpoint.

379.text: Step 1, self-play: ask the current model for fresh data. From round 2 onward it is sampling from a distribution its own earlier output helped shape.

380.text: Generate the round's candidates from the arm's current weights. Nothing external is consulted; this is the model's own opinion of what a name looks like.

382.text: Step 2: score every candidate with the verifier. This explicit score table is the only thing separating filtered self-training from naive bootstrapping.

383.text: Every candidate is paired with a verifier score before any retraining happens. This explicit score table is what separates filtered self-training from naive bootstrapping.

384.text: Sort best-to-worst so the kept set is literally the top slice under the verifier.

385.text: The keep fraction turns a scored list into a hard selection boundary. max(1, ...) guarantees at least one survivor even if the fraction rounds down to zero.

386.text: The kept set: the top slice under the verifier. In the unfiltered arm keep_fraction is 1.0 and this is simply the whole candidate list, which is the entire difference between arms 1 and 2.

387.text: Score the full candidate pool, not just the kept slice. This is the honest read on what the model currently generates; measuring only the kept names would report the filter's selectivity as if it were the model's quality.

389.text: Step 3: build the retraining stream. The subtlety is that the number of self-generated slots (45 of 300 with the defaults) is usually fewer than the number of names kept (60), so which of the kept names actually get used is a real choice, not a formality.

395.text: How many of the retraining steps see a self-generated name. Everything about how self-referential the loop becomes is set by this one number.

396.text: The normal case: fewer slots than kept names.

397.text: random.sample draws the slots uniformly and without replacement from the whole kept set. Walking kept in score order instead would silently use only the top 15% of candidates and discard the rest, a second invisible filter stacked on top of the intended one.

401.text: The other branch, reached only by raising MIX_RATIO: more slots than kept names, so a few names get repeated across many steps. Watch the "distinct" count in the per-round printout to see how much amplification is actually happening.

402.text: The remaining steps sample uniformly from the real corpus. That anchor is what keeps the model from drifting off the real distribution entirely, and it is also why the control arm exists: real data alone, same budget.

403.text: Shuffle the mixed stream so real and self-generated examples are interleaved; otherwise the model would see a blocky curriculum each round.

406.text: Step 4: retrain, deliberately shorter and at a lower learning rate than the initial fit. Each round is meant to nudge the model, not to overwrite it.

409.text: Step 5: resample after retraining. This is the only measurement that closes the loop, since everything before it describes the data rather than the model.

410.text: The quality score, which is the number that goes up.

411.text: The unique fraction and the most-repeated name, which is the number that goes down. Printing these two lines next to each other is the whole lesson of the lab.

412.text: And novelty, which catches the other failure: scoring well by reproducing training names verbatim.

414.text: Persist every round's numbers so the loop can be read as a trajectory rather than a before-and-after pair. A non-monotonic trajectory is itself information here.

420.text: How many distinct names ended up in the self-generated slots. When the kept set itself fills with copies of one high-scoring string this collapses even though the slot count does not, which is collapse caught one step upstream of the output.

421.text: Store the pre-retraining candidate quality alongside the post-retraining score, so each round shows both ends of itself and a round that went backwards is visible as such.

435.text: The per-round line carries all of it at once: how selective the filter was, how much variety survived into the retraining stream, quality before and after, unique fraction, the most-repeated name with its count, and novelty. Any one of those columns alone tells a misleading story.

449.text: Arm 1, the filtered loop, the one this lab is nominally teaching and the one that turns out to collapse.

452.text: Arm 2, the naive loop that keeps every generation. Folklore says this is the dangerous one; at this mix ratio it is the arm that keeps its diversity.

455.text: Arm 3, the control: real data only, same seeds, same step budget. Without it, "quality improved" cannot be distinguished from "we trained for another 1800 steps".

462.text: The filtered arm's audit trail, printed in full before the three arms are compared. The per-round table is where the divergence between quality and diversity is easiest to see.

465.text: Kept count, candidate quality, post-retraining quality, delta against baseline, unique fraction, most-repeated name, novelty. Seven columns because six of them are needed to stop the seventh from lying.

473.text: One row per round. Read left to right: the quality columns improve while the unique column falls and one name's count climbs.

483.text: The last round's score as the headline, since the question is where the loop ended up, not how good its best round looked.

487.text: Final quality and final unique fraction on the same line, deliberately. Reporting the first without the second is exactly the mistake the lab is about.

488.text: Total improvement next to the change in unique fraction. Both signs matter: the metric went up and the diversity went down, in the same run, from the same cause.

496.text: Quality per round for all three arms side by side. The filtered arm leads this table, which is precisely why it needs the next one.

503.text: The same table for the unique fraction, and the one that inverts the conclusion: the filtered arm's diversity falls round after round while the unfiltered and control arms hold roughly steady.

510.text: The final summary row per arm: quality, delta, unique, novel, and the most-repeated name with its count. Four columns and an example, which is the minimum needed to describe what a self-training loop actually did.

519.text: Generating final names for side-by-side comparison with baseline. Visually inspecting the names is often more informative than the aggregate score.

520.text: The baseline names with their scores are the reference point for judging whether the self-improvement loop actually helped.

522.text: Printing each name with its score lets you verify the scorer is sensible: do high-scoring names actually look like real names?

525.text: A fresh sample from the filtered model, so the collapse is legible as text and not only as a percentage. Twenty names is enough to see the same string several times.

527.text: The final sample list is the qualitative counterpart to the score table, showing what the evolved generator now tends to produce.

530.text: Count the distinct names in that final sample. The qualitative and quantitative views should agree, and printing both is how you find out when they do not.

533.text: The same sample from the unfiltered model, for contrast. This is the arm that was supposed to degenerate.

545.text: Pull out the control and unfiltered endpoints so the closing text can quote all three arms rather than just the one that looks best.

549.text: Which arm ended up least diverse is computed, not asserted. The answer depends on the seed, the scorer and the round count, and hard-coding the expected winner is how a lab ends up teaching the opposite of what it runs.

555.text: The share of the sample taken by a single name. This is the number that makes "the metric improved" and "the model died" obviously the same event.

556.text: Goodhart's law, printed with the run's own numbers. The verifier scores names one at a time, so a model that finds one high-scoring string and repeats it beats a model producing many plausible different names. The loop optimized what was measured; the measurement was incomplete.

595.text: The four-step summary: Generate, Score, Filter, Retrain. This is the self-improvement loop in its simplest form.

607.text: The conventional wisdom, left in and then contradicted by the numbers directly above it. Filtering does reduce the risk of amplifying errors, and here it caused mode collapse rather than preventing it, because selection pressure toward a narrow optimum is what selection is.

619.text: Do not memorize the ordering of the three arms: it moves with the seed, the scorer and the number of rounds. Memorize the habit of printing all three columns, because "quality went up" cannot by itself tell you whether the loop learned or narrowed.

624.text: The closing notes tie the toy loop back to real research. The mechanism is simplified, but the control structure is the same.

files.code:
"""
microGPT: Self-improving model edition.

A tiny character-level GPT that iteratively improves itself by generating
candidate outputs, scoring them with a verifiable quality function, and
retraining on its own best generations alongside the original data.

This implements a simplified form of filtered self-training, closest in spirit
to "STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning" (Zelikman et al., 2022,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465), which keeps only verified-correct
self-generated rationales. Karpathy's autoresearch project
(https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch) applies the same
generate-evaluate-keep loop to hyperparameter optimization. Broader related
work includes "Self-Rewarding Language Models" (Yuan et al., 2024,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.10020), which uses a learned self-judge rather
than a fixed scorer, and "SPIN" (Chen et al., 2024,
https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01335), which uses distribution-matching self-play.

This lab uses a fixed handcrafted scorer (bigram statistics) as the verifier,
which is simpler than the learned judges in Self-Rewarding LMs or the
distribution-matching in SPIN. No external LLM is needed. The verifier is
built from a held-out split of the corpus, so it scores names the model has
never trained on.

The interesting result here is a failure, and the lab is built to show it.
The loop runs three arms from identical starting weights and identical seeds:
filtered (keep the top 20%), unfiltered (keep everything), and a control that
retrains on real data only with the same step budget. Every round prints the
quality score AND two things the quality score cannot see: the fraction of
unique names and the most-repeated name with its count. Watch the quality
metric rise while diversity falls. That is Goodhart's law, on screen, in a
loop small enough to read in one sitting.
"""

import copy
import itertools
import math
import os
import random
from collections import Counter

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
char_to_id = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(uchars)}
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Held-out split: the verifier must not read the model's training data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The original version of this lab built the bigram verifier from the same
# corpus the model trained on, so a high "quality" score could simply mean the
# model had memorized the training set. Splitting the corpus fixes that: the
# model only ever sees train_docs, the verifier only ever sees heldout_docs.
# A generated name now has to look like names the verifier has seen and the
# model has not.
HELDOUT_SIZE = 3000
heldout_docs = docs[:HELDOUT_SIZE]
train_docs = docs[HELDOUT_SIZE:]
train_set = set(train_docs)  # used to measure novelty (is the name actually new?)
print(f"train docs: {len(train_docs)}, held-out docs (verifier only): {len(heldout_docs)}")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Quality scorer: the "verifier" that decides which self-generations to keep
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# We build a bigram model from real names the model never trains on (the
# held-out split). This serves as a ground-truth quality signal: generated
# names that match real-name statistics score higher. In STaR, the verifier
# checks logical correctness; here it checks "does this look like a real name?"
#
# Important limitation to keep in mind while reading the results: this verifier
# scores each name in isolation. It has no opinion about the *distribution* of
# names, so a model that emits one very high-scoring name over and over gets a
# great score. Phase 2 measures exactly that failure.


def build_bigram_scorer(names):
    """Build a log-probability scorer from bigram statistics of real names."""
    counts = {}
    for name in names:
        seq = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in name] + [BOS]
        for a, b in itertools.pairwise(seq):
            counts[(a, b)] = counts.get((a, b), 0) + 1
    # Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing: P(b|a) = (count(a,b) + 1) / (count(a) + V)
    total_per_context = {}
    for (a, _), c in counts.items():
        total_per_context[a] = total_per_context.get(a, 0) + c
    log_probs = {}
    for (a, b), c in counts.items():
        log_probs[(a, b)] = math.log((c + 1) / (total_per_context[a] + vocab_size))
    # Default for unseen bigrams: use per-context denominator when available
    default_lp_per_context = {a: math.log(1 / (t + vocab_size)) for a, t in total_per_context.items()}
    # Fallback for completely unseen contexts
    default_lp_unknown = math.log(1 / vocab_size)
    return log_probs, default_lp_per_context, default_lp_unknown


def score_name(name, log_probs, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk):
    """Score a generated name by average bigram log-probability with length penalty."""
    if len(name) < 3 or len(name) > 15:
        return -10.0  # reject too-short or too-long names
    seq = [BOS] + [char_to_id.get(ch, 0) for ch in name if ch in char_to_id] + [BOS]
    total = 0.0
    for a, b in itertools.pairwise(seq):
        total += log_probs.get((a, b), default_lp_ctx.get(a, default_lp_unk))
    # A sequence of N tokens contains N-1 bigrams, so that is what we average
    # over. Dividing by len(seq) (the token count) would quietly shrink every
    # score toward zero, more so for short names.
    avg_lp = total / (len(seq) - 1)
    # Penalize names far from the typical length (mean ~6 chars in the dataset)
    length_penalty = -0.1 * abs(len(name) - 6)
    return avg_lp + length_penalty


bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk = build_bigram_scorer(heldout_docs)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model (same architecture as lab 03)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
n_embd = 32
n_head = 4
n_layer = 1
block_size = 16
head_dim = n_embd // n_head


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, _dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, n_head, head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x)))


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention()
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.mlp = MLP()

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.mlp(self.norm2(x))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block() for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        tok_emb = self.wte(idx)
        pos_emb = self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.norm_in(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Training and generation helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
temperature = 0.5


def train_on_data(model, data, num_steps, base_lr=1e-2, verbose=True):
    """Train the model on a list of name strings."""
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=base_lr, betas=(0.85, 0.99), eps=1e-8)
    total_loss = 0
    for step in range(num_steps):
        doc = data[step % len(data)]
        tokens = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
        input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device)
        targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)
        logits = model(input_ids)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        lr_t = base_lr * (1 - step / num_steps)
        for pg in optimizer.param_groups:
            pg["lr"] = lr_t
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
        if verbose and ((step + 1) % 200 == 0 or step == 0):
            print(f"  step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")
    return total_loss / num_steps


@torch.no_grad()
def generate_names(model, n_samples=100):
    """Generate n_samples names from the model."""
    model.eval()
    names = []
    for _ in range(n_samples):
        tokens = [BOS]
        for _ in range(block_size):
            idx = torch.tensor([tokens[-block_size:]], device=device)
            logits = model(idx)
            logits = logits[0, -1] / temperature
            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
            token_id = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        name = "".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:])
        if name:
            names.append(name)
    model.train()
    return names


def evaluate_quality(names):
    """Compute average quality score for a list of names."""
    scores = [score_name(n, bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk) for n in names]
    return sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else -10.0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The metrics the quality score cannot see
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Average quality is a per-name statistic, so it is blind to two failure modes
# that matter more than the score itself:
#   diversity: a collapsed model emits the same high-scoring string forever
#   novelty:   a model can score well by parroting its training corpus
# Both are one line of Python each. Printing them next to the quality score is
# the difference between "the loop worked" and "the loop found a shortcut".


def diversity_stats(names):
    """Return (unique fraction, most-repeated name, its count)."""
    if not names:
        return 0.0, "", 0
    counts = Counter(names)
    top_name, top_count = counts.most_common(1)[0]
    return len(counts) / len(names), top_name, top_count


def novelty(names):
    """Fraction of generated names that do not appear verbatim in the training corpus."""
    if not names:
        return 0.0
    return sum(1 for n in names if n not in train_set) / len(names)


# ===========================================================================
# Phase 1: Initial training on real data
# ===========================================================================
print("=" * 60)
print("PHASE 1: Initial training on real data")
print("=" * 60)

model = MicroGPT().to(device)

NUM_ROUNDS = 6
SAMPLES_PER_ROUND = 300
KEEP_TOP_FRACTION = 0.2  # filtered arm: keep the top 20% of self-generated names
RETRAIN_STEPS = 300
MIX_RATIO = 0.15  # 15% self-generated, 85% real data in retraining


def run_arm(keep_fraction, mix_ratio, label):
    """
    Run the generate -> score -> filter -> retrain loop for NUM_ROUNDS and
    measure quality, diversity and novelty after every round.

    Three settings of the two knobs give us three arms of one experiment:
      keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.15 -> the filtered loop this lab teaches
      keep_fraction=1.0, mix_ratio=0.15 -> the naive loop (keep everything)
      keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.0  -> control: real data only, same budget
    The control matters. Without it, we cannot tell whether the self-generated
    data helped or whether 1800 extra training steps would have done the same.
    """
    # Same seeds and the same starting weights for every arm, so the arms
    # differ only in what data they retrain on.
    random.seed(4242)
    torch.manual_seed(4242)
    arm_model = MicroGPT().to(device)
    arm_model.load_state_dict(copy.deepcopy(initial_state))

    stats = []
    for round_idx in range(NUM_ROUNDS):
        # Step 1: Generate candidates
        candidates = generate_names(arm_model, SAMPLES_PER_ROUND)

        # Step 2: Score and filter, keeping the best `keep_fraction` of them
        scored = [(name, score_name(name, bigram_lp, default_lp_ctx, default_lp_unk)) for name in candidates]
        scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
        n_keep = max(1, int(len(scored) * keep_fraction))
        kept = [name for name, _ in scored[:n_keep]]
        all_quality = evaluate_quality(candidates)

        # Step 3: Mix self-generated data with real data for retraining.
        # mix_ratio sets how many retraining steps see a self-generated name
        # (45 of 300 with the defaults), and that is usually fewer than the
        # number of names we kept (60). So we sample the self-generated slots
        # uniformly from the whole kept set. Walking `kept` in score order
        # instead would silently use only the top 15% and discard the rest.
        n_self = int(RETRAIN_STEPS * mix_ratio)
        if n_self <= len(kept):
            self_slots = random.sample(kept, n_self)
        else:
            # More slots than kept names: reuse them, so a few names influence
            # many steps. This is what happens if you raise MIX_RATIO.
            self_slots = [random.choice(kept) for _ in range(n_self)]
        mixed_data = self_slots + [random.choice(train_docs) for _ in range(RETRAIN_STEPS - n_self)]
        random.shuffle(mixed_data)

        # Step 4: Retrain on mixed data
        avg_loss = train_on_data(arm_model, mixed_data, RETRAIN_STEPS, base_lr=5e-3, verbose=False)

        # Step 5: Evaluate quality, plus the two things quality cannot see
        post_names = generate_names(arm_model, EVAL_SAMPLES)
        post_quality = evaluate_quality(post_names)
        unique_frac, top_name, top_count = diversity_stats(post_names)
        novel_frac = novelty(post_names)

        stats.append(
            {
                "round": round_idx + 1,
                "candidates": len(candidates),
                "kept": n_keep,
                "slots": n_self,
                "distinct_fed": len(set(self_slots)),
                "all_quality": all_quality,
                "post_quality": post_quality,
                "unique": unique_frac,
                "top_name": top_name,
                "top_count": top_count,
                "novel": novel_frac,
                "avg_loss": avg_loss,
            }
        )

        # The "slots" figure is how many of the RETRAIN_STEPS steps see a
        # self-generated name, and "distinct" is how many different names those
        # slots contain. When the kept set itself fills up with copies of one
        # high-scoring name, "distinct" drops even though "slots" does not.
        print(
            f"  {label} round {round_idx + 1}: "
            f"kept {n_keep:3d}/{len(candidates)}, self slots {n_self:3d} ({len(set(self_slots)):2d} distinct), "
            f"quality {all_quality:.4f} -> {post_quality:.4f}, "
            f"unique {unique_frac:5.1%}, top '{top_name}' x{top_count:<3d} "
            f"novel {novel_frac:5.1%}, loss {avg_loss:.4f}"
        )

    return arm_model, stats


print(f"\nthree arms, {NUM_ROUNDS} rounds each, identical seeds and identical step budgets")
print(f"every round: generate {SAMPLES_PER_ROUND}, filter, retrain {RETRAIN_STEPS} steps, evaluate {EVAL_SAMPLES}\n")

print(f"arm 1, FILTERED: keep top {KEEP_TOP_FRACTION:.0%} of self-generations, mix {MIX_RATIO:.0%} into retraining")

print(f"""
The filtered loop moved the quality metric by {total_improvement:+.4f} and the
unique fraction by {final_unique - baseline_unique:+.1%} ({baseline_unique:.1%} -> {final_unique:.1%}).
One name, '{final_top_name}', accounts for {final_top_count} of {EVAL_SAMPLES} samples ({top_share:.1%}).

That is Goodhart's law in 400 lines: the metric can improve while the model
dies. The verifier scores names one at a time, so a model that discovers a
single high-scoring string and emits it over and over gets a better average
score than a model that produces many plausible different names. The loop
optimized what we measured, and we measured the wrong thing.

Note which arm ended up least diverse in this run: {least_diverse}. The
folklore says the UNFILTERED loop is the dangerous one, and at large mix ratios
it is. But filtering is itself a distribution-narrowing operation: taking the
top {KEEP_TOP_FRACTION:.0%} by a per-name score deliberately throws away the tails, so with
only {MIX_RATIO:.0%} of the retraining stream coming from the model, the filtered arm is the
one that concentrates. Selection pressure toward a narrow optimum is not a bug
in the filter, it is what the filter does.

The control arm (real data only, same seeds, same step budget) reached
{control_quality:.4f} vs the filtered arm's {final_quality:.4f}, so the
self-generated data is doing real work on the metric, and the problem is not that
the loop does nothing, it is that the metric it improves is incomplete.

The per-round quality trajectory is also not monotonic. Do not expect a clean
staircase: each round retrains on a fresh random sample, and the loop has no
revert-on-regression rule, so rounds can and do go backwards.

Fixes that would make this loop trustworthy, none of them implemented here:
  - score the distribution, not just each name (penalize repeats)
  - deduplicate the kept set before retraining
  - keep a diversity floor as a hard constraint, not a hope
  - revert a round when any tracked metric regresses
""")

print(f"""
{"=" * 60}
HOW SELF-IMPROVEMENT WORKS
{"=" * 60}

The self-improvement loop has four steps per round:

  1. GENERATE: Model produces {SAMPLES_PER_ROUND} candidate names
  2. SCORE:    Bigram quality function + length penalty rates each candidate
     (the verifier is built from {len(heldout_docs)} held-out names the model never trains on)
  3. FILTER:   Keep only the top {KEEP_TOP_FRACTION:.0%} (verified good outputs)
  4. RETRAIN:  Mix {MIX_RATIO:.0%} self-generated + {1 - MIX_RATIO:.0%} real data, train {RETRAIN_STEPS} steps

Keeping only VERIFIED good outputs reduces the risk of collapse. Naive
self-training (keeping all outputs) lets the model amplify its own errors.
The quality filter mitigates this, though it does not fully prevent mode
collapse, and the numbers above show it did not prevent it here either.
Diversity controls, quality thresholds, and revert-on-regression would
strengthen the loop further.

Measured in this run:
  filtered    quality {final_quality:.4f}, unique {final_unique:.1%}
  unfiltered  quality {unfiltered_quality:.4f}, unique {unfiltered_unique:.1%}
  control     quality {control_quality:.4f}, unique {control_unique:.1%}

Do not memorize the ordering of those three numbers: it depends on the seed,
the scorer, and how many rounds you run. Memorize the habit of printing all
three columns, because "quality went up" on its own cannot tell you whether
the loop learned or narrowed.

This is a simplified version of the pattern behind:
  - STaR: keep self-generated rationales only if the answer is correct
  - Karpathy's autoresearch: keep code changes only if loss improves
  - Self-Rewarding LMs use a learned judge (not a fixed scorer like here)
  - SPIN uses distribution-matching self-play (a different mechanism)
""")

2.text: The title marks this as a self-improvement lab: the base model architecture stays familiar, but the training loop starts consuming its own filtered outputs.

4.text: The core idea: the model generates outputs, scores them for quality, keeps only the best, and retrains on those. This is the generate-evaluate-retrain loop.

5.text: Verification is explicit here. The model does not automatically trust its own samples; each candidate must pass an external quality check first.

6.text: Retraining mixes accepted self-generated names back with the original corpus so the loop can improve without fully drifting off-distribution.

8.text: Filtered self-training is the central mechanism: generate candidates, verify them, then feed only the survivors back into training.

9.text: STaR (Self-Taught Reasoner) showed that keeping only verified-correct self-generations prevents the model from amplifying its own mistakes.

10.text: STaR is the closest ancestor here because its core safeguard is exactly the same one this lab uses: keep only verified-good self-generated data.

11.text: Karpathy’s autoresearch is relevant because it uses the same keep-or-discard feedback loop, just over code and hyperparameters instead of text samples.

14.text: Self-Rewarding LMs extend the idea: the model itself acts as both generator and judge, creating a self-reinforcing improvement cycle.

19.text: The verifier is handcrafted rather than learned, which keeps the self-improvement loop transparent enough to inspect line by line.

20.text: That simplification matters pedagogically: the verifier here is cheap, explicit, and stable enough to understand without adding another model.

22.text: A fixed handcrafted scorer keeps the lab self-contained, with no external LLM and no learned judge to debug, and it is built from a held-out split, so a high score cannot just mean the model memorized its own training set.

25.text: The result this lab is built around is a failure, and it is the filtered arm that fails. Read the diversity column next to the quality column throughout: the metric improves while the model dies.

37.text: Math is only needed for the verifier. The model itself is standard PyTorch; the self-improvement novelty lives in the scoring loop.

38.text: The lab still uses the shared local dataset so the verifier and the model judge the same distribution.

42.text: PyTorch handles the model and optimizer. The interesting part is how its outputs get recycled back into training.

43.text: Module definitions let this lab reuse the same small GPT skeleton as the earlier PyTorch labs.

44.text: Functional helpers like softmax and cross-entropy stay in `F`, keeping the training loop compact.

46.text: Fixing both RNGs is important because the whole point is to compare the model before and after self-improvement under repeatable sampling.

47.text: Fixed seeds ensure reproducibility so you can compare results across runs and verify the self-improvement trend is real.

52.text: Resolve the shared corpus path relative to this lab so the script can run from its own directory.

53.text: If the dataset is missing, fetch it once. That keeps the lab self-contained without bundling a large text file.

56.text: The verifier should be grounded in real data, so the downloaded corpus is the same names dataset used everywhere else in the series.

59.text: The training corpus is still the anchor dataset. Self-improvement starts from real examples rather than replacing them.

60.text: Shuffle before the split, not after. The held-out slice is taken off the front of this list, so an unshuffled corpus would hand the verifier an alphabetical prefix and the model everything else.

63.text: Build the vocabulary once from the real corpus so both training and verification speak the same token language.

64.text: Building the character vocabulary from the actual data. The sorted set ensures a deterministic mapping from characters to token IDs.

65.text: The BOS token doubles as both start and stop marker, which keeps sampling and scoring aligned on where names begin and end.

66.text: BOS (beginning/end of sequence) token is placed after all real characters. It signals where names start and end during generation.

78.text: 3000 names withheld from training, reserved for the verifier alone. The earlier version of this lab built the verifier from the same corpus the model trained on, which meant a rising "quality" score could simply mean the model had memorized the training set.

79.text: The verifier's corpus. The model never sees these names, so scoring well on them requires generalizing rather than reciting.

80.text: The model's corpus. The split is the only thing that makes the quality number mean anything: a generated name now has to look like names the verifier has seen and the model has not.

81.text: A set of the training names, so novelty can be checked in O(1) per generated name. Without this the loop could score beautifully by parroting its own training data back.

86.text: This section builds the verifier. The model will not trust its own generations blindly; every candidate has to clear this external score.

87.text: The verifier, and a deliberately simple stand-in for a judge model: bigram statistics of real names the model never trains on. In STaR the verifier checks logical correctness; here it checks the narrower question "does this look like a real name?", which is answerable exactly and cheaply.

92.text: The limitation that ends up dominating the whole experiment: this verifier scores each name in isolation. It has no opinion about the distribution of names, so a model that emits one very high-scoring string forever earns a great average score. Everything the loop does downstream is a consequence of this one blind spot.

98.text: This function is the external judge. It compresses the real-name distribution into a cheap statistical model that can score every generated sample.

99.text: Docstring: build a log-probability scorer from bigram statistics. It is called with heldout_docs, never the training split, so the character pairs it learns come from names the model has never been shown.

100.text: Counts store how often each ordered character pair appears in the real dataset. That becomes the backbone of the quality score.

101.text: Iterate over real names only. The verifier must be anchored in genuine data before any self-generated samples enter the loop.

102.text: Wrap each name with BOS on both sides so the scorer learns realistic starts and stops, not just interior letter transitions.

103.text: Walk the name as overlapping character pairs. itertools.pairwise yields (a,b), (b,c), (c,d) and so on, and these adjacent pairs are the bigrams whose counts become the verifier.

104.text: Counting all adjacent character pairs (bigrams). These counts form the basis of the quality scorer.

105.text: Laplace smoothing ensures the verifier can still assign a finite score to rare or unseen bigrams instead of collapsing to negative infinity.

106.text: Collapse pair counts down to per-context totals so each transition can be normalized into a conditional probability.

107.text: Summing counts per context character to compute conditional probabilities: P(next_char | current_char).

108.text: Aggregate counts by left context so each bigram can later be normalized into a conditional probability.

109.text: Store verifier scores in log-space because self-generated names may be long enough for raw probability products to underflow.

110.text: Convert raw counts into log-probabilities so long sequences can be scored without underflow.

111.text: This is the smoothed conditional probability `P(next | current)` for every bigram actually seen in the real corpus.

112.text: Add-1 (Laplace) smoothing prevents zero probabilities for unseen bigrams. Log-space avoids floating-point underflow when multiplying many small probabilities.

113.text: Per-context fallback probabilities let the scorer degrade gracefully when a start character is known but a specific transition was never observed.

114.text: Keep a fallback for contexts that exist but whose particular continuation never appeared in the data.

116.text: The scorer returns both explicit seen-transition log-probs and fallbacks, which is what makes it usable as a robust filter instead of a brittle lookup table.

119.text: The scoring function is the heart of the self-improvement loop -- it decides which generated names are 'good enough' to retrain on.

121.text: The one hard constraint in the scorer. Everything else here is a smooth preference, but a name outside 3 to 15 characters is rejected outright rather than scored, which is why a degenerate one-character string cannot win on a flattering per-bigram average.

122.text: A fixed floor, far below anything the bigram term produces for a plausible name, so a rejected candidate sorts to the bottom and the top-fraction filter can never select it. The same value is the fallback in evaluate_quality when a batch is empty.

123.text: Unknown characters are dropped before scoring so the verifier judges only over the vocabulary it actually knows how to score.

124.text: Accumulate bigram scores across the whole name. Better names are the ones whose local transitions keep matching the real corpus.

125.text: Walk the name as overlapping character pairs. itertools.pairwise yields (a,b), (b,c), (c,d) and so on, and these adjacent pairs are the bigrams whose counts become the verifier.

126.text: Sum of bigram log-probabilities measures how well the generated name matches the statistical patterns of real names.

130.text: A sequence of N tokens contains N-1 bigrams, so that is what we average over. Dividing by the token count instead would quietly shrink every score toward zero, and shrink short names most, a length bias hiding inside the normalizer.

131.text: Length penalty keeps the filter from rewarding degenerate very short or very long strings that happen to get decent local bigram scores.

132.text: A soft preference for the dataset's typical length (about 6 characters), which stops the filter rewarding degenerate very short or very long strings that happen to score well per bigram.

133.text: Final score = language-model plausibility plus a soft preference for the dataset’s typical length.

136.text: Build the verifier once, from the held-out split, before any training happens. Fixed for the whole run: a moving scorer would make the round-over-round quality numbers incomparable, and a scorer fitted on the model's own training data would make them meaningless.

138.text: From here on the code is a plain small GPT. The lab's novelty lies in what happens after generation.

141.text: Use a slightly wider embedding than the earlier toy models so the self-improvement loop has enough capacity to move.

142.text: Four heads keep the attention shape conventional and make the comparison to the PyTorch baseline easier.

143.text: One transformer block is enough here because the experiment is about the data loop, not model scale.

144.text: The context window stays tiny because names are short. That keeps repeated retraining rounds cheap.

145.text: Head width is derived from the chosen embedding size and head count, just like the earlier transformer labs.

148.text: RMSNorm stays identical to the earlier labs so the reader is not juggling a second architectural change.

157.text: Attention also stays standard causal self-attention. The self-improvement experiment should isolate the training-data feedback loop.

167.text: Queries are split into attention heads here, but unlike the verifier logic this is just the standard transformer machinery reused from earlier labs.

170.text: Scale attention scores by head width just as in the baseline transformer; otherwise the logits would get too sharp.

178.text: The MLP block is unchanged. Again, the point is to keep the core model familiar while the outer loop changes.

188.text: Each transformer block is residual attention plus residual MLP, same template as the earlier autoregressive labs.

197.text: Residual connections are unchanged. The model backbone stays conventional so the experiment isolates the effect of the outer self-improvement loop.

202.text: The top-level model is intentionally boring here. That makes it easier to attribute changes in output quality to the self-improvement loop itself.

205.text: Token embeddings map integer ids into vectors. These are the same embeddings later sampled through autoregressive generation.

206.text: Position embeddings keep order information explicit so the model can tell early letters from later ones.

207.text: Normalize the summed token and position embeddings before they enter the transformer stack.

213.text: All linear layers and embeddings get the same small Gaussian init so the loop starts from a stable baseline.

217.text: Forward is standard next-token prediction: embed, add position, run the transformer, project back to vocabulary logits.

218.text: The batch and sequence dimensions are unpacked for readability. This lab never hides tensor shapes from the reader.

220.text: Position ids are generated on the fly from sequence length, just like in the earlier PyTorch labs.

230.text: Everything runs on CPU. The model is small enough that the cost of this lab is the number of generate-score-retrain rounds, not the arithmetic inside any one of them.

231.text: Temperature 0.5 for every generation call in the loop. It stays fixed across arms and rounds, so any change in output diversity is the model's doing rather than the sampler's.

234.text: This helper trains the model on any list of strings -- real data, self-generated data, or a mix. The flexibility is key for the self-improvement loop.

236.text: Each retraining phase creates a fresh optimizer, so self-improvement is happening through new data exposure rather than optimizer-state carryover.

237.text: Track average loss over the mini-run so each phase can report a comparable training signal.

239.text: Cycling through the training docs with modulo ensures every sample gets used even if num_steps exceeds the dataset size.

240.text: Teacher forcing stays unchanged. The self-improvement idea lives entirely in how the training examples are chosen, not in a different objective.

241.text: Clip the example to the context window, leaving one token over for the shifted target. Names are short so this rarely bites, but it is what stops a long name indexing past the position embedding table.

242.text: Pack one short name into a batch of size 1. The lab stays simple on batching so the outer generate-filter-retrain logic remains easy to follow.

244.text: One forward pass produces next-token logits at every position at once. That is what makes teacher forcing cheap: a name of n tokens yields n training signals from a single pass.

245.text: Cross-entropy is still the learning signal. What changes across rounds is the curation of the data feeding into that same loss.

248.text: Linear decay remains in place during retraining so later self-improvement rounds make smaller, more conservative parameter updates.

249.text: Write the decayed rate into every parameter group so the optimizer picks it up on this step.

254.text: Periodic loss prints let you see whether each retraining phase is still learning from the mixed data rather than destabilizing.

255.text: Returning average loss lets us track whether the model is actually learning from the mixed data in each self-improvement round.

258.text: No gradients anywhere in generation. Candidates are treated as data, not as a differentiable path back into the model, which is exactly what separates this loop from ordinary training.

259.text: Generation is kept separate from training because the model alternates between acting as a teacher and acting as a student.

264.text: Each name starts from the BOS token, just like during training. The model then predicts characters one at a time.

265.text: Generation is capped at block size so the model proposes full candidate names but cannot wander into arbitrarily long degenerate strings.

266.text: Only the most recent context window is fed back in. The generation routine is standard autoregressive sampling.

268.text: Temperature scaling controls randomness: dividing logits by temperature < 1 sharpens the distribution, making high-probability characters more likely.

270.text: Sampling rather than argmax keeps candidate diversity high enough for filtering to matter.

274.text: Convert token IDs back to characters, skipping the initial BOS. This is the raw generated name that will be scored.

275.text: Drop empty strings. A sample whose very first token is BOS decodes to nothing, and letting those through would pad the candidate pool with names that score the rejection floor by definition.

277.text: Put the model back in training mode before returning, since the same object goes straight into train_on_data for the next round.

281.text: Aggregate quality is the loop-level metric. The lab judges improvement by whether batches of sampled names look more like the real corpus over time.

284.text: Average score across all names gives one number to compare: baseline quality vs. post-self-improvement quality.

298.text: Diversity, in three lines. Average quality is a per-name statistic and cannot see repetition at all, so the unique fraction and the most-repeated name are printed alongside it every round.

304.text: Return the unique fraction plus the single most-repeated name and its count. The count is what makes collapse legible: "46% unique" is abstract, "one name 97 times out of 200" is not.

307.text: Novelty: the other thing quality cannot see. A model can score well by reciting its training corpus verbatim, which is memorization dressed up as improvement.

311.text: One line, using the training-set membership check built earlier. Cheap enough that there is no excuse for not printing it every round.

321.text: Train one ordinary supervised model first. Self-improvement should start from a competent baseline, not random noise.

324.text: The initial fit, longer than any single retraining round below. Every arm starts from the weights this produces, so the loop is only ever asked to improve a model that already works.

325.text: Phase 1 trains on real data only. This gives the model a reasonable starting point before self-improvement begins.

335.text: A baseline sample taken before any self-improvement, so every later round has something to be compared against on all three metrics, quality, diversity and novelty, rather than only the first.

336.text: Baseline quality is the number to beat. If self-improvement works, post-loop quality should be measurably higher than this.

348.text: Phase 2 is the actual experiment: three arms from identical weights and identical seeds, differing only in what data they retrain on. The aim is to show what the quality metric hides while it rises, which takes more than showing the loop working.

351.text: Six rounds. Enough for a trend to appear, few enough that the whole three-arm experiment runs in about a minute.

352.text: 300 candidates per round: enough for a top-20% filter to have real selection pressure, cheap enough to re-run.

353.text: The filtered arm keeps the top 20% by verifier score. Read that as what it is: a distribution-narrowing operator. Top-k selection deliberately throws away the tails, and in this run it is the filtered arm that collapses while the unfiltered arm holds its diversity, the opposite of the folklore.

354.text: Retraining is intentionally short and local. The lab is modeling iterative improvement, not a full second training run.

355.text: 15% of retraining steps see a self-generated name and the rest stay real. That real-data majority is why the naive arm survives here, and at higher mix ratios the unfiltered loop does become the dangerous one. Which arm collapses is a function of this knob rather than a law.

358.text: One function, three arms. keep_fraction=0.2, mix_ratio=0.15 is the filtered loop this lab teaches; 1.0, 0.15 is the naive loop that keeps everything; 0.2, 0.0 is the control that retrains on real data only at the same step budget. The control is what makes the other two interpretable, since without it there is no way to tell whether the self-generated data helped or whether 1800 extra training steps would have done the same.

372.text: Reseed to the same value at the top of every arm, and load the same snapshot weights below. The arms have to differ in exactly one thing or the comparison is worthless.

378.text: One round: generate, score, filter, mix, retrain, measure. Six of these per arm, with quality, diversity and novelty recorded after every one so the trajectory is visible rather than just the endpoint.

379.text: Step 1, self-play: ask the current model for fresh data. From round 2 onward it is sampling from a distribution its own earlier output helped shape.

380.text: Generate the round's candidates from the arm's current weights. Nothing external is consulted; this is the model's own opinion of what a name looks like.

382.text: Step 2: score every candidate with the verifier. This explicit score table is the only thing separating filtered self-training from naive bootstrapping.

383.text: Every candidate is paired with a verifier score before any retraining happens. This explicit score table is what separates filtered self-training from naive bootstrapping.

384.text: Sort best-to-worst so the kept set is literally the top slice under the verifier.

385.text: The keep fraction turns a scored list into a hard selection boundary. max(1, ...) guarantees at least one survivor even if the fraction rounds down to zero.

386.text: The kept set: the top slice under the verifier. In the unfiltered arm keep_fraction is 1.0 and this is simply the whole candidate list, which is the entire difference between arms 1 and 2.

387.text: Score the full candidate pool, not just the kept slice. This is the honest read on what the model currently generates; measuring only the kept names would report the filter's selectivity as if it were the model's quality.

389.text: Step 3: build the retraining stream. The subtlety is that the number of self-generated slots (45 of 300 with the defaults) is usually fewer than the number of names kept (60), so which of the kept names actually get used is a real choice, not a formality.

395.text: How many of the retraining steps see a self-generated name. Everything about how self-referential the loop becomes is set by this one number.

396.text: The normal case: fewer slots than kept names.

397.text: random.sample draws the slots uniformly and without replacement from the whole kept set. Walking kept in score order instead would silently use only the top 15% of candidates and discard the rest, a second invisible filter stacked on top of the intended one.

401.text: The other branch, reached only by raising MIX_RATIO: more slots than kept names, so a few names get repeated across many steps. Watch the "distinct" count in the per-round printout to see how much amplification is actually happening.

402.text: The remaining steps sample uniformly from the real corpus. That anchor is what keeps the model from drifting off the real distribution entirely, and it is also why the control arm exists: real data alone, same budget.

403.text: Shuffle the mixed stream so real and self-generated examples are interleaved; otherwise the model would see a blocky curriculum each round.

406.text: Step 4: retrain, deliberately shorter and at a lower learning rate than the initial fit. Each round is meant to nudge the model, not to overwrite it.

409.text: Step 5: resample after retraining. This is the only measurement that closes the loop, since everything before it describes the data rather than the model.

410.text: The quality score, which is the number that goes up.

411.text: The unique fraction and the most-repeated name, which is the number that goes down. Printing these two lines next to each other is the whole lesson of the lab.

412.text: And novelty, which catches the other failure: scoring well by reproducing training names verbatim.

414.text: Persist every round's numbers so the loop can be read as a trajectory rather than a before-and-after pair. A non-monotonic trajectory is itself information here.

420.text: How many distinct names ended up in the self-generated slots. When the kept set itself fills with copies of one high-scoring string this collapses even though the slot count does not, which is collapse caught one step upstream of the output.

421.text: Store the pre-retraining candidate quality alongside the post-retraining score, so each round shows both ends of itself and a round that went backwards is visible as such.

435.text: The per-round line carries all of it at once: how selective the filter was, how much variety survived into the retraining stream, quality before and after, unique fraction, the most-repeated name with its count, and novelty. Any one of those columns alone tells a misleading story.

449.text: Arm 1, the filtered loop, the one this lab is nominally teaching and the one that turns out to collapse.

452.text: Arm 2, the naive loop that keeps every generation. Folklore says this is the dangerous one; at this mix ratio it is the arm that keeps its diversity.

455.text: Arm 3, the control: real data only, same seeds, same step budget. Without it, "quality improved" cannot be distinguished from "we trained for another 1800 steps".

462.text: The filtered arm's audit trail, printed in full before the three arms are compared. The per-round table is where the divergence between quality and diversity is easiest to see.

465.text: Kept count, candidate quality, post-retraining quality, delta against baseline, unique fraction, most-repeated name, novelty. Seven columns because six of them are needed to stop the seventh from lying.

473.text: One row per round. Read left to right: the quality columns improve while the unique column falls and one name's count climbs.

483.text: The last round's score as the headline, since the question is where the loop ended up, not how good its best round looked.

487.text: Final quality and final unique fraction on the same line, deliberately. Reporting the first without the second is exactly the mistake the lab is about.

488.text: Total improvement next to the change in unique fraction. Both signs matter: the metric went up and the diversity went down, in the same run, from the same cause.
