496.text: Quality per round for all three arms side by side. The filtered arm leads this table, which is precisely why it needs the next one.

503.text: The same table for the unique fraction, and the one that inverts the conclusion: the filtered arm's diversity falls round after round while the unfiltered and control arms hold roughly steady.

510.text: The final summary row per arm: quality, delta, unique, novel, and the most-repeated name with its count. Four columns and an example, which is the minimum needed to describe what a self-training loop actually did.

519.text: Generating final names for side-by-side comparison with baseline. Visually inspecting the names is often more informative than the aggregate score.

520.text: The baseline names with their scores are the reference point for judging whether the self-improvement loop actually helped.

522.text: Printing each name with its score lets you verify the scorer is sensible: do high-scoring names actually look like real names?

525.text: A fresh sample from the filtered model, so the collapse is legible as text and not only as a percentage. Twenty names is enough to see the same string several times.

527.text: The final sample list is the qualitative counterpart to the score table, showing what the evolved generator now tends to produce.

530.text: Count the distinct names in that final sample. The qualitative and quantitative views should agree, and printing both is how you find out when they do not.

533.text: The same sample from the unfiltered model, for contrast. This is the arm that was supposed to degenerate.

545.text: Pull out the control and unfiltered endpoints so the closing text can quote all three arms rather than just the one that looks best.

549.text: Which arm ended up least diverse is computed, not asserted. The answer depends on the seed, the scorer and the round count, and hard-coding the expected winner is how a lab ends up teaching the opposite of what it runs.

555.text: The share of the sample taken by a single name. This is the number that makes "the metric improved" and "the model died" obviously the same event.

556.text: Goodhart's law, printed with the run's own numbers. The verifier scores names one at a time, so a model that finds one high-scoring string and repeats it beats a model producing many plausible different names. The loop optimized what was measured; the measurement was incomplete.

595.text: The four-step summary: Generate, Score, Filter, Retrain. This is the self-improvement loop in its simplest form.

607.text: The conventional wisdom, left in and then contradicted by the numbers directly above it. Filtering does reduce the risk of amplifying errors, and here it caused mode collapse rather than preventing it, because selection pressure toward a narrow optimum is what selection is.

619.text: Do not memorize the ordering of the three arms: it moves with the seed, the scorer and the number of rounds. Memorize the habit of printing all three columns, because "quality went up" cannot by itself tell you whether the loop learned or narrowed.

624.text: The closing notes tie the toy loop back to real research. The mechanism is simplified, but the control structure is the same.

units.title: Evolutionary Self-Improvement
units.tagline: A population of model variants competes, mutates, and evolves.
units.description:
Instead of improving one model's outputs (Lab 23), this lab improves the model itself through population-based evolution. A population of tiny GPT variants, each with different hyperparameters, compete for survival across generations.

Each generation: train all models briefly, evaluate fitness (validation loss), keep the best, replace the rest with mutated copies of the winners. Children can inherit trained weights from parents (the 'exploit' step) while exploring new hyperparameter settings (the 'explore' step).

This is a simplified evolutionary hyperparameter search in the spirit of Population Based Training, the same pattern behind Karpathy's autoresearch and DeepMind's FunSearch, though not a full PBT implementation, which would copy weights in place, keep optimizer state across generations, and perturb continuous schedules. The lab is careful about the headline: the evolutionary run spends thousands of training steps against the single baseline's 500, so beating it is mostly budget. It therefore also compares the two configurations at matched per-model budget and adds a random-search arm with the same total budget as evolution. It archives the best model globally, because the final population is often worse than its peak generation, and it prints distinct architectures per generation, because top-k truncation on a population of 8 collapses the gene pool fast and a population with one architecture left is not searching any more.
learning_objectives: Implement population-based training with selection and mutation
Analyze the exploit-explore tradeoff in evolutionary optimization
Compare evolved configurations against random baselines at matched compute, not matched run count

exercises.prompt: Double the population size from 8 to 16. Does evolution find better configurations, and how does the compute cost scale?
exercises.hint: Larger populations explore more configurations per generation but cost more compute. Track both the best fitness and total training time.

exercises.prompt: Add weight inheritance even when the architecture changes, by copying overlapping parameters. Does this speed up evolution?
exercises.hint: When n_embd changes, copy the intersection of the weight matrices. The inherited knowledge may give the child a head start on training.

units.code:
"""
microGPT: Evolutionary self-improvement edition.

Instead of improving a single model's outputs (Lab 23), this lab improves the
model itself through population-based evolution. A population of tiny GPT
variants -- each with different hyperparameters -- compete for survival.
The fittest are selected, mutated, and the cycle repeats across generations.

This implements Population Based Training (PBT) as described in "Population
Based Training of Neural Networks" (Jaderberg et al., 2017,
https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09846). PBT combines random hyperparameter search
with online selection: instead of training one model to completion, train many
in parallel, periodically replacing the worst with mutated copies of the best.

Related approaches include "FunSearch: Making new discoveries in mathematical
sciences using large language models" (Romera-Paredes et al., 2023,
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06924-6), which uses an evolutionary
loop over LLM-generated programs, and Karpathy's autoresearch
(https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch), which runs a sequential version
of the same pattern: mutate config, train, evaluate, keep or discard.

This lab uses no external LLM. Mutations are random perturbations of
hyperparameters (learning rate, embedding dimension, number of heads). The
fitness function is validation loss on held-out names. Evolution discovers
good configurations that a single random guess would likely miss.

Note: this is a simplified evolutionary hyperparameter search inspired by
PBT, not a full PBT implementation. Canonical PBT copies weights into
underperformers in-place, preserves optimizer state across generations, and
perturbs continuous schedules. Here we use a discrete search space, fresh
optimizers per generation, and deepcopy survivors.

Three things this lab measures that toy evolution demos usually skip, because
each one deflates the headline number:
  - Global elitism. The best model of the run is archived when it is found.
    The best member of the FINAL population is often worse, because the
    population regresses after its peak generation.
  - The compute ledger. The evolutionary run spends thousands of training
    steps; the single random baseline spends 500. Beating it is mostly budget.
    So we also compare the two configurations at matched per-model budget,
    and add a random-search arm with the same total budget as evolution.
  - Diversity. Distinct architectures per generation is printed, because
    top-k truncation on a population of 8 collapses the gene pool quickly,
    and a population with one architecture left is not searching any more.
"""

import copy
import math
import os
import random

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

random.seed(42)
torch.manual_seed(42)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dataset & Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
input_path = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "..", "data", "input.txt")
if not os.path.exists(input_path):
    import urllib.request

    url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/karpathy/makemore/refs/heads/master/names.txt"
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, input_path)

docs = [l.strip() for l in open(input_path).read().strip().split("\n") if l.strip()]
random.shuffle(docs)
print(f"num docs: {len(docs)}")

uchars = sorted(set("".join(docs)))
char_to_id = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(uchars)}
BOS = len(uchars)
vocab_size = len(uchars) + 1
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size}")

# Split into train/val
val_size = 1000
val_docs = docs[:val_size]
train_docs = docs[val_size:]

# Fitness is evaluated on a fixed prefix of the validation split, not all of it.
# 200 names is enough to rank models while keeping the search affordable: this
# lab evaluates ~150 models, so every extra sample costs 150 forward passes.
VAL_SAMPLES = 200
print(f"train: {len(train_docs)}, val: {len(val_docs)} (fitness uses the first {VAL_SAMPLES})")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Flexible model (hyperparameters are configurable)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
device = "cpu"
block_size = 16


class RMSNorm(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, eps=1e-5):
        super().__init__()
        self.eps = eps

    def forward(self, x):
        return x * torch.rsqrt(x.pow(2).mean(-1, keepdim=True) + self.eps)


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_embd, n_head):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_head = n_head
        self.head_dim = n_embd // n_head
        self.wq = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wv = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)
        self.wo = nn.Linear(n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q = self.wq(x).view(B, T, self.n_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        k = self.wk(x).view(B, T, self.n_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        v = self.wv(x).view(B, T, self.n_head, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        out = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.wo(out)


class Block(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_embd, n_head):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(n_embd, n_head)
        self.norm2 = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_embd, 4 * n_embd, bias=False)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(4 * n_embd, n_embd, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x))
        x = x + self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(self.norm2(x))))
        return x


class MicroGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_embd, n_head, n_layer):
        super().__init__()
        self.wte = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd)
        self.wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)
        self.norm_in = RMSNorm(n_embd)
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([Block(n_embd, n_head) for _ in range(n_layer)])
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(n_embd, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    @staticmethod
    def _init_weights(module):
        if isinstance(module, (nn.Linear, nn.Embedding)):
            nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.08)

    def forward(self, idx):
        B, T = idx.shape
        x = self.norm_in(self.wte(idx) + self.wpe(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)))
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        return self.lm_head(x)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Evolution primitives
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Hyperparameter search space
HP_SPACE = {
    "n_embd": [16, 24, 32, 48, 64],
    "n_head": [1, 2, 4],
    "n_layer": [1, 2],
    "lr": [5e-3, 8e-3, 1e-2, 1.5e-2, 2e-2],
    "beta1": [0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95],
}


def random_config():
    """Sample a random hyperparameter configuration."""
    cfg = {k: random.choice(v) for k, v in HP_SPACE.items()}
    # Ensure n_embd is divisible by n_head
    while cfg["n_embd"] % cfg["n_head"] != 0:
        cfg["n_head"] = random.choice(HP_SPACE["n_head"])
    return cfg


def mutate_config(cfg):
    """Mutate one or two hyperparameters of a configuration."""
    new_cfg = dict(cfg)
    n_mutations = random.choice([1, 1, 2])  # usually 1, sometimes 2
    keys_to_mutate = random.sample(list(HP_SPACE.keys()), min(n_mutations, len(HP_SPACE)))
    for key in keys_to_mutate:
        new_cfg[key] = random.choice(HP_SPACE[key])
    # Ensure n_embd divisible by n_head
    while new_cfg["n_embd"] % new_cfg["n_head"] != 0:
        new_cfg["n_head"] = random.choice(HP_SPACE["n_head"])
    return new_cfg


def build_model(cfg):
    """Build a model from a configuration."""
    return MicroGPT(cfg["n_embd"], cfg["n_head"], cfg["n_layer"])


def train_model(model, cfg, train_data, num_steps, verbose=False, start_step=0):
    """Train a model for a fixed number of steps, return avg loss.

    `start_step` is where in `train_data` this call picks up. A model that has
    already seen 400 names must continue at name 400, not restart at name 0 --
    otherwise every generation re-reads the same first STEPS_PER_GEN names and
    "more steps" buys memorisation of a tiny slice rather than more data.
    """
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=cfg["lr"], betas=(cfg["beta1"], 0.99), eps=1e-8)
    total_loss = 0
    for step in range(num_steps):
        doc = train_data[(start_step + step) % len(train_data)]
        tokens = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
        input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]], device=device)
        targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]], device=device)
        logits = model(input_ids)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        total_loss += loss.item()
        if verbose and ((step + 1) % 100 == 0 or step == 0):
            print(f"  step {step + 1:4d} / {num_steps} | loss {loss.item():.4f}")
    return total_loss / num_steps


@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate_model(model, val_data, max_samples=VAL_SAMPLES):
    """Evaluate validation loss (fitness = negative val loss)."""
    model.eval()
    total_loss = 0
    n_samples = min(max_samples, len(val_data))
    for i in range(n_samples):
        doc = val_data[i]
        tokens = [BOS] + [char_to_id[ch] for ch in doc] + [BOS]
        n = min(block_size, len(tokens) - 1)
        input_ids = torch.tensor([tokens[:n]])
        targets = torch.tensor([tokens[1 : n + 1]])
        logits = model(input_ids)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, vocab_size), targets.view(-1))
        total_loss += loss.item()
    model.train()
    return total_loss / n_samples


@torch.no_grad()
def generate_names(model, n_samples=10, temperature=0.5):
    """Generate sample names from a model."""
    model.eval()
    names = []
    for _ in range(n_samples):
        tokens = [BOS]
        for _ in range(block_size):
            idx = torch.tensor([tokens[-block_size:]])
            logits = model(idx)[0, -1] / temperature
            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
            token_id = torch.multinomial(probs, 1).item()
            if token_id == BOS:
                break
            tokens.append(token_id)
        names.append("".join(uchars[t] for t in tokens[1:]))
    model.train()
    return names


# ===========================================================================
# Phase 1: Random baseline, train one random configuration
# ===========================================================================
print(f"\n{'=' * 70}")
print("PHASE 1: Random baseline (single random configuration)")
print("=" * 70)

BASELINE_STEPS = 500

baseline_cfg = random_config()
print(f"config: {baseline_cfg}")
baseline_model = build_model(baseline_cfg)
n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in baseline_model.parameters())
print(f"params: {n_params}")

# 500 steps is a small budget, and that matters for every comparison below.
# The evolutionary run further down spends thousands of steps across its whole
# population, so "evolved beats this baseline" would mostly be a statement
# about compute. The results section therefore also compares the two configs
# at matched per-model budget, and adds a random-search arm with the same total
# budget as evolution.
train_model(baseline_model, baseline_cfg, train_docs, BASELINE_STEPS, verbose=True)
baseline_val_loss = evaluate_model(baseline_model, val_docs)
print(f"val loss: {baseline_val_loss:.4f}")
print(f"samples: {', '.join(generate_names(baseline_model, 5))}")

# ===========================================================================
# Phase 2: Population-Based Evolution
# ===========================================================================
print(f"\n{'=' * 70}")
print("PHASE 2: Population-Based Training (evolutionary self-improvement)")
print("=" * 70)

POP_SIZE = 8
NUM_GENERATIONS = 6
STEPS_PER_GEN = 200
TOP_K = 3  # keep top-k, replace the rest

# Initialize population with random configurations
population = []
for i in range(POP_SIZE):
    cfg = random_config()
    model = build_model(cfg)
    # "steps" is the cumulative training this member's weights have received.
    # It is not the same for every member: survivors keep their weights and
    # keep accumulating, while a child whose architecture changed starts from
    # scratch at 0. Without this counter, within-generation fitness silently
    # confounds configuration quality with lineage age.
    population.append({"id": i, "cfg": cfg, "model": model, "val_loss": float("inf"), "steps": 0})

print(f"population size: {POP_SIZE}")
print(f"generations: {NUM_GENERATIONS}")
print(f"steps/generation: {STEPS_PER_GEN}")
print(f"selection: top-{TOP_K} survive, rest are replaced by mutated copies\n")

generation_stats = []
evolution_steps = 0  # total training steps spent by the whole population

# Global elitism: an archive of the single best model ever evaluated. Without
# it the "evolved best" is just whatever happens to be in the final
# population, which is not the same thing as the best the search found,
# in this lab the population regularly peaks in a middle generation and then
# regresses.
best_ever = {"val_loss": float("inf"), "cfg": None, "model": None, "gen": 0, "steps": 0}

for gen in range(NUM_GENERATIONS):
    # Train each member for STEPS_PER_GEN
    for member in population:
        # start_step: this member resumes at the name after the last one it saw.
        train_model(member["model"], member["cfg"], train_docs, STEPS_PER_GEN, start_step=member["steps"])
        member["steps"] += STEPS_PER_GEN
        evolution_steps += STEPS_PER_GEN
        member["val_loss"] = evaluate_model(member["model"], val_docs)

    # Sort by fitness (lower val loss = better)
    population.sort(key=lambda m: m["val_loss"])

    best = population[0]
    worst = population[-1]
    avg_loss = sum(m["val_loss"] for m in population) / len(population)

    # How much variety is actually left in the population? Two counts: distinct
    # architectures (what changes the parameter count) and distinct full
    # configs (architecture plus lr and beta1).
    n_archs = len({(m["cfg"]["n_embd"], m["cfg"]["n_head"], m["cfg"]["n_layer"]) for m in population})
    n_cfgs = len({tuple(sorted(m["cfg"].items())) for m in population})

    if best["val_loss"] < best_ever["val_loss"]:
        best_ever = {
            "val_loss": best["val_loss"],
            "cfg": dict(best["cfg"]),
            "model": copy.deepcopy(best["model"]),
            "gen": gen + 1,
            "steps": best["steps"],
        }

    gen_stat = {
        "gen": gen + 1,
        "best_loss": best["val_loss"],
        "worst_loss": worst["val_loss"],
        "avg_loss": avg_loss,
        "best_cfg": dict(best["cfg"]),
        "best_params": sum(p.numel() for p in best["model"].parameters()),
        "best_steps": best["steps"],
        "n_archs": n_archs,
        "n_cfgs": n_cfgs,
    }
    generation_stats.append(gen_stat)

    print(
        f"gen {gen + 1:2d}: "
        f"best {best['val_loss']:.4f} (id={best['id']}, {best['steps']} steps), "
        f"worst {worst['val_loss']:.4f}, "
        f"avg {avg_loss:.4f}, "
        f"distinct archs {n_archs}/{POP_SIZE}, configs {n_cfgs}/{POP_SIZE}, "
        f"best cfg: embd={best['cfg']['n_embd']}, heads={best['cfg']['n_head']}, "
        f"layers={best['cfg']['n_layer']}, lr={best['cfg']['lr']:.4f}"
    )
    # Cumulative steps next to val loss, so you can see the confound directly.
    for rank, m in enumerate(population):
        c = m["cfg"]
        print(
            f"       rank {rank + 1}: val {m['val_loss']:.4f}  steps {m['steps']:5d}  "
            f"embd={c['n_embd']:2d}, heads={c['n_head']}, layers={c['n_layer']}, "
            f"lr={c['lr']:.4f}, beta1={c['beta1']}"
        )

    # Evolution: replace bottom members with mutated copies of top members
    survivors = population[:TOP_K]
    new_population = copy.deepcopy(survivors)  # keep survivors as-is (with their trained weights)

    for i in range(POP_SIZE - TOP_K):
        # Pick a random survivor as parent
        parent = random.choice(survivors)
        child_cfg = mutate_config(parent["cfg"])

        # If architecture changed, need a new model (can't inherit weights)
        arch_changed = (
            child_cfg["n_embd"] != parent["cfg"]["n_embd"]
            or child_cfg["n_head"] != parent["cfg"]["n_head"]
            or child_cfg["n_layer"] != parent["cfg"]["n_layer"]
        )

        child_model = build_model(child_cfg)
        if not arch_changed:
            # Same architecture: inherit parent's weights (the PBT "exploit"
            # step), and inherit the parent's accumulated step count with them.
            child_model.load_state_dict(parent["model"].state_dict())

        new_population.append(
            {
                "id": POP_SIZE * (gen + 1) + i,
                "cfg": child_cfg,
                "model": child_model,
                "val_loss": float("inf"),
                # A child with a new architecture is untrained: 0 steps. A child
                # that inherited weights starts where its parent left off.
                "steps": 0 if arch_changed else parent["steps"],
            }
        )

    population = new_population

# ===========================================================================
# Results
# ===========================================================================
print(f"\n{'=' * 70}")
print("EVOLUTION RESULTS")
print("=" * 70)

# Final evaluation: train and evaluate all members of the last population
# (children spawned in the last generation haven't been trained yet)
for member in population:
    if member["val_loss"] == float("inf"):
        train_model(member["model"], member["cfg"], train_docs, STEPS_PER_GEN, start_step=member["steps"])
        member["steps"] += STEPS_PER_GEN
        evolution_steps += STEPS_PER_GEN
        member["val_loss"] = evaluate_model(member["model"], val_docs)
        if member["val_loss"] < best_ever["val_loss"]:
            best_ever = {
                "val_loss": member["val_loss"],
                "cfg": dict(member["cfg"]),
                "model": copy.deepcopy(member["model"]),
                "gen": NUM_GENERATIONS,  # spawned in the last generation, trained here
                "steps": member["steps"],
            }

population.sort(key=lambda m: m["val_loss"])
final_best = population[0]  # best in the final population
best_evolved = best_ever  # best ever seen, which is what we report
evolved_val_loss = best_evolved["val_loss"]

print(
    f"\n{'Gen':>4s}  {'Best Loss':>9s}  {'Avg Loss':>8s}  {'Worst Loss':>10s}  "
    f"{'Steps':>6s}  {'Archs':>5s}  {'Cfgs':>4s}  {'Best Config'}"
)
print("-" * 100)
for s in generation_stats:
    c = s["best_cfg"]
    print(
        f"{s['gen']:>4d}  {s['best_loss']:>9.4f}  {s['avg_loss']:>8.4f}  {s['worst_loss']:>10.4f}  "
        f"{s['best_steps']:>6d}  {s['n_archs']:>5d}  {s['n_cfgs']:>4d}  "
        f"embd={c['n_embd']}, heads={c['n_head']}, layers={c['n_layer']}, lr={c['lr']:.4f}"
    )
print("(Steps = cumulative training steps of that generation's best member.")
print(" Archs/Cfgs = distinct architectures and distinct full configs in the population.)")

# The best of the final population is not the best of the run. Say so with numbers.
print(f"\nbest in final population: {final_best['val_loss']:.4f} ({final_best['steps']} steps)")
print(
    f"best ever seen:           {best_ever['val_loss']:.4f} (generation {best_ever['gen']}, {best_ever['steps']} steps)"
)
gen_best_curve = ", ".join(f"{s['best_loss']:.4f}" for s in generation_stats)
print(f"per-generation best:      {gen_best_curve}")
if best_ever["gen"] < NUM_GENERATIONS:
    print(
        f"  -> the search peaked at generation {best_ever['gen']} and then regressed. "
        "Global elitism is why we can still report the peak."
    )

# ===========================================================================
# Was any of this fair? The compute ledger
# ===========================================================================
print(f"\n{'=' * 70}")
print("COMPUTE LEDGER: the headline number is mostly budget")
print("=" * 70)

# Arm A: the same 500-step baseline, but let its config keep training so we can
# compare configurations at matched per-model budget instead of comparing
# 500 steps against a whole population's worth of training.
MATCHED_STEPS = 1200
CHECK_EVERY = 200


def budget_curve(cfg, total_steps=MATCHED_STEPS, check_every=CHECK_EVERY, seed=7):
    """
    Train one config from scratch and record val loss every `check_every` steps.

    Each chunk builds a fresh optimizer, exactly as a generation of evolution
    does, so this curve is the like-for-like comparison rather than a single
    long run with persistent Adam state.
    """
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = build_model(cfg)
    curve = []
    for chunk in range(total_steps // check_every):
        train_model(m, cfg, train_docs, check_every, start_step=chunk * check_every)
        curve.append(evaluate_model(m, val_docs))
    return curve


print(f"\nSame two configs, trained from scratch, val loss every {CHECK_EVERY} steps:")
base_curve = budget_curve(baseline_cfg)
eval_curve = budget_curve(best_evolved["cfg"])
header = "  ".join(f"{(i + 1) * CHECK_EVERY:>7d}" for i in range(MATCHED_STEPS // CHECK_EVERY))
print(f"\n{'config':>16s}  {header}")
print("-" * (18 + 9 * (MATCHED_STEPS // CHECK_EVERY)))
print(f"{'baseline':>16s}  " + "  ".join(f"{v:>7.4f}" for v in base_curve))
print(f"{'evolved':>16s}  " + "  ".join(f"{v:>7.4f}" for v in eval_curve))
matched_delta = min(base_curve) - min(eval_curve)
print(f"\nbest-of-curve: baseline {min(base_curve):.4f}, evolved {min(eval_curve):.4f}, delta {matched_delta:+.4f}")
print("That delta is the configuration advantage at matched per-model budget.")

# Arm B: random search at (almost) the same total training budget as evolution.
# This is the control that tells you whether selection and mutation earned
# anything, or whether spending the same compute on independent random configs
# would have done as well. POP_SIZE x NUM_GENERATIONS configs at STEPS_PER_GEN
# steps each is slightly less compute than the evolutionary run (which also
# trains the children spawned in the last generation), so the comparison is
# conservative in evolution's favour.
# This is the most expensive block in the lab. It is also the only reason the
# headline number below can be trusted.
rs_configs = POP_SIZE * NUM_GENERATIONS
print(
    f"\nRandom search control: {rs_configs} random configs x {STEPS_PER_GEN} steps = {rs_configs * STEPS_PER_GEN} steps"
)
rs_best = {"val_loss": float("inf"), "cfg": None, "model": None}
for i in range(rs_configs):
    cfg = random_config()
    m = build_model(cfg)
    train_model(m, cfg, train_docs, STEPS_PER_GEN)
    vl = evaluate_model(m, val_docs)
    if vl < rs_best["val_loss"]:
        rs_best = {"val_loss": vl, "cfg": cfg, "model": m}
    if (i + 1) % 10 == 0:
        print(f"  {i + 1:3d}/{rs_configs} configs sampled, best so far {rs_best['val_loss']:.4f}")
print(f"random search best: {rs_best['val_loss']:.4f} (config: {rs_best['cfg']})")

print("\n--- training steps spent ---")
print(f"  single random baseline:      {BASELINE_STEPS:>7,d}")
print(f"  evolution (whole run):       {evolution_steps:>7,d}  ({evolution_steps / BASELINE_STEPS:.0f}x the baseline)")
print(f"  random search (matched):     {rs_configs * STEPS_PER_GEN:>7,d}")
print(f"  matched-budget head-to-head: {MATCHED_STEPS:>7,d}  per config")

print("\n--- comparison ---")
print(f"random baseline ({BASELINE_STEPS} steps):  val_loss={baseline_val_loss:.4f} (config: {baseline_cfg})")
print(f"evolved best (best ever):     val_loss={evolved_val_loss:.4f} (config: {best_evolved['cfg']})")
print(f"random search (equal budget): val_loss={rs_best['val_loss']:.4f}")
improvement = baseline_val_loss - evolved_val_loss
print(
    f"\nevolved vs {BASELINE_STEPS}-step baseline:   {improvement:+.4f}  <- NOT a fair comparison, {evolution_steps / BASELINE_STEPS:.0f}x the compute"
)
print(
    f"evolved vs equal-budget search: {rs_best['val_loss'] - evolved_val_loss:+.4f}  <- what evolution bought over random search"
)
print(f"config advantage, matched budget: {matched_delta:+.4f}  <- the honest per-config number")

# Generate from both
print("\n--- random baseline samples ---")
for i, name in enumerate(generate_names(baseline_model, 10)):
    print(f"  {i + 1:2d}: {name}")

print("\n--- evolved best samples ---")
for i, name in enumerate(generate_names(best_evolved["model"], 10)):
    print(f"  {i + 1:2d}: {name}")

# Show the evolutionary tree
print("\n--- population diversity (final generation) ---")
for i, member in enumerate(population):
    c = member["cfg"]
    n_p = sum(p.numel() for p in member["model"].parameters())
    print(
        f"  rank {i + 1}: val_loss={member['val_loss']:.4f}, steps={member['steps']:5d}, "
        f"params={n_p:,}, "
        f"embd={c['n_embd']}, heads={c['n_head']}, layers={c['n_layer']}, "
        f"lr={c['lr']:.4f}, beta1={c['beta1']}"
    )

final_archs = len({(m["cfg"]["n_embd"], m["cfg"]["n_head"], m["cfg"]["n_layer"]) for m in population})
final_cfgs = len({tuple(sorted(m["cfg"].items())) for m in population})
final_sizes = {sum(p.numel() for p in m["model"].parameters()) for m in population}
final_shapes = len({(m["cfg"]["n_embd"], m["cfg"]["n_layer"]) for m in population})
arch_curve = ", ".join(str(s["n_archs"]) for s in generation_stats)
avg_curve = ", ".join(f"{s['avg_loss']:.4f}" for s in generation_stats)
print(f"\ndistinct architectures per generation: {arch_curve} (final population: {final_archs}/{POP_SIZE})")
print(f"distinct full configs in final population: {final_cfgs}/{POP_SIZE}")
print(f"distinct model sizes in final population: {len(final_sizes)}/{POP_SIZE} ({sorted(final_sizes)} params)")
print(f"population average val loss per generation: {avg_curve}")
if len(final_sizes) == 1 or final_shapes == 1:
    print(
        "\n  -> Read those lines again: every surviving member is the same size.\n"
        "     Whatever variety is left is in lr, beta1 and the head count, none of\n"
        "     which changes the parameter count. There is effectively no\n"
        "     architectural diversity left to select from. Top-k truncation with a\n"
        "     low mutation rate collapses a gene pool this small very fast.\n"
        "     A real search needs a diversity floor: forbid duplicate genomes, keep\n"
        "     a fraction of random immigrants, or raise the mutation rate when\n"
        "     variance drops. None of that is implemented here, and measuring it first\n"
        "     is the point."
    )
if generation_stats[-1]["avg_loss"] > generation_stats[0]["avg_loss"]:
    print(
        f"\n  -> The population AVERAGE got worse over the run "
        f"({generation_stats[0]['avg_loss']:.4f} -> {generation_stats[-1]['avg_loss']:.4f}).\n"
        "     Children with fresh architectures are untrained, so a population that\n"
        "     keeps mutating keeps paying a restart cost. 'Evolution improved the\n"
        "     population' is not a claim this run supports."
    )

# ===========================================================================
# Explanation
# ===========================================================================
print(f"""
{"=" * 70}
HOW EVOLUTIONARY SELF-IMPROVEMENT WORKS
{"=" * 70}

Population Based Training (PBT) evolves model configurations:

  1. INITIALIZE: Create {POP_SIZE} models with random hyperparameters
  2. TRAIN:      Each model trains for {STEPS_PER_GEN} steps
  3. EVALUATE:   Measure validation loss (fitness)
  4. SELECT:     Keep the top {TOP_K} models (survivors)
  5. MUTATE:     Create {POP_SIZE - TOP_K} children by mutating survivors' configs
  6. INHERIT:    If architecture unchanged, children inherit parent weights
  7. REPEAT:     Go to step 2 for {NUM_GENERATIONS} generations

Key differences from Lab 23 (self-improving model):
  - Lab 23 improves the MODEL'S OUTPUTS (better training data)
  - Lab 24 improves the MODEL ITSELF (better architecture/hyperparameters)
  - Lab 23 uses one model; Lab 24 uses a competing population
  - Lab 23 is like STaR; Lab 24 is like natural selection

The "exploit + explore" balance:
  - EXPLOIT: children inherit trained weights from successful parents
  - EXPLORE: hyperparameter mutations introduce diversity

This is the same pattern behind:
  - PBT (Jaderberg et al.): evolve learning rates and augmentation during training
  - Karpathy's autoresearch: sequential mutate-train-evaluate-keep loop
  - FunSearch: evolve programs scored by a fitness function
  - Neural Architecture Search: evolve network topologies

THREE THINGS THIS RUN MEASURED, WHICH ARE EASY TO GET WRONG:

  1. The headline is mostly compute. Evolution spent {evolution_steps:,} training
     steps against the baseline's 500. At matched per-config budget the
     configuration advantage was {matched_delta:+.4f}, not {improvement:+.4f}.

  2. Fitness within a generation is not a clean config comparison. Survivors
     keep their weights and keep accumulating steps; children with a new
     architecture restart at zero. The "steps" column shows the confound.
     Each generation gives every member the same NUMBER of new steps, which
     is not the same as giving them the same total training.

  3. Diversity dies quietly. Distinct architectures per generation:
     {arch_curve}. Once that hits 1, selection has nothing left to select.

The reported winner comes from a best-ever archive, not from the final
population, because the two are frequently not the same model.

At production scale, PBT discovers training schedules that would take
human researchers weeks of manual tuning. It also runs with populations large
enough, and mutation rates high enough, that the gene pool survives, which is
exactly the part a toy run at this size cannot show you for free.
""")

2.text: The title shifts the focus from single-model refinement to population-level search over many candidate models.

4.text: Lab 23 improved outputs; this lab improves the configuration itself. The object being optimized changes from data to model population.

5.text: The key insight: instead of improving one model's outputs, we improve the model population itself through evolutionary pressure.

6.text: Each variant has different hyperparameters -- this diversity is what gives evolution something to select from.

7.text: Selection and mutation repeat over generations, so improvement comes from many small inherited changes rather than one optimizer run.

9.text: PBT is the core algorithm here: train many models in parallel, periodically replacing the worst with mutated copies of the best.

10.text: PBT is the direct template: train a population briefly, rank by fitness, then let strong members seed the next generation.

11.text: PBT combines hyperparameter search with ongoing training, so good settings can prove themselves under learning dynamics rather than static scoring.

12.text: Online selection is what distinguishes PBT from a static hyperparameter sweep: weak configs are replaced while training is still underway.

13.text: The population is not just ranked once. Replacement happens generation after generation, so search and learning are intertwined.

15.text: These related systems matter because they show the same outer-loop idea can optimize many kinds of candidates, not only neural net hyperparameters.

17.text: FunSearch is included as a conceptual cousin: both systems use an evolutionary outer loop to search over candidates scored by an objective.

18.text: Autoresearch provides the same narrative in sequential form: propose a change, measure it, and keep only the improvements.

22.text: No LLM needed for mutations -- simple random perturbations of numeric hyperparameters are enough for effective search.

23.text: The search space is intentionally small and interpretable, so each evolved improvement can be traced back to a concrete hyperparameter choice.

24.text: Validation loss is our fitness function -- evolution will minimize it by discovering good hyperparameter combinations.

25.text: That is the motivation for population search: a good region of configuration space can be found by repeated selection even when a single draw would likely miss it.

27.text: The docstring is explicit about scope: this lab teaches the exploit-explore control loop, not every engineering detail of production PBT.

28.text: Canonical PBT would overwrite weak population members in place; this lab keeps the same idea but expresses it with simpler rebuild-or-inherit logic.

29.text: Optimizer-state carryover is omitted here for simplicity, which makes inheritance easier to explain but slightly less faithful to industrial PBT.

30.text: Discrete choices keep the search space small and legible. You can point to every possible architectural value the loop is allowed to explore.

31.text: Fresh optimizers per generation keep the implementation small, even though production PBT would usually preserve optimizer momentum too.

33.text: Three measurements that toy evolution demos usually skip, each one because it deflates the headline number. They are the reason this lab's reported improvement is much smaller than the first number it prints.

35.text: Global elitism. Without an archive, "the evolved model" is whatever happens to be sitting in the final population, which is regularly worse than the best the search actually found, because the population peaks and then regresses.

38.text: The compute ledger. The evolutionary run spends thousands of training steps against the baseline's 500, so beating it is mostly budget. Hence a matched-per-config comparison and an equal-total-budget random-search arm.

42.text: Diversity. Top-k truncation on a population of 8 collapses the gene pool within a few generations, and a population with one architecture left has stopped searching. So the distinct-architecture count is printed every generation.

47.text: Copying whole model states is part of the exploit step: strong survivors can seed the next generation.

48.text: Math is only needed for the usual transformer computations and reporting of loss values.

50.text: Fixed seeds ensure reproducibility -- every run produces the same evolutionary trajectory for fair comparison.

52.text: PyTorch provides the model and optimizer, while the evolutionary logic stays plain Python around it.

53.text: Modules still matter because architecture itself is part of the search space in this lab.

54.text: Functional helpers like cross-entropy keep the training loop compact so the evolutionary wrapper stays readable.

56.text: Fix seeds so the population trajectory is reproducible enough to compare baseline and evolved runs meaningfully.

62.text: Resolve the shared names corpus so every candidate model is judged on the same data distribution.

63.text: Fetch the dataset only if necessary. The experiment should be runnable from a clean checkout.

66.text: All population members train on the same underlying corpus. The only thing that changes is model configuration.

67.text: Auto-downloading keeps the experiment runnable from a fresh checkout, which matters because population methods already add enough moving parts on their own.

69.text: Every individual in the population ultimately trains on this same underlying corpus, which is what makes fitness comparisons meaningful.

70.text: Shuffle once before splitting so the held-out set is not a biased prefix of the alphabetically ordered names file.

71.text: Corpus size is printed up front so you can reason about how much data each generation is sampling from.

73.text: The vocabulary stays fixed across the whole population so models compete on architecture and optimization, not tokenization differences.

74.text: Character-to-ID mapping stays deterministic so every population member trains and validates on exactly the same tokenization.

75.text: One token id past the last character, serving as both start and end marker. It is fixed before the search begins, so no genome can change what the models are being asked to predict.

76.text: Vocabulary size is fixed before the search begins; evolution is not allowed to cheat by changing the token set.

77.text: Printing vocab size confirms that the evolutionary search is not changing the task itself, only the model and optimizer configuration.

79.text: A held-out split is essential because evolution needs a fitness signal that rewards generalization rather than memorized training loss.

80.text: Hold out 1,000 names so the fitness signal measures unseen-data performance.

81.text: Validation documents are kept separate from the search process so the population competes on unseen data.

82.text: Everything after the validation slice is the training pool, shared by every member of every generation. Data is therefore never a confound between candidates; only configuration and accumulated compute are.

87.text: Fitness is measured on the first 200 validation names, not all 1000. That is a deliberate cost/precision trade: this lab evaluates roughly 150 models, so each extra validation name costs ~150 forward passes. 200 names is enough to rank candidates, which is all selection needs.

88.text: Printing the split sizes — and how much of the validation split the fitness signal actually uses — makes the search budget explicit: one pool for training, one pool for selection, and a stated sample size for the number that decides who survives.

93.text: Everything runs on CPU to keep the example local and deterministic. The evolutionary idea does not depend on accelerators.

94.text: The context window is fixed for the whole population so sequence length does not become another hidden variable.

97.text: RMSNorm stays unchanged from the earlier labs. Evolution is changing macro configuration, not swapping in new layer types.

98.text: RMSNorm remains parameter-free and unchanged; the search is over macro configuration, not normalization variants.

99.text: The normalization layer itself has no learned weights here, so widening the model changes surrounding matrices more than it changes normalization.

106.text: Attention now takes `n_embd` and `n_head` as parameters because those are evolvable traits in the search space.

107.text: Attention receives dynamic width and head-count arguments because those two architectural choices are part of the evolvable genome.

108.text: The attention module is rebuilt to match each sampled genome, which is why architectural mutation naturally changes parameter count too.

109.text: Store head count on the module because both tensor reshaping and legality checks depend on it.

111.text: Query projection width grows and shrinks with embedding size, so larger genomes pay for more expressive attention with more parameters.

116.text: The attention forward pass stays standard even though the model size changes. Evolution is selecting among architectures, not inventing new operators.

117.text: Unpack batch, time, and channel dimensions so the tensor geometry stays visible while the model size changes.

118.text: Queries are always projected at full head count. Evolution changes head count by rebuilding the module, not by changing the attention rule.

119.text: Keys follow the same head geometry as queries because this lab changes capacity through width and depth, not by introducing KV-sharing tricks.

120.text: Values mirror keys so attention remains standard scaled dot-product attention regardless of which genome is active.

121.text: Scaled dot-product attention is still standard. Evolution is not discovering a new attention rule here.

122.text: The causal mask is unchanged across the population. Evolution compares model sizes and learning rates, not different generation rules.

129.text: Blocks become parameterized because architecture depth and width are now part of the genome, not compile-time constants.

132.text: Each block carries the sampled width and head count through both attention and MLP, so a genome affects the full transformer stack.

135.text: The MLP expansion still uses the usual 4x multiplier. Capacity changes through `n_embd` and `n_layer`, not an extra search dimension.

136.text: The second linear layer contracts the 4x hidden expansion back to model width, making parameter count very sensitive to the sampled embedding dimension.

138.text: The block's forward pass is fixed: pre-norm attention added back to the residual stream, then a pre-norm MLP added back the same way. Evolution changes a block's width and head count, and how many blocks there are, never what a block does.

144.text: The top-level model constructor exposes the exact architectural knobs that evolution is allowed to search over.

145.text: MicroGPT accepts n_embd, n_head, and n_layer as constructor arguments, making the architecture evolvable.

146.text: The full model is assembled from the genome here: embeddings, transformer depth, and output head all depend on the sampled configuration.

147.text: Embedding tables scale with `n_embd`, so wider models immediately cost more parameters.

150.text: Depth comes straight from the genome: one or two blocks, each built at the sampled width. Along with n_embd and n_head this is one of the three knobs that changes tensor shapes, so mutating it forces the child to start from random weights.

157.text: Small init std (0.08) keeps initial outputs low-entropy -- important so all population members start trainable.

160.text: Sequence length is still inferred at runtime, so genomes change capacity without changing the caller interface.

161.text: Position embeddings still use the same fixed context length. This keeps comparisons between candidates fair.

171.text: This discrete table is the search landscape. Evolution can only step among these predefined choices.

172.text: The search space is deliberately discrete and small so the reader can reason about every possible mutation.

173.text: Embedding size is the main capacity knob. Larger values increase both model expressiveness and parameter count.

174.text: Number of attention heads: 1, 2, or 4. Must evenly divide n_embd, which the code enforces.

175.text: Depth is part of the genome too, which lets the search compare shallow and slightly deeper tiny GPTs under the same budget.

176.text: Learning rate varies by 4x across the space -- this is often the most impactful hyperparameter to tune.

177.text: Beta1 controls momentum in Adam -- lower values make the optimizer more responsive to recent gradients.

181.text: Random initialization samples a fresh genome for a new individual in the population.

182.text: A fresh genome is just a dict sampled from the search space; evolution later decides which of these simple objects deserve to survive.

183.text: A configuration is one genome in the population: architecture depth/width and optimizer settings all become evolvable traits.

184.text: This repair step prevents illegal genomes from surviving sampling or mutation, which keeps the search focused on runnable candidates.

185.text: This legality check prevents the search from proposing invalid head layouts where embedding width cannot be split evenly across heads.

186.text: Constraint repair: if n_embd isn't divisible by n_head, resample n_head until the constraint is satisfied.

190.text: Mutation starts from an existing survivor genome rather than from scratch, which is why the search can improve cumulatively.

192.text: Mutation starts by copying the parent genome so only the selected fields change and the rest of the inherited design stays intact.

193.text: Most children mutate only one trait, which keeps the search local enough for successful parents to pass on useful structure.

194.text: Sampling mutation keys without replacement means one generation cannot accidentally mutate the same hyperparameter twice in opposite directions.

195.text: Mutation is plain resampling from the discrete search space. There is no gradient for these choices, only selection pressure.

198.text: After mutation, the same divisibility guard runs again so children stay architecturally valid.

199.text: Repair after mutation matters most when width changed, because that can invalidate the current head-count choice.

203.text: build_model() is a factory: given a config dict, it returns a fresh MicroGPT with those hyperparameters.

204.text: Model construction is factored out because evolution repeatedly instantiates architectures from sampled genomes.

205.text: Genome-to-model translation is a separate step so survivors can be copied, mutated, and rebuilt cleanly.

208.text: Training is intentionally short and fixed-length. Evolution needs many comparable partial runs, not one full convergence run. start_step is what makes those runs consecutive rather than repeated.

209.text: A fixed number of steps per call, so every member gets the same amount of new training each generation. That is not the same as equal total training, and the step counter tracked in the population is what exposes the difference.

211.text: The subtle part of population-based training. Without an offset, every generation would restart at name 0, so a member with 1200 steps would have read the same 200 names six times over. "More compute" would then buy memorisation of a tiny slice, and the matched-budget curves further down would measure overfitting rather than learning.

216.text: Adam's hyperparameters come straight from the genome, so evolution tunes the optimization dynamics alongside the architecture.

217.text: Average training loss is tracked per member mainly for observability; survival itself is still based on validation loss.

219.text: Each member walks the corpus in the same order, but resumes at its own offset, so a longer-lived member has seen strictly more data rather than the same data more often. Data is still not a confound between members at equal step count; compute and lineage age are.

220.text: Like the self-improving lab, names are still encoded as BOS-delimited character sequences before training.

222.text: Inputs stay on CPU here so population search can run in a minimal environment without distributed orchestration.

223.text: Targets are the inputs shifted by one, so every position predicts the next character. The objective is identical for every member of the population, so the search ranges over configuration rather than over what the models are trying to do.

225.text: Training loss drives weight updates inside a generation, but it is not the survival criterion. That distinction matters.

232.text: Returning average loss lets us monitor training quality, though fitness is measured separately on validation data.

235.text: @torch.no_grad() disables gradient tracking during evaluation -- we only need forward passes for fitness.

236.text: Validation loss is the fitness signal. Lower is better, so evolution selects candidates that generalize best — as judged on the fixed 200-name sample declared above.

237.text: Validation loss is the fitness function. Lower loss means a genome earns the right to survive and reproduce.

240.text: Cap evaluation samples to keep selection cheap. The goal is a stable ranking signal, not a perfect benchmark.

242.text: Walk the validation set in order rather than sampling from it, so every member is scored on exactly the same names in the same sequence. Fitness comparisons across a population are worthless if the evaluation set moves between members.

245.text: Evaluation reuses the same autoregressive objective, but on held-out names so the search favors generalizing configurations.

251.text: Average validation loss is the fitness score. The evolution loop will sort the population by this value.

254.text: Sampling from a model after evolution sits outside fitness, but it helps verify that lower validation loss corresponds to plausible-looking names.

255.text: Autoregressive generation: predict one token at a time, append it, and feed the growing sequence back in.

260.text: Each sample starts from BOS, keeping generation behavior aligned with how the models were trained.

262.text: Generation is only for qualitative inspection. Fitness is decided numerically by validation loss, not by cherry-picked samples.

263.text: Scale logits by temperature before sampling so sample diversity can be inspected without changing the learned model.

265.text: Multinomial sampling exposes the actual learned distribution of the winner instead of forcing greedy outputs.

266.text: BOS token acts as both start and end marker -- generating BOS means the name is complete.

277.text: Phase 1 is a single randomly configured model trained once. It is the number the evolutionary run will be compared against, and the compute ledger further down is what stops that comparison from being a fiction.

281.text: 500 steps is a small budget, and that matters for every comparison in this file. The evolutionary run below spends roughly twenty times as much across its population, so "evolved beats this baseline" is mostly a statement about compute. The results section therefore also compares the two configurations at matched per-model budget and adds an equal-budget random-search arm.

283.text: One random draw from the search space, as the thing to beat. A single sample is a weak reference point on purpose, since the honest comparisons are the matched-budget curve and the random-search arm rather than this one.

285.text: Instantiate the baseline from the sampled config so later improvement can be measured against a single-run search.

286.text: Counting parameters shows model capacity -- evolution might discover that smaller or larger models work better.

295.text: Train the baseline once. Everything downstream that quotes an improvement against this run has to also quote the step counts, which is why the ledger section exists.

296.text: The baseline's fitness, measured the same way the population's will be: validation loss on held-out names.

297.text: The baseline validation score becomes the denominator for the final improvement claim: evolution should beat this single random trial.

298.text: Five samples from the baseline, so the loss numbers further down have something legible beside them rather than standing on their own.

307.text: Population size controls how much diversity the search can maintain at once.

308.text: Six generations. Long enough for the gene pool to collapse, which is one of the things the run is measuring.

309.text: Each generation only gets 200 training steps. That is enough to rank candidates without making the demo too slow.

310.text: Top-3 of 8 survive; the other five are replaced by mutated copies. This truncation ratio is aggressive for a population this small, and the diversity diagnostics at the end are the bill for it.

312.text: This is the initial population: multiple independently sampled genomes enter the search before any selection has happened.

313.text: The population container holds each individual’s identity, genome, model weights, and most recent fitness.

314.text: Population initialization: create POP_SIZE individuals, each with a random config and fresh model.

317.text: steps is the cumulative training this member's weights have received, and it is deliberately not the same for every member. Survivors keep their weights and keep accumulating; a child whose architecture changed restarts at zero. Without this counter, within-generation fitness silently confounds configuration quality with lineage age.

322.text: New members start at infinite validation loss, so an unevaluated member can never be mistaken for a fit one by the sort below, and at zero steps.

329.text: Generation stats accumulate a compressed history of the search so the final report can show trend, not just the winner.

330.text: Total training steps spent by the whole population. This counter is the entire reason the headline improvement can be put in context rather than quoted bare.

332.text: Global elitism: an archive of the single best model ever evaluated, kept outside the population. Before this existed the lab reported whatever survived to the last generation, which meant it could report a worse model than it had already found and discarded.

337.text: The archive itself: loss, config, a deep copy of the weights, and which generation produced it. The generation number is what lets the closing text say whether the search peaked early and regressed.

339.text: Each generation repeats the same cycle: train, evaluate, sort, keep the best, and repopulate.

340.text: Within a generation, every member gets trained before any survivor decision is made. Selection is based on a synchronized snapshot of the population.

343.text: Every member gets the same number of new steps this generation, resuming at the name where it left off. It does not follow that they are equally trained: a survivor arrives here with several generations of weights behind it and a fresh-architecture child arrives with none. The competition is therefore partly about lineage age, not only configuration quality — which is what the steps column is printed to show.

344.text: Accumulate into this member's lifetime step count, so the confound stays visible instead of being reset each generation.

345.text: And into the run total, which the compute ledger divides by the baseline's 500.

346.text: Fitness is updated immediately after training so ranking reflects the current generation, not stale scores from earlier rounds.

348.text: Sorting by validation loss makes the best candidate land at index 0 and the worst at the end.

349.text: Sorting by validation loss creates the selection pressure. Once ordered, survivors and replacees are obvious.

351.text: Once sorted, `best` is both the current champion and the most likely parent source for the next generation.

352.text: The worst member as well as the best. Printing the tail matters: a population whose best improves while its average and worst degrade is not improving.

353.text: Average population loss matters because evolution can improve the frontier while still collapsing diversity, and this metric helps reveal that.

355.text: How much variety is actually left, counted two ways: distinct architectures (what changes the parameter count) and distinct full configs (architecture plus learning rate and beta1). The second stays higher than the first long after the search has stopped exploring anything structural.

358.text: Distinct architectures in the population. Once this reaches 1 the search has nothing structural left to select between, whatever the config count says.

359.text: Distinct full configs, including the optimizer knobs. Useful as a contrast: lr and beta1 keep mutating happily while the architecture space has already collapsed.

361.text: Update the archive whenever this generation's best beats everything seen so far. Three lines, and they are the difference between reporting the search's peak and reporting its last gasp.

370.text: Record generation-level telemetry so the search can be inspected as a trend in best, average, and worst population quality.

377.text: The best member's cumulative step count, stored per generation so the results table can put it next to that generation's best loss. A loss that improves alongside a rising step count has not told you much about the configuration.

378.text: Diversity goes into the per-generation record too, so the collapse can be printed as a curve rather than as a single final number.

384.text: The per-generation printout exposes the whole exploit-explore story in one line: who won, how bad the tail is, and what genome led the field.

385.text: The generation's champion, with its cumulative steps alongside its loss. Survivors keep their trained weights across generations, which is the PBT "exploit", and that is exactly why the step count has to be printed next to the fitness.

388.text: Distinct architectures and configs, printed every generation rather than only at the end. Diversity dies quietly, and a single end-of-run number cannot tell you when it happened.

392.text: The whole population, ranked, with cumulative steps next to each validation loss. This is where the lineage-age confound is visible directly: read down the steps column and check whether the ranking tracks configuration or training time.

396.text: Loss, cumulative steps and the full genome, one row per member. The steps column is the reason this table exists: by the last generation a member on 1200 steps is ranked against a fresh child on 200, and that gap is training time, not a better configuration.

401.text: The evolutionary step starts here. Survivors stay; everyone else is replaced by mutated descendants.

402.text: The top-K slice is the survivor pool. These members are the only ones allowed to pass structure into the next generation.

403.text: Deep-copy the survivors so their trained weights persist into the next generation instead of being overwritten in place.

405.text: Exactly `POP_SIZE - TOP_K` children are created so population size stays constant across generations.

406.text: Parents are chosen from survivors only, which means every child descends from a genome that already proved itself on validation loss.

407.text: Random parent selection from survivors: each child descends from one of the top-K. This spreads good genes.

408.text: Each child starts from a successful parent genome, then explores nearby configurations by mutation.

411.text: Only the three architecture knobs decide whether weights can be inherited. A mutation that touches lr or beta1 alone leaves the tensor shapes intact, so the child keeps its parent's learning for free.

417.text: If shape changed, exploration wins completely and the child starts from fresh random weights.

418.text: The clean split between exploit and explore: inherit weights when the shape allows it, start from scratch when it does not. A child that restarts pays a real cost, and it shows up as a rising population average later in the run.

419.text: Same architecture, so the child loads the parent's parameters, and inherits the parent's accumulated step count with them on the next line. Copying one without the other is how the confound gets hidden.

421.text: When shape is unchanged, the child inherits learned weights. This is the exploit step that makes PBT more efficient than restarting every trial.

423.text: Each child re-enters the population with a new identity and an unknown fitness, even if it inherited strong weights.

425.text: Each child gets a unique ID for tracking lineage across generations.

429.text: A child with a new architecture is genuinely untrained, so its step count starts at zero; a child that inherited weights starts where its parent left off. Keeping these two cases honest is what makes the steps column mean anything.

444.text: This final pass avoids a subtle reporting bug: the last batch of spawned children has been created but not yet trained unless you evaluate them here.

446.text: The children spawned in the last generation have never been trained, so evaluating the final population without this pass would compare trained survivors against random initializations.

452.text: And those late children get a shot at the archive too. A model discovered on the very last pass should still be reportable as the run's best.

461.text: Sort the final population so it can be listed and so final_best is well defined. Note what this sort does not decide: the reported winner comes from the archive, not from index 0 here.

462.text: The best of the final population, kept only so it can be printed against the archive. The gap between these two lines is the whole argument for elitism.

463.text: best_evolved is the fittest individual discovered across the entire run, and that claim is now true because it reads the elitist archive rather than the surviving population. Before the archive existed this line took population[0], which meant the lab could report a model measurably worse than one it had already found and thrown away.

466.text: The generation table: best, average and worst loss, cumulative steps of the best member, and the two diversity counts. Six columns because the best-loss column on its own is the one that flatters the method.

471.text: The summary table gives a generation-by-generation view of search progress, which is the clearest way to see whether evolution is genuinely converging.

478.text: Spell out what the steps column means in the output itself, since a cumulative count next to a loss is easy to misread as a per-generation budget.

482.text: Best in the final population, with its step count.

484.text: And the best ever seen, with the generation that produced it. When these two lines differ, which they usually do, the second is the honest answer to "what did the search find?"

486.text: The full per-generation best curve, so a non-monotonic search is visible as a shape rather than hidden behind a minimum.

488.text: If the peak was not the last generation, say so explicitly. "The search peaked and then regressed" is a normal outcome for top-k truncation on a small population, and elitism is the only reason the peak is still reportable.

497.text: The compute ledger. The first improvement number this lab could print is mostly a statement about training budget, and this section is what turns it into an honest one.

504.text: 1200 steps per config, matched. Comparing the baseline's 500 steps against a whole population's worth of training is not a configuration comparison, so run both configs at the same budget instead.

505.text: Check the validation loss every 200 steps rather than only at the end, because a single endpoint cannot distinguish a better configuration from a luckier stopping point.

508.text: Train one config from scratch and record a curve. Deliberately from scratch: reusing the evolved model's weights would smuggle its extra training back into the comparison.

512.text: Each chunk builds a fresh optimizer, exactly as a generation of evolution does. Without that, this curve would be a single long run with persistent Adam state and would not be like-for-like.

520.text: Each 200-step chunk resumes where the previous one stopped, so 1,200 steps means 1,200 distinct names. Without the offset every chunk would re-read the same first 200, and the curve would measure how fast a model memorises a tiny slice rather than how it improves with budget.

526.text: The baseline config's curve at matched budget.

527.text: And the evolved config's, same budget, same seed, same chunking. Any gap here is attributable to the configuration and nothing else.

533.text: Best point on each curve, not the last point. Neither curve descends cleanly — each chunk trains on one name at a time and rebuilds Adam from scratch, so single-example gradient noise moves the validation loss around by more than the trend does — and taking endpoints would turn that noise into a result.

535.text: This delta is the honest per-config number, and it is a fraction of the headline improvement. Everything above it in the ledger is budget.

537.text: The control that decides whether selection and mutation earned anything at all: spend the same total compute on independent random configs and see how close they get.

546.text: POP_SIZE x NUM_GENERATIONS configs at STEPS_PER_GEN steps each is slightly less compute than the evolutionary run, which also trains the children spawned in the last generation. The comparison is therefore conservative in evolution's favour.

550.text: Track only the best random config found. Random search gets the same elitism the evolutionary arm does, or the comparison would be rigged.

556.text: Keep the incumbent whenever a sample beats it. This is what makes random search a real baseline rather than a straw man: it is evolution with the selection and mutation removed and nothing else changed.

560.text: The equal-budget random-search result. How close this lands to the evolved best is the measure of what selection and mutation actually bought.

562.text: The step counts, printed side by side. Once these four numbers are visible, the improvement figures below can be read for what they are.

564.text: Evolution's whole-run cost, and its ratio to the baseline. This is the multiplier that the headline comparison quietly spends.

568.text: The headline question: did evolutionary search beat a single random configuration trained once?

569.text: The unfair comparison first, labelled as such rather than omitted.

570.text: The evolved best, taken from the archive, which is why this line can quote a model that no longer exists in the population.

574.text: The number a less careful version of this lab would have stopped at, printed with the compute multiplier attached so it cannot be quoted alone.

577.text: What evolution bought over random search at the same total budget. Much smaller, and this is the number that actually says something about selection and mutation.

579.text: And the configuration advantage at matched per-model budget: the honest per-config figure. Three numbers for one question, and the largest of them is the one with 21x the compute behind it.

581.text: Side-by-side samples keep the numerical improvement grounded in generated outputs, not just in lower validation loss.

586.text: Sample from the evolved winner so the improvement is visible in the output, not just in the loss number.

591.text: The final population, listed in full. Whether several genome families survived or selection collapsed everything onto one configuration is not something a best-loss number can tell you.

593.text: Pull this member's genome out so the row below can print every knob next to the loss, not just the winner's.

596.text: Loss, cumulative steps, parameter count and genome per surviving member. The parameter column is the one to watch: identical counts across the whole population mean the architecture search is over, whatever the config column shows.

602.text: Distinct architectures left at the end, counted on the three shape knobs.

604.text: Distinct model sizes, the strictest of the three diversity counts. Parameter count depends only on n_embd and n_layer, so n_head, lr and beta1 can all keep mutating without moving it, which is why the run can end with two distinct architectures and still only one distinct size.

606.text: The architecture count as a curve across generations. Collapse is a trajectory, and this line is the diagnostic the lab exists to print.

608.text: Print the curve and the final count together, so an end state of one or two architectures can be traced back to the generation where the pool narrowed.

611.text: Population average per generation, alongside the diversity curve. A rising average with a falling architecture count is a search that has stopped exploring and started churning.

612.text: If every survivor is the same size, say so in plain language. Top-k truncation with a low mutation rate collapses a gene pool this small very fast, and a real search needs a diversity floor: forbid duplicate genomes, keep random immigrants, or raise the mutation rate when variance drops. None of that is implemented here, and measuring it first is the point.

624.text: And if the population average got worse over the run, print that too. Children with fresh architectures restart untrained, so a population that keeps mutating keeps paying a restart cost, and "evolution improved the population" stops being a claim this run supports.

641.text: The numbered recap restates the algorithm as a control loop: initialize, train, evaluate, select, mutate, inherit, repeat.

652.text: Lab 23 improves training data (output quality); Lab 24 improves the model architecture and optimizer settings.

655.text: Lab 23 is like self-play refinement (STaR); Lab 24 is like natural selection -- fundamentally different strategies.

657.text: Exploit means reusing what already works; explore means mutating it enough to discover a better region of the search space.

658.text: Exploit: children inherit trained weights from successful parents, getting a head start on learning.

659.text: Explore: random hyperparameter mutations keep the population from settling into a local optimum.

662.text: PBT was originally designed to evolve learning rate schedules and data augmentation during training.

664.text: FunSearch uses the same pattern but evolves LLM-generated programs instead of numeric hyperparameters.

669.text: The compute point, restated with the run's own numbers: the matched-budget configuration advantage against the raw improvement figure. The gap between the two is what a compute ledger is for.

673.text: The lineage-age point. Equal new steps per generation is not equal total training, and the steps column is where that shows.

679.text: The diversity point, with the per-generation architecture curve inline. Once it reaches 1, selection has nothing left to select.

682.text: And the reason the reported winner comes from the archive rather than the final population: the two are frequently not the same model.

685.text: The closing claim is deliberately modest. Production PBT does discover schedules that would cost a researcher weeks, with populations large enough and mutation rates high enough that the gene pool survives, which is exactly the part a run at this size cannot show for free.
